articles.title: TRADES' UNIONS AND POLITICS.
articles.text:
TRADES' UNIONS AND
POLITICS.

TRADES' SOCIETIES POLITICAL
UNION.

Wimm are Trades' Unions? What are their
principles and objects? How can they be
made most available to advance their principles
and objects? The reply to the two first queries
are easily made. A trades' union is an associa-
;Lion of men in any particular trade; its prin-
ciples and objects being, the defence of the
customs and privileges of the trade, the main-
tenance, or attainment, of a remunerative
scale of wages, the regulation of the
hours of labcur, and the general advancement
of the interests of its members. The third
question is one more difficult of solution.
It must be painfully evident to all
reflecting unionists that, under the pre-
sent system, a trades' union rarely
succeeds in advancing the interests of its
members by increased wages, or reduction of
the hours of labour, and that it is only by
dint of great perseverance and self-sacrifice
that it is enabled to maintain its defensive
position. Why is this? Simply because, as
a body, the members of a trades' union,
deprived of the suffrage, have no political
power or influence; while their employers,
being in possession of the suffrage, have both.
Trade' unionists, having no vote' have no
power to influence members of Parliament in
favour of their claims; these members natu-
rally inclining to serve the interests of those
who have the power to send them to Parlia-
ment, or unseat them if they feel so disposed.
Trades' unions, therefore, to be made available
for carrying their principles and objects to a
successful issue, must obtain for their members
the protected suffrage, which, having obtained,
members of the House of Commons will
be found not only willing to listen to their
complaints, but ready to bring their grievances
before Parliament, and to defend their
actions. Another question then arises.
How are the members of trades' unions to
obtain the suffrage? The most direct and
effectual way would be by making use of that
organisation which they now too often fritter
away in fruitless attempts •to improve their
condition by social efforts alone. But I am
here met with the stereotyped objection—
" That if we interfere in politics our union will
be destroyed." Better that it should be des-
troyed than continue to exist as a sham, as a
"mockery, a delusion,and a snare." But I deny
that by a trades' union making use of its organi-
sation, simply to obtain the suffrage for its mem.
bers, it would be in any danger of destruction;
on the contrary, like a child released from its
swaddling clothes, it would increase in strength
and power. I have no desire to see trades'
unions turned into debating societies for the
discussion of the many political questions
of the day, upon which great diversity of
opinion must necessarily exist; this I admit
would be fatal to their existence. But they
are not asked to do this; they are only asked
to take up the question of the suffrage, about
which, amongst working men, there cannot be
any difference of opinion. Every working
man—every trade unionist—will admit that he
has a natural right to have a voice in the
elections of those men who tax him, and make
the laws he is bound to obey; and by claiming
for their members the right of voting, the union
would only be carrying out the principle it
daily practices, in allowing all its members who
pay towards its support an equal voice in the
management of its affairs. If only a few
intelligent and determined men in each union
would bring this subject fairly- before the
members, at a proper time, I feel convinced that
in the great majority of cases they woald carry
the union with them, in spite of the timidity
of some men, and the antiquated prejudice of
others. The ball once set in motion, it would
roll on, gathering force as it went, until its
progress became irresistible. That this course
will ultimately be pursued, I have little doubt,
and the silly cry of "Trades' unions have
nothing to do with politics" will become one
of the past. This, however, will be a work of,
time, and will only be acted upon in many
unions when they find that their existence is
endangered, not by their interference in politics.
but by the interference of political power with
them. This period may probably come sooner
than expected.
In the meantime, by the formation of the
Trades Societies'Political Union, the member-
ship of which is to be confined to trades'
unionists, and whose excellent address appeared
in the BEE-HIVE of November 22, an oppor-
tunity is afforded to all trades' unionists to
exert themselves for the attainment of the
franchise, without running counter to the
feelings or prejudices of those of their fellow
unionists who act on the cry of" No politics."
The programme of this association was adopted,
at a meeting of the members held on Tuesday
evening last, and its objects are confined solely
to the attainment of manhood suffrage pro-
tected by the ballot. The rules provide
for those cases where a trade society may be
prevented. joining, as a society, by ignorance,
timiditY, or Prejudice b Rule 5 says—" That
societies, and members of societies, be invite d
to form branches of this association, and
send representatives for the purpose of form-
ing a political council to work out its objects,"
&c. Thus, for example, if a society, by the '
necessary majority of its members, should
decide upon joining the association, it would
become a branch, and entitled to send a
'delegate to represent them on the council.
Again, where a society declines to join, but a
number of its members are favourable to the
principle, they can, independently of
their society, hold a meeting, form them—
selves into a branch, and be represented
by. a delegate at the council. There is
thus no excuse for any one professing to hold
the principles of the association holding back
from its ranks. The promoters of the associa-
tion are men generally well known in the ranks
°l* union as "good men and true," veterans
in the eau' se, aided by recruits of fair promise,
who have
entered on their task as a labour of
love as well as duty, and not likely to be deter-
red bY danger or difficulty. If the association
is well
.Worked,
bt it
ea of which there can be little
doU.) nnot fail of speedily becoming ,a most
effective instrument in obtaining the suffrage,
not alone for trades f th
mass of the unenfran
unionists but or e great
chised., Rally romid it,
then, trades unionists! and prove by the sup-
Port you render it, that you fully appreciate
the efforts made in Your behalf. Keep aloof
from it, or give it only a lukewarm support,
•and
You will well de-
serve"tou. will still be kept, as
be kept, in a state of political serfdom,
struggling
on, and struggling vainly, through
your trades societies *alone, to obtain your proper
social position. Such, at least, after many
years experience as a member of a trades union,
is the opinion of
December 4th 1862.

articles.title: • A WEEKLY NEWSPAPER OF GENERAL INTELLIGENCE, AND TRADES', FRIENDLY SOCIETY, AND CO-OPERATIVE JOURNAL.
DISTRESS IN LANCASIIIRE.
articles.text:
DISTRESS IN LANCASIIIRE.

LONDON WORKING MEN'S CENTRAL
COMMITTEE.

The general meeting of the trades delegates from
the above committee, was held on Wednesday evening
at the BEEHIVE office (the room being granted gratu-
itously). The president, Mr. KilUnpack, of the Lou-
don Pressmen's Society, in the chair.
Mr. Jarvis, from the North London Carpenters, and
Mr. Cremer' from the Amalgamated Carpenters'
Society, took their seats as delegates.
Mr. Applegarth who had consented to act as secretary
of the committee at its formation, being compelled to
resign the appointment owing to pressure of business,
Mr. Hornsby, of the Friends of Freedom Society of
Carpenters, was elected to the office. A letter was
read from the secretary of the Pickwick Histrionic Club
offering their services to give an entertainment on
behalf of the fund, and the secretary was instructed to
acknowledge its receipt.
Mr. Ryan introduced a deputation from the Over.
lookers' Association of Lancashire.

Mr. Lang, on behalf of the deputation, stated that
the overlookers, seeing no prospect of any improve-
ment in the cotton trade, were desirous of emigrating.
The Queensland Cotton Company have offered send
out 75 adults free to that colony, and advance £2 per
head towards an outfit; and they desired to know
whether this committee would aid this object.
After same discussion, the question stood adjourned
for further consideration.

Mr. Cremer moved that before any funds were sent
into Lancashire, full inquiries should take place as to
the action of the existing committees in that locality.
It would be the duty of the committee to see that their
funds were sent to those districts where they were
most needed.

At long discussion ensued, and it was ultimately re-
solved, the subject being of so much importance, and
so many contradictory reports being published, that
Messrs. (Cremer and Burn should visit certain dis-
tricts in Lancashire, with the view of making inquiry
and report the result to the next meeting of the com-
mittee prior to any funds being sent away.
The remuneration of the delegates, who will be absent
only a few dayi, was fixed at 6s. per day, with lodging
and travelling expenses.
After the transaction of some routine business, the
committee adjourned until next Wednesday.
The sub-committee will meet at the BEEHIVE Office,
on Saturday evening (to-night), from seven till nine
o'clock, to receive subscriptions. The sub-committee
will meet every Saturday evening for the same object
until further notice.

The following letter has been sent to the treasurer
of the above committee by the persons who have up to
the present time been collecting and forwarding the
weekly subscriptions in Woolwich Dockyard to the
BEEHIVE. It requires no comment. It is another
lesson for working men; though it is highly desirable
they should learn those already set them :
Woolwich Dockyard, Dec. 3, 1862.
Sir,—Tt is with extreme regret that I have to announce
that the present small amount is the last that I shall
have the pleasure of forwarding to you from the Wool-
wich Dockyard. Not that we are about to discontinue
our efforts for the amelioration of the distressed Lan-
cashire Weavers. It arises from the fact of the prin-
cipal officers having organised and headed a general
collection throughout the yard, and which will be for-
warded through another channel. I hope working
men are beginning to see the importance of supporting
the BEEHIVE as the true representative of their feel-
ings, wants, and actions; and that they are at last
learning-the hard lesson that the true way of improving
their social condition is by taking their own affairs into
their own hands' and not leave them to those who can-
not possibly feel so much interest in their welfare as
they do themselves. IL M.'

EAST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL OPERATIVES'

RELIEF FUND

The Executive Committee —Met for business as
usual on Monday, at Speak-buildings, Padiham.
The Rev. E. A. Verity, 8.D., in the chair. The fol-
lowing deputies were also present :—John Pinder,
James Crompton, Lawrence Shackleton (Burnley),
H. Whitehead, James Heap, George Hargreaves
(Habergham), J. Denbigh, John Haworth, W. Wil-
kinson (Treasurer), Joseph Peacock (Secretary).
The minutes of the last meeting were confirmed, and
the Secretary gave.in his report.
The thanks of the Committee were voted to Mr.
Potter, of the BEER IVI3, who sent £3O; to Mr.
Strother, of Middlesborough on Tees for the first
instalment of a fund collected there; and to Mr.
Dyson, of Leeds, who sent a collection made by him
of 9s. 6d. More is promised.

The thanks of the Executive were heartily voted
to the London Trades' Council for the unanimous
response given to the appeal, and the feeling dis-
played towards their destitute brethren.
On the proposal of Mr. Shackleton, seconded by
Mr. James Denbigh, it was resolved to send them,
through Mr. Potter, a balance sheet of the Central
Operatives' Fund from the beginning, and to appeal
to them for increased funds to carry out the scheme
of more largely aiding the 'poor workmen of East
Lancashire.

Mr. Peacock thought that if East Lancashire
could be supplied by the United Trades of the
kingdom with sufficient funds to supplement the aid
now given, North and South Lancashiie might be
added to the list. (Hear, hear.)
Mr. Heap, and Mr. John Haworth, the deputies ,to
Liverpool, then delivered in their report, and the
thanks of the meeting was accorded them.
The Chairman observed that he thought after the
generous and noble example of the London Trades,
Liverpool, Edinbro', and Dublin, as well as Bristol,
would not delay . to join, as it was essential the
response should be general and unanimous. (Hear,
hear.)

The Secretary said that there had been an error
in the statement of some friends, who supposed that
the middle-class committees in East Lancashire
were giving food in relief to the amount of '2s. 2d.
per head. He wished to correct the statement ;
Is. 6d. was the highest, and 6d. the lowest amount
given; therefore the average would be is. per head.
The poor-law guardians at Padiham, Burnley, and
other places only, in some instances, gave 4d., and
in others as much as Is. 4d. per head. He knew not
why it varied.
Mr. Pinder thought it disgraceful to stamp the
clothing, and make it a loan from the Manchester
Central and London Committees. It was felt to be
an insult by many poor people, and, he thought,
unjust, because the clothing was a gift and not a
loan.

It was resolved- to send copies of the reported
meeting of the London Trades' Council to all other
cities and towns.

The Chairman read a letter from thct,engineers of
Newcastle touching the starving co-operatives, for
whom much sympathy was everywhere felt.
The usual grants were then distributed to Padi-
ham, llabergham, and Burnley, after which the
meeting separated.

The Prince of Wales hai subscribed £l,OOO for the
Lancashire Distress Fund.

articles.title: LONDON, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 6, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 6, 1862.

.7R4 DES' SOCIEIIES POLITICAL

UNION.

A meeting of this association was held on Tuesday
everling last, at the Brown Bear, Broad-street, Blooms-
bury, for the purpose of adopting the programme and
address, and on other business. There was a very
good attendance, and much interest displayed in the
success of what will, doubtless, become a most impor-
tant society. _ _ I _

Mr. GeOrge Odgers having ten the chair, ex-
plained the reason why he, and those associated with
him, had exerted themselves in getting up this associa-
tion. As trades' unionists, they felt the desirability of
Lecoming possessed of the franchise. The speaker
then reviewed the various attempts that had been
made, of late years, to pass a Reform Bill through
Parliament, and intimated that Lord Palmerston was
the great stumbling block in the way. The Govern-
ment, of which he was the head, had grossly violated
the pledge they had given, on turning out Lord
Derby's administration, and the House of Commons
had broken all the promises made at the last election.
Under these circumstances, it became the duty of
working men, especially trades' unionists, to take up
the quession for themselves, and if they did so
earnestly and honestly, he had no doubt they would be
successful.

Mr. Facey, the secretary, read a resume of the pro-
ceedings of the society from its conimencement.
Mr. Eglington then moved that the programme and
address which had been printed and circulated should
be adopted by the association. They proposed to
confine their exertions to those points only, the
attainment of a registered manhood suffrage, and the
protection of the vote by 'ballot. The speaker on-
forced the motion by some very pertinent remarks.
Mr. Graham seconded the resolution. lie contended
that no country could be truly great and prosperous
where the working dames were kept in political
slavery._

Mr Cremer supported the reselution in a speech of
considerable power. He contended that the right to
the suffrage was born in man; he combatted the
assertion that manhood suffrage would produce a bad
House of Commons; it was a libel upon the working
classes, who were, as a body, quite as intelligent poli-
tically as the present electors, who could not boast
much of the composition of the house returned by
them. He thought, even if there might be some
danger in the experiment, to use the words of the
Roman author, that Liberty with danger, was pre-
ferable to Safety with slavery.' (Hear.)
Mr. Petherbridge also supported the resolution, con-
fining his remarks to the advocacy of the vote by
ballot, which he thought would be absolutely necessary
with manhood suffrage. Having spent some years in
Australia, both before and since the introduction of
the ballot in that country, he could testify to the great
improvement in the political hemisphere under that
system,_

- Mr. Howell, in supporting the resolution, pointed
out how imcortant it was for the security of these
trades' societies, and the safety of their social rights,
that working men should be in possession of the fran-
chise. The men who had started this association meant
to persevere with it, and not allow it to fall through.
(Cheers.) He advocated, at great length, the necessity
of trades unions making use of their organisation to
obtain the suffrage.
Mr. Bligh, who attended as a deputation from the
Tower Hamlets' Manhood Society, wished to know
who were eligible to become members of the associa-
tion now meeting, and how far they were prepared to
co-operate with other societies having the same objects
in view.

Mr. Davis, deputed by the No. 19 Lodge of Amalga-
mated Painters, having said a few words in support of
the resolution,
Mr. Facey, in reply to Mr. Bligh, said, it was in-
tended to confine the association to trades unionists
only, for very apparent reasons; but, at the same time,
it was prepared to aid and co-operate with any other
society formed for the attainment of the same objects.
The resolution was then unanimously agreed to.
Some formal business was then transacted, a great
number of cards of membership taken .up, and the
meeting then adjourned until Tuesday, the 16th inst.,
at eight o'clock, when a paper will be read on the
' Suffrage,' and discussion invited.

We have received a great many letters upon the
above subject, some really approving of the movement
now inaugurated, but find it impossible to give them
in full • we, however, make the following extracts. A
Bristolian' writes :—` I was much pleased to read in
your paper of the 22nd, the resolutions of the Trades'
Political Union' and their address to the Trades'
Unionists of the United Kingdom. The address is an
able piece of writing, and I hope, and believe that it
will make a powerful and permanent impression on
the mind of every reflective man who reads it.'
J. Stedman, writes Sir,—As an old reformer,
I heard with pleasure the address issued by the trades,
amongst whom my respected brother brush, Mr. Facey,
has taken a very prominent part in times past. I have
always maintained that political emancipation was the
key stone to the social building, and I feel heartily
glad to see this truly grand and important movement
initiated.'

Mr. Samuel Tomkins writes Sir,—lt is cheering
to find that steps are being taken to induce the members
of trade societies to move in the matter of Parliamentary
Reform. To me it has been a source of amazement
that working men have refrained from using their
Powerful organisations to obtain, at least, a portion of
their rights as men. The letters on the subject in
your piper, and especially the address of the London
Trades Political Union, show there is a possibility of
their throwing their timidity to the winds, and em-
barking in a cause demanding the most thoughtful
attention and best energies of every rational creature.'
The only objective letter received has been one from
Mr. Thomas Vize, in which he complains of the word-
ing of the address and its length, winding up with
some remarks depreciatory of Mr. Facey, the secretary.
Whether these remarks are deserved or not we are not
aware, but as they contain no definite charge we re-
frain from inserting them. Mr. Vize does not say in
his letter whether he is in favour of or opposed to the
movement.

FIRE AT PETROLEUM OIL WORKS AT ROTKERRITHE.—
On Tuesday night the Patent Petroleum Oil Works,
belonging to Messrs. Rossell and Co., in Rotherhithe-
street, caught fire. The fire commenced in a brick
building used as one of the oil refineries. Adjoining
this extensive building were a number of open yards
and sheds piled with casks, &c., and it was feared that
the flames would have extended to those portions of
the works. A number of steam and other engines soon
arrived, and were set to work from the river Thames
and from a tidal ditch, but such was the inflammable
nature of the goods on the premises that a considerable
time elapsed before the brigade could do more than cut
off the progress of the flames in the direction of the
adjoining buildings. Before nine o'clock Captain Shaw
sent the principal portion of the engines home to their
respective stations, thereby allaying all fears of any
further ex.tension of mischief, and shortly afterwards
the flames were entirely extinguished. The damage
done, however, is very considerable.

articles.title: HR. VIIITOENT ON DALY AND GARIBALDI:
articles.text:
HR. VIIITOENT ON DALY AND
GARIBALDI:

On Thursday Mr. Vincent delivered his third
oration at the Broadmead Rooms, Bristol, his sub-
ject being Italy and Garibaldi, which attracted a
large audience. Mr. Jacques occupied the chair.
Mr. Vincent, in the earlier part of his oration,
vividly portrayed the condition of Italy as she once
was, referring to some of her foremost men, paying
a tribute especially to Cavour and Mazzini ; and he
next pictured her progress through her struggle for
liberty, referring to the position France took in the
matter and speaking in not too complimentary terms
of Louis Napoleon and of diplomatists. The con-
cluding portion of his address, which was the most
loudly, applauded, was that which more especially
referred to Garibaldi, the hero of Aspromonte, who
transcended in valour allother heroes—the majestic
right arm of the Italian enterprise, the magnificent,
incorruptible, noble-minded citizen. Alluding to
his last enterprise, which, he (the lecturer) argued,
had been stayed by secret French intervention, he
said Garibaldi's plan' whatever it was, had to be
executed, and would be. Whatever his plan might
have been, it had not been defeated. He had been
shot down, not in arms against the King, but for the
King, by an Italian bullet, though he should have
been honoured with the shield of Italian protection
as the first of italian citizens, and should have been
preserved, even if his preservation had cost the fall
of the throne. (Applause.) He had accepted his
situation with touching and beautilul meekness;
he seemed to say uncomplainingly, 'Oh, bullet,
thou art the patriot's reward!' In conclusion Mr.
Vincent said if Garibaldi visited London in March
next, as there was every reason to believe, he would
have such a reception as the country had never
given to any public man. Each of the trades of the
metropolis had organised a committee, and intended
to form in grand procession upon his arrival, trust-
ing also that there would be deputations from other
cities and towns in England. Every shop in Lon-
don would hang out banners in his honour, and he
had the admiration, not only of the workpeople and
of tht. middle classes, but also of the aristocracy. At
the palace at Sydenham he would be entertained at
such a banquet as would make the genius of abso-
lutism everywhere tremble. (Loud applause.) The
lecturer concluded with an eloquent aspiration
regarding Italy and Garibaldi.

articles.title: HORRIBLE HURDERS AT SEA.
articles.text:
HORRIBLE HURDERS AT SEA.

At the Southampton Police court on Wednesday,
Ferdinand° Petriana, an Austrian, and late carpenter
and second mate on board the ship Winthrop, an Ame-
rican-built ship, sailing under the British flmg—was
charged with havingmurdered the captain of the vessel,
together with his wife and the first mate, whilst on the
voyage from Rio to Monte Video. The prisoner had
been landed at Southampton on the previous day from
the steam-ship Oneida, in which vessei he had been sent
home in custody. The witnesses were also landed at
the same time. The evidence of the following witness
contains full particulars of the horrible occurrence :
Peter Ronja, a Dutchman, said: I was an able sea-
man aboard the ship Winthrop, belonging to Halifax,
Nova Scotia. The prisoner was carpenter and second
mate aboard the same vessel. The captain's name was
Nicola Liperi, an Italian. I shipped at Monte Video.
The name of the first mate was Jones, an American.
The captain's wife, who was an Englishwoman, was
also on board. We left San Francisco on the 20th of
September laden with timber. About fourteen days
after that, on a Friday, at between one and two
in the morning, I was keeping watch on deck,
and standing by the mate near the cabin door.
The mate went into the cabin, where there was
a light, for the purpose of seeing the time, and
when he came out he said it was half-past one.
When the mate opened the door I saw the captain
lying asleep on the sofa. After the mate came
out we continued talking far a few minutes, when we
saw the light suddenly extinguished in the captain's
cabin. The mate opened the door to see who put the
light out, when he saw the prisoner in the cabin.
The mate said to the prisoner, What did you put out
the light for?' and immediately afterwards the pri-
soner fired a pistol from the cabin. I and the mate
ran away, and the prisoner can after us and fired a
second, the ball of 'which struck the mate in the back.
The mate ran a few steps further, and then fell in the
forecastle. The prisoner followed the mate into the
forecastle, and I went forward. Directly afterwards
the prisoner came out again, and, as he passed me on
the deck, he said, lam going to jump overboard.' I
then went down the forecastle and saw the mate lying
there dead, and the captain's wife was also there lying
across a chest. At this time the prisoner came back
with a pistol in one band and an augur in another, and
told me to stand out of his way. The prisoner then
ran up and down the deck exclaiming, I am captain
now.' lie then called the cook, and told him to make
a good breakfast, and Called to me to heave the mate
overboard. A few minutes after this the prisoner put
his pistols away, and as soon as we saw that we got
hold of him, bound him, and secured him in the hold.
We kept him there till we arrived at Rio Grande,
which was about five days afterwards. The wife, who
was badly wounded, died the next day, and we threw
her overboard on the Sunday, not being able to keep
her any, longer. The prisoner, who is a fine dark-
looking nian, in the prime of life, was then remanded,
to await orders from the Board of Trade.

MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN HYDR PARK.
—A. distressing case of alleged murder andiottempted
suicide took place in Hyde Park, on Monday night,
under the subjoined circumstances :—About 10.30 two
men crossing Kensington-gardens bridge were at. tracted by loud shrieks and cries for helpfrom a female
voice. They immediately called for assistance, and
hurried to the spot from whence the screams pro-
ceedeqt, John Parsons, boatman to the Royal
Hung& Society, hearing the alarm, at once went
roinid to the south shore of the Serpentine, and got
there just as one of the men had succeeded
in getting hold of a woman's clothing, and was in
the act of dragging her by that means to the
shore. The woman was removed, under the direc-
tion of Parsons, to the society's receiving•house, in
a state of insensibility, and placed in a warm bath
without delay. Dr. Christian attended, and had
all the necessary means applied for restoring anima-
tion, and succeeded in accomplishing the object so far
as to enable the unfortunate creature to open her eyes
about half-past two on Tuesday, when she made
the startling announcement that she had drowned her
child. Parsons at once returned to the spot in a boat,
accompanied by another boatman, and dragged for the
body of the child until six o'clock, but without success.
At eleven o'clock they went oub again, and finally suc-
ceeded in recovering the body of a male child, nicely
dressed, and apparently about a month old. The
wretched woman and the dead body of her infant were
removed to St. George's Workhouse, Mount-street,
Grosvenor-square, where the former lies in a very
precarious state. The woman, who gives the name of
Jane Hunt, but refuses her address, admits having
drowned the child, and that she At OW same time itp
tended self-destruction.

articles.title: PRICE Two PENCE,
articles.text:
PRICE Two PENCE,

FRIGHTFUL BOLLER EXPLOSION
NEAR SHEFFIELD.

Seniors Loss OF LIFE.—An explosion of a most
fearful character occurred at Messrs. Beatson and
Co.'s, the Midland Iron Works, adjoining the Midland
Railway Station, Masbro', on Wednesday, about
half-past six o'clock. Most fortunately the men
employed on the night turn had just gone off,
and those to be employed during the day had only
arrived in small numbers, or the consequences must
have been much more serious. The cause of the
fearful calamity was the bursting of an horizontal
boiler, adjoining which were three furnaces, one
being a ball furnace situate at one end, and
at the other were two puddling furnaces. These are
completely demolished, and the roofs of nine others
entirely stripped away. The length of the mill is about
140 yards, in which were numerous sheds covering fur-
naces in daily use. These sheds were covered over
with slates and sheet iron and were supported by mas-
sive iron pillars and girders, with massive
beams. All these are entirely swept away, and the
mass of debris is of an indescribable character. Mr.
Hartley, the manager, was on the spot, and rendered
every aid. He succeeded in extricating one of the men
from his fearful position in an inanimate state, and
immediately swooned away. The bodies of five men
were shortly recovered, all being dead, and near twenty
others in a fearfully lacerated state. Two of these
have since died, and the others are in a precarious
state. The names of those killed are —Joseph Adams,
puddler, married man and family; James Fitzgerald,
labourer, single man, about 20; George Copley, married,
with one ciild, about 27; William Curvoy, labourer,
single man. 25 ; William Cawthorne, single, labourer,
17 ; John Ellis, engine tenter; and Charles Woodcock.
All the medical gentlemen of the neighbourhood were
in attendance upon the injured workmen, several of
whom were conveyed to the Sheffield Infirmary.

articles.title: SUICIDE OF A YOUNG WIFE.
articles.text:
SUICIDE OF A YOUNG WIFE.

On Monday evening Mr. William Carter held an
inquest at the King's Arms Tavern, St. George's
Bridge, Albany-road, Camberwell, on the body of
ElizAbeth Jeffery, aged 18, the wife of a porter.
Mr. William Pike proved that on Saturday night,
about ten o'clock, he went upon the bank of the Surrey
Canal, near St. George's Bridge, where he found a
bonnet and a mantle lying on the ground. He pro-
cured the drags, and in about three minutes he brought
the body of deceased to the bank.

Mary-Davis, the mother of the deceased, said she
last saw her daughter alive about half-past nine o'clock
on Saturday night at her (witness's) house. The
husband was out of work, but the deceased had some
employment as an ironer, and shared her earnings with
hiai.—David Davis, the father of the deceased, stated
that he kept the husband with him three quarters of
an hour alter the deceased left home to prevent any
disputes. lied seen the husband strike his daughter,
but he did not do so on the Saturday night.—The jury
returned a verdict to the effect, Tnat the deceased
committed suicide while in an unsound state of mind.'

articles.title: SOUIHAMPTON ELECTION.—THE NaMINATION.
articles.text:
SOUIHAMPTON ELECTION.—THE
NaMINATION.

The imiination took pl ice in the Guildhall at
10 o'clozk on Wednesday. The proceedings throughout
were of a most noisy character. Captain Mangles was
proposed by Colonel Tryon and seconded by Mr. J. T.
Tucker. The Lord Mayor (Mr. Alderman Rose) was
proposed by Mr. W. J. Lefeuvre, and seconded by
Mr. Joseph Lobb. Mr. Scrase nominated the Hon.
W. F. Cowper, but there was no seconder. Captain
Mangles and the Lord Mayor spoke amidst a scene of
indescribable confusion. The show of hands was
declared to be in favour of the Lord Mayor, and a
poll was demanded on behalf of Captain Mangles.

Mr. WILLIAMS, M.P., AND HIS C ONSTITUENTS.
According to his annual custom, Mr. W. Williams,
M.P. for Lambeth, on Monday evening addressed a
meeting of his constituents at the Horns Tavern,
Kennington, for the purpose of rendering an account
of his stewardship for the last session, and of express-
ing his views upon the current political questions of
the day. The meeting was very fully attended. Mr.
Stratton was called to the chair. Mr. Williams hav-
ing reviewed at length the proceedings of Parliament
during the last session, and explained the part which
he had taken in them, touched upon the subject of
financial reform, and said his practical experience in
the House of Commons was that there was no sincere
or earnest desire in that body for economy. He con-
demned the waste of money now taking place on
fortifications; and our colonial possessions ought, he
contended, to be self-supporting, and not to be a bur-
den on this country to the extent of £3,000,000 per
annum. He next referred to the great distress exist-
ing in the manufacturing districts, arising out of the
unfortunate war in America, and which the wholel
country were doing their duty in alleviating, and sat
down without giving any expression of his opinion on
the American question. A resolution, expressing the
entire confidence of the electors in the hon. member,
and their thanks to him for his conduct as their re-
presentative, was adopted.

SINGULAR CASE OF MANSLAUGHTER.—An inquiry
was held on Monday evening by Mr. W. Payne,
coroner, at Guy's Hospital, respecting the death of
Alexander Norden, aged 29, which took place on Friday
last from injuries inflicted on him by William Cairns.
Frederick Holley said he was a carpenter, and was
employed at Mr. Ashley's, No. 24, Bishopsgate-street.
On the 31st of July last witness threw a potato at
Alexander Norden, a shopmate. Norden threw some-
thing back at witness, who ran out of the shop. An-
other workman, William Cairns, returning from his
dinner, opened. the shop•door to go in, when at that
instant Norden, supposing it to be witness, flung a
piece of wood which struck the door. Cairns flung
something into the shop and entered. Witness heard
a scuffle, and upon going in found his own chile
sticking deep in Norden's back, A man took it
out, and deceased fell. Another witness said that
Cairns threw the chisel at the deceased a distance of

12 or 14 feet. Mr. Holmsdale, house surgeon, said the
deceased was athnitted with a very deep wound
between the 10th ant 11th ribs, which penetrated the
lung. Death resulted from empyema, the consequence
of the wound' ill the lung. In reply to a question from
the coroner, Fienry Norden said he went to the station,
but the polio'.) persuaded him not to give Cairns in
charge, saying it would all blow over,' and he had
better do nothing. Deceased died consequently
without t' /taking any deposition, but he told witness
what hall happened between him and Cairns. The
coroner said that would not be evidence, as Cairns was
not Iwo sent. The conduct of the police was most ex-
traord. tnary. The coroner having summed up, the jury
ratur tied a verdict of Manslaughter against William
eair as, and expressed their condemnation of the con-
duc tof the police. The coroner issued his warrant
: the apprehension and committal of Cairns for
icrial at the next sessions of the Central Criminal Court.

THE LANCASHIRE DISTRESS AND
THE TIMES.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE "13EE•IIIVE."

Sin,—lt has been with great satisfaction that I
have seen that the BEE-HIVE., as an influential
organ of the working classes, has refrained from
joining in the cry which has been raised in certain
quarters against the Lancashire millowners. You.
have left it to the Times, and Mr. Kingsley, and
others, who hate the employers more than they care
or the men, to avail themselves of this opportunity
for making mischief. Those persons have no
scruples about throwing water on the kindling sym-
pathy of England, if they can but cast some
discredit upon political opponents, and retard the
progress of industrial civilisation by stirring up
jealousy and suspicion between the leaders and the
soldiers of labour. The ornamental classes and their
literary champions feel instinctively that when that
civilisation shall have established itself, their day
will be over; and we cannot be surprised that they
should avail themselves of every means, fair and
foul, to retard its approach. But their tactics on
this occasion are too transparent to deceive any
one. In the battle which working men have bad
to tight for their rights, political and social, they
know on which side they have always found the
squires and parsons. It will take a great deal to
convince your readers that the Times is the friend
of the working man. When they see its articles
garnished with all the cla?-trap phrases of the
vulgarest socialist demagogues, they will remember
certain other articles last year. A little common
honesty in the matter of the builders' lock out would
have been worth all this venomous philanthrophy.
As a general rule we may expect to see the upper
classes take the part of the -master against the
workman. But the cotton manufacturers are a
powerful body. They have dealt heavy blows at
the aristocracy and the Church. They have shown
more disposition than other employers to fraternise
with their men, and to become what they ought to
be—true and conscientious chieftains of industry.
Hence they are especia Ily dreaded and bated by
. . .

he upper classes, and it is felt that the present is -a
golden opportunity for calumniating them, and
weakening their influence. The attempt, I ant
convinced, will fail, as it deserves. Lancashire men
are not slow to complain when they are wronged;
but not all the malicious endeavours of the Times
and its correspondents have availed to produce
the slightest discontent among the suffering
operatives. They see and know that the
employers (speaking generally) are making
unheard-of sacrifices, that they may do
their duty towards their men. In theory and talk
these manufacturers have been too apt to treat
political economy as if it was a code of morals. In
their obstinate British way they have taken a sort of
perverse pleasure in painting themselve as stony-
hearted money-grubbers. But their practice is
better than their doctrine. They could not create
that magnificent industrial organisation without
feeling that responsibility, and that pride in the
well-being of the whple body from highest to lowest,
which belongs to a true ruler. It is on the growth
and extension of this sentiment among employers,
and the corresponding loyalty which it will evoke
among the workmen, that the future of industry
depends. It has begun, I verily believe, when in-,
dustry is organised on a grand scale. Our London
friends must not judge the question by their exper-
ience of scrambling ill-organised trades, such as that
of the builders. To take one instance out of many.
Sir Elkanah Armitage has fed and clothed his work-
men since the commencement of the distress, and has
declared that he will share his last sixpence with
them. Can you fancy Messrs. Kelk and Lucas doing
anything like that? I believe this cotton-famine,
with all its horrors, will have a glorious result. Not
merely will workmen, who have been generously
dealt with, ever retain a noble loyalty towards their
chiefs, but the employer who has sacrificed his thou-
sands and tens of thousands to keep his workmen
alive, and to prevent the break-up of the industrial
kingdom (if I may be allowed the expression), which
was the pleasure and pride of his life—the employer,.
I say, will have passed through experiences during
this sharp agony, will have known sensations such
as purify the heart, from what taint of selfishness
may have afflicted it before. He will confess to
himself manfully, what before he almost condemned
himsrlf for feeling, that the good of society should
be his conscious aim in the conduct of his business,
and that the acquisition of wealth is the least part
of the satisfaction to be reaped from the direction of
a just industrial enterprise.
I began this letter by remarking that you, Sir,
have abstained from echoing the upper-class clamour
against the millowners. But my chief object in
writing was to remonstrate with you for what I
conceive to be a step in the wrong direction. In
advocating a working man's relief fund for the Lan-
cashire distress, you allege that relief has been re-
fused to co-operators, or marked workmen. Now
this is a serious charge to make, and I hold that you
ought either to give names and circumstances, or say
nothing about it. If the Times had mentioned by
name those manufacturers who are behaving meanly
—as no doubt there are some—it would have been

doing real service. It is the vague charges against
a class, offering no opportunity for examination, whick
are o unjust and mischievous. I for one withhold
my belief from all such charges, until I see them in,
a more distinct shape.—l am, &c.,
E. S. BEESLY.
University Hall, Gordon Square.

Dee. 2nd, 1862
The case mentioned by Professor Beesly, was.
distinctly stated in our advertising page.]

articles.title: CABMEN AND THEIR G.RIEV.ANCES..
articles.text:
THE CABMEN AND THEIR
G.RIEV.ANCES..

The cabmen have held their aggregate meeting,
which was a great and legitimate success,, both in
point of numbers and in tone and feeling. There Nyas.a
spirit of order and quiet determination pervading the
meeting, auguring well for the ultimate success of the
movement. One of the great features of the evening
was the attendance of a large number of influentiaL
proprietors, holding, in the aggregate, many hundred
numbers, who in the main, cordially agreed. with the
proceedings of the drivers' delegates, and,theadoptkin
of a resolution appointing an equal number of pro-
prietors to sit with the drivers' delegates to further
prosecute the movement. There is no doubt the
agitation will be carried forward. with spirit, and
with all the more chances of ultimate success from the
united effort that will now be brought to boar, upon.
the question,. The exact mode in w,hich., the future
agitation will be carried on, will of course rest with
the united delegates, but we would suggest that they
should first get their petition for parliameatary inquiry
extensively signed through the trade, by proprietors.
as well as drivers, and that obtained the committee
must be prepared with slaoh, a body of evidence to. lay
before it by competent witnesses, as will carry con-
viction with it, and prepare the way for a favourable
report, upon which rests any chance for the success
of the new bill to, be brought before the Rouse of
Commons. We need hardly say that we wish them
all success, and that they may rely upon our hearty
support so long as they pursue the same wise and
moderate COUXI3O they have hitherto adopted. One
hopeful sign is that every daily paper, with the ex-
ceptioa of the Times, on Thursday morning contained
a_rerort of the meeting sent to them.

At the great Lancashire county meeting, held at
Manchester, on Tuesday last, the large sum of £60,000
was subscribed in the room, tae Earl of Derby healing
the list with £5,000. Other contributions were pro,
mised, swelling; the total up to the large azaeltnt of
£130,000.

articles.title: A2'HE METROPOLITAN RAILWAY.
articles.text:
A2'HE METROPOLITAN RAILWAY.

•
Nothing definite has yet transpired as to the openiug
of this line of railway. The repeated delays and post-
ponements which have taken place in the matter have
led to some very unfavourable comments as to the con-
dition of the line. Mr. Fowler, the engineer, in his
last report to the directors, stated most confidently that
everything would be ready for the opening by the Ist
of October last. The bursting of the Fleet sewer was
assigned as a cause of delay, and when all the damage
occasioned by this accident had been repaired, a further
cause for postponement was found in the necessity for
arranging or adapting the system of working the
eignals. Then it was found that the carriages which
had been built for the railway were too wide, and that
the doors could not in consequence be opened in the
tunnel. They were, in fact, made some ten inches
wider than the ordinary carriages of the Great
'Western R tilway. This blunder has, we believe,
been slow rectified by reducing the width of the
carriages. One reason for not opening the line
was, however, put forward, which, unlike any of those
already mentioned, had really no foundation, viz., that
the delay was occasioned by difficulties interposed by
the Great Western Railway, who had undertaken to
work the line. So far from this being the case, the
Great Western Company have been prepared at any
time, within the last three months, to undertake the
working of the railway, and no blame whatever can be
attributed to them in this respect. The Great Western
Company are prepared to abide by, and to carry out
the working arrangements in the fairest and most
'honourable manner. Among the rumours which have
been current during the last week, as to the cause of
delay, are some of a very grave nature. It was stated
that the works connected with the new Fleet sewer
were not sufficiently strong, that a very large portion
of the bank of the cutting near the Sessions-house,
Clerkenwell, had given way, and that the reconstruc-
tion of a large part of the retaining wall in some other
parts near the line of the sewer would be necessary.
This last report, we are glad to learn, has been
considerably exaggerated, There is a portion of
the line between the station and the mouth of
the Coppice-row tunnel, the retaining wall of which
had not been built up of brickwork. It was a part at
which the branch line to run under Smithfield was to
diverge, and here the bank was kept up only by a short
wall and come piling. A portion of the earth slipped,
but it was only to a trifling extent, and scarcely suffi-
cient to interfere with the line on the permanent way.
There are other reports of an unsatisfactory nature as
to the condition of some part of the brickwork in the
tunnel, but we are unable to ascertain whether there is
any foundation for this report. It is impossible to say
with certainty when the line will be opened for traffic.
No day for the officiel inspection has yet been named.
The directors of the Great Western Company have
done all in their power to complete the arrangements,
the station masters and guards and porters are ap-
pointed, and the answer now given to all inquiries on
the subject is that the opening day will not be delayed
beyond the middle of next month.

DECISION ON TilE BETTING' ACT.

• LIVERPOOL.
No little commotion has existed amongst the police
authorities in connection with a number of summonses
which had been issued against several of the Liverpool
betting men.
Some time ago a number of innkeepers in Liverpool
were summoned for allowing betting in their houses,
and convicted upon the evidence of policemen, who, in
plain clothes, went to their places of business' and made
bets upon different horse-racing events, depositing
money at the time.
On the 29th, a man named Edward Richardson, the
landlord of the Saddle Vaults, a beer-house, was sum-
moned, and the evidence against him was that of a
police-officer named Weetcott, who said that on Friday,
the 7th instant, he went to the defendant's premises,
when the latter bet him six halt-crowns to one against
Dulcibella for the Liverpool cup. Defendant booked
the bet, and witness gave him haif-a-crown.
In cross-examination by Mr. Cobb, solicitor, who
-appeared for the defendant, the witness said that the
half-crown with which be made the bct was the
proporty of the corporation.
His evidence was corroborated by another officer,
named Hugh M'Allan.

Mr. Cobb contended that there was no case within
the meaning of the act. The act religing to betting
houses was passed some time since in order to put down
houses which were springing up in all parts of 'London,
and which were usel solely for the purposes of betting.
The act had no reference to be(r houses such as that
kept by the defendant, where people went for refresh-
ment. The act was made for the suppression of betting
how( s' not public houses.
Mr. Robertson Gladstone (brother of the Chancellbr
of the Exchequer), who was on the bench along with
Mr. Hyslop, in adjudicating upon the case, said,—With
regard to this case, I believe we are both of the same
opinion, though I may be a little stronger in my views
than my brotner magistrate. "We think that this is
not a case coming under the act for the suppression of
betting houses. The act of parliament was intended
for the suppression of an evil existing. I. look upon
such betting as has been spoken of in this case as inci-
dental to a beer house, but the business of a beer house is
the trade of the place. As far as my judgment goes,
therefore, I do not think that tne case comes within
the meaning of the act. The upp,-r classes could prac-
tise the evil of betting to any extent they chose, yet,
when it descended to other people, not so well off in
this world's goods, the parties offending could be
brought into court. There were club-houses in Lon-
don, and in Liverpool too, where betting was con-
stantly practised. In every club in London it was the
practice to allow betting and card-playing and bets
were made Upon every game. What justice was there
in allowing one class of society to do one thing and
not giving the same privilege to other classes?
As Mr. Gladstone again at on the bench the next
day it was considered that the same decision would
be given in the cases. After some conversation
amongst the prosecuting officials, it was agreed that
all the summonses should be withdrawn.

articles.title: SPIRIT PHOTOGRAPHS 17
articles.text:
SPIRIT PHOTOGRAPHS 17

AMERICA.

Our American friends (says the Leeds Mercury), who
,21aira to be ahead of us in many things, have certainly
distanced us completely in the practice of spiritualism
and photography. The good people in I.!oston can not
only call up the spirits of their departed friends and
bold conversations with them—through a suitable.
'medium' of course—but they can take the portraits of
the spirits! The operation requires to be performed
by a medium who combines a spiritual nature with a
competent knowledge of photography, and Mr. William
H. Mumler, of the city of Boston, seems to be the only
person possessing those qualities in the necessary
degree who has yet become known to fame. This
lucky individual, who seems to be in a fair way to
snake a fortune out of the spirits, gives the following
account of his discovery :—A few Sundays since, he
being alone in the photograph saloon of Mrs. Stuart,
258, Washineton-street, trying some new chemicals,
and amusing himself by taking a picture of himself,
which, when produced, to his great astonishment and
wonder, there was on the plate, not a'one a picture of
himself; as he supposed, but also a picture of a young
woman sitting in a chair that stood by his side. He
said that, while standing for his picture, he felt a
Peculiar sensation and a tremulous motion in his
riga arm, and afterwards felt very much exhausted.
This was all he experienced that was unusual. While
looking upon the strange ~henomenon—the picture of
two persons upon thuplat. tnstead of one—the thought
and the conviction flashed epon his mind that this was
.the picture of a spirit. And in it he recognised the
likeness of his deceased cousin, which is also said to
he correct by all those who knew her. Since this dis-
covery has been made a great many bereaved relatives
have been furnished with pictures of the dead, taken in
,groups with those of living sitters, the picture of the
spirit being fainter and less distinct than that of the
one who sits.' The Boston paper, from which we take
the above extract, assures us that the most searching
investigations have been mile with the view of finding
out any deception' but without success. After this
the claims of the Boston folks to be considered:;, an
'advance people' will hardly be disputed.

DROWNED WHILE SKATING.—A weaver of the name
of James Chew, of Oakenshaw, near Blackburn, while
skating on a lodge near his house on Wednesday night,
was suddenly immersed beneath' the ice and drowned,
Owing to its breaking as he passed over it. Twelve or
fourteen companions who were with him at the time
happily escaped. They made strong efforts to rescue the
deceased, but did not succeed until ten o'clock, the body
having been drawn several yards beneath
POWERS OF ENDERANCE.—Captain C. F. Hall has
just been narrating before the Anierican Geographical
Society his recent Arctic experience while in search of
traces of the Franklin expedition, and took the oppor-
tunity of introducing to the society the Esquimaux man
whom he brought away with him—a hardy hunter,
who has been known to stand for three days and nights
motionless on the ice beside a seal-hole. Captain Hal I
described the ability of the Esquimaux to go without
food as striking him as quite astounding. He has
known them to do so for weeks. He heard of an instance
in which a party of these intrepid seal-hunters were
floated off from the mainland on a pack of ice, and could
not return for thirty days' during witieh time they had
not a morsel of food; yet they survived, although even
their faithful and wonderful dogs succumbed to the
pangs of hunger.

articles.title: B.EAUTIFUL HETEO.R.
articles.text:
A B.EAUTIFUL HETEO.R.

A. letter in the Times, signed E. J. Lowe, describes a
beautiful meteor seen from the railway station at
Grantham :—The following observations are as accurate
as it is possible to make them under such difficult cir-
circumstances, and when many features have to be
noticed in so brief a space of time. I consider, however,
there cannot be an error of five seconds in time, nor of
one minute in space :—Hour of appearance, sh. 46m.
575. G. 21. T.; hour of disippearance, sh. 47m. ssec.
G. M. T. Motion slow. Duration, Bsec. Greatest dia-
meter, Oleg. 31min. ; length longitudinally, ldeg.
17min. Colour, blue; form, kite-shaped. Position
near B Ceti—right ascension, 36 minutes 39 seconds:
south declination, 18 degrees 45 minutes. Position
near Fomalhaut right ascension, 22h. 50 minutes
1 second; south declination, 30degs. 20 min. 50-ecs.
The meteor was somewhat kite-shaped, being nearly
equal to the moon in breadth, and ab.pve tviice, her
diameter in length (this estimate being. taken-by looking
at the meteor and the Inooll at the same time). The
light was an intense blue, but only intensely bright in
the front, mostly as a crescent, buteccasionally expand-
ing almost to a circle; the remaining portion milky
white and dim in comparison. A train of sparks was
left in its path, yet it only lasted from one to two
seconds; balls of a blue colour, of large size (almosc
equal to the apparent diameter of Mars) also fell from
the head of the meteor perpendicularly downwards, not
continuously, but at frequent intervals. These balls
threw out other smaller balls, which burst into star-
like sparks of a yellowish colour, not unlike the shower
from a rocket when seen from a distance. The meteor
gradually increased in size, but not uniformly—An
occasional decrease in size and brightness taking place.
It vanished at its maximum brightness; not bursting,
but as if going behind some opaque body.

articles.title: SMITHFIELD CLUB CATTLE STIOW.
articles.text:
SMITHFIELD CLUB CATTLE STIOW.

As the opening day draws near, the arrangements at
the Agricultural Hall are rapidly approaching comple-
tion. All is huitle and activity-throughont the I.ll4a-
ing, from the rooms in which the officials are swiftly
writing their orders to the galleries in which the sound
of the workman's hammer may still be heard. -Every
day fresh implements are sent for exhibition. Applica-
tions for space have had to be refused. Ploughs,
drills, root-crushers, chaff-cutters, thrashing and reaping
in.:chines—all kinds of complicatecl.contrivances—begin
to .crowd the galleries set apart,for them. 4ibme of
them, still enclosed in canvas, ara Anzzls to thi un-
initiated, who can scarcely determine 'whether they
are statues .or. pumps; but others
.are gay and
glaring with al/ the glory of that particular red
paint which seems specially destined for the decora-
tion of agricultural implements. The show in the
galleries is certain to be a fine one; and there are
also many machines which, from their weight being in
excess of two tons, are obliged by the regulations to be
shown on the ground floor. Of the hall itself, and its
ample proportions, we have frequently Ispoken already;
and there can be no doubt that its general effect improves
upon further acquaintance. Considering its size, the
roof is remarkably light and graceful; and although it
Might, perhaps, be wished that a somewhat more liberal
employment of colour had been resorted to, yet in our
dim December days there would probably be but little
sunshine to light it up, and much good work might
have been comparatively wasted. The arrangements
for lighting are, as we have said before, most
excellent; and as the evening closes in, the effect
of the sudden illumination is really a very striking
one. Indeed, although utility has of course been
the chief thing studied, it is certain that even as a
spectacle the approaching show will be worth a
visit. Pacing along through the galleries, past hundreds
of machines for almost every agricultural purpose and
need, the visitor will have a clear and unbroken view of
the hall below, with the mellow light falling alike upon
the bustling crowd and the patient cattle. A brilliant
assemblage is expected—and no doubt with reason—on
the opening day. London has now returned to town;
and it is therefore tolerably certain that on Monday
week the Upper Ten' will be well represented at
Islington. The question as to whether the aristocracy
will come to a place so distant from the homes is
sufficiently answered by the fact that they did so in the
case of the Dog Show; and as regards the general
public, upon whom, after all, the success of the enter-
prise • mainly depends, it cannot be too often repeated
that the most ample facilities for locomotion will be pro-
vided. In point of fact, Islington will be at least as
easy of access as Brompton, and perhaps even more so, '
as many of the omnibuses will set down their passengers
at the very doors of the building. The arrangements for
the comfort and convenience of the visitors have been
carefully planned and ably carried out; and many useful
hints have, of course, been suggested by recent ex-
perience at the International Exhibition. Of that dis-
play, indeed, the approaching show will in some respects
a continuation, as most of the implements have been
brought direct from one to the other, and still bear the
placards recording the fact that they have received either
medals or honourable mention. One of the chief attrac-
tions of the Exhibition—one which became so popular as
to draw an almost impassable crowd about it every day
—will probably have as great a success in its new
quarters. We allude to Messrs. Aubert and Linton's
piping bullfinch, which will resume its song near the
Islington-green entrance to the building. The sum
realised by this metallic minstrel will be devoted, as
before, to the Lancashire Distress Fund, and in all
probability a handsome donation will result.
The arrangements in the gallery will secure an unin-
terrupted promenade to the visitor. Seeds and other
farm produce will be exhibited in cases against the wall;
between these and the implements there will be a clear
passage; and there will be another avenue between the
implements themselves and the outer railings of the gal-
lery. Many of the stands, some of them remarkably
neat in appearance, are already being erected, and will
be ready to receive their contents in a day or two. It
was feared that the lights—which, with a view of show-
ing the roof to the best advantage, had been kept as
high as possible—might not be sufficient to illuminate
the basement so completely as is desirable; but this has
been remedied by fixing a second circlet to the tubes
that run from the galleries, and by placing fresh lights
on every alternate standard holding the iron work of the
cattle pens. The awards of the judges will be made on
Saturday, and about eight o'clock in the evening the
building will be opened .for a private view by members
of the club and other privileged persons. On Monday
it will be open to the public at 55., and on the four fol-
lowing days at is., finally closing on Friday evening,
Dec. 12.

The Vienna Post Office authorities call the attention
of the letter-writing public to the necessity for giving
the name of the street in which persons live as well ,as

DARLNG ESCAPE.—On Thursday night a prisoner,
named John Hobson, who had been committed to take
his trial at the assizes to be held this week, on a charg
of coining, escaped from the Nottingham House of
Correction, under the following remarkable circum-
stances :—The prisoner was employed as a shoemaker
in his cell, and he availed himself of his opportunities
to partially cut the panel out of the door. After the
turnkey had left him, at half-past eight o'clock, he
broke the door panel out, and, having made a rope of
his bedclothes, he fastened it to the prison wall and let
himself down into the street, a distance of about 30
feet. He succeeded in getting clear away, and has not
yet been re-captured. The prisoner is a most daring
character, and passes by a number cf aliases.
ANCONA.—NO Ancona is not a pleasant city in its
outward physiognomy. It has all the annoyances and
disagreeables of a seaport, without any of the agreeables
that should belong to the coast. There is no possibility
of pleasant rambles along the shore; all exit to the south--
ward being absolutely forbidden not only by the cliff
itself, but by fortresses and walls, and sentries act &Ifni-
tun& ; and exit to the north leading only to the crowded
mile or so of causeway between the city and the railway
station, and beyond that to a flat and very ugly shore,
cut up by little creeks, and hedged in by the railway.
There is no shipping of any interest in the offing. There
is not even any fish to eat—or none worth, that is, eating.
—A _Lenten Journey, by Anthony Trollope.
ORIGIN OF PETROLEUM. The flow of oil from
mineral springs is by no means new either to science
or commerce. Herodotus has recorded that the island
of Zante furnished large quantities, while Pliny and
Disoscorides describe the oil obtained from Agri-
gentum, a small town in Sicily. The Persian springs
at Bakoum have yielded to the value of 600,000 dols.
' annually; and the earth oil from Rangoon, in Burmah,
has been exported to the extent of 400,000 hogsheads
yearly. The streets of Genoa and Amiens were formerly
lit by a petroleum obtained from Parma. In 1847, a
spring was discovered in Yorkshire, which was success-
fully worked by Mr. James Young, of Glasgow, until
exhausted, when he turned his attention to the distilla-
tion of coal, and discovered paraffin oil. The marvel-
lous oil springs of the New World, however, far
surpass in extent and interest all previous discoveries,
and the quantity already yielded, wit:lout apparently
diminishing the supply, shows that this will be a most
important article of commbrce for some nears to come.
In Canada the oil rises from the saturateo: corniferous
limestones; in the States it is principally' obtained
from Devonian sari lstonea, while in Westent Virginia
and Ohio it rises directly from the coal-mean tres. In
all cases it no doubt arises from the decompoe ition of
coal by temperature and pressure, and is lifted by the
percolation of water under it to cavities and fissa Teti in
rocks till it approaches the surface, and it is gent, 'rally
accompan= ty quantities of coal gas.—Dr, j, B.

The union of Stockport contains 17 townships, within

articles.title: SCOTTISII .HOSPITAL.
articles.text:
THE SCOTTISII .HOSPITAL.

The anniversary dinner of this society—which is
usually held on St. Andrew's Day, but which, owing to
that day falling this year on a Sunday, could 'not- be
kept, in accordance with the custom of the society in
this respect—took place on Monday, at the Freemasons'
Tavern, and was attended by about 150 of the friends
and supporters of the excellent charity in question. The
Great Hall, where the banquet was served, was decorated
with banners and various devices, most judiciously ani
tastefully arranged by Mr. Douglas, an officer of the
Scottish Society, the banner of the society holding a
prominent position over the Chairman's seat.

- Sir John Heron Maxwell, Bart., presided on the
occasion, and was supported on his right and left by Dr.
Webster, Dr. Alison, Sir Walter Stirling the Rev. Dr.
Cumming, Dr. Thompson, Professor Kerr, Professor
Donaldson, David Roberts, Esq., R. A. Kirk, Esq., Scp.
The cloth baying been drawn, and grace—' For these
and all thy mercies given '—h tying been chanted.by the
vocalists, Miss Ran.stord, Mr. Young, Mr. W. E. Rans-
ford, and Mr. Ransford, the latter of whom had the
directicn of the musical arrangement,
The Chairman rose to propose the toast of Her Ma-
jesty.' . _ _

- The toast was received with great enthusiasm.
The Chairman, in giving ` His Royal Highness
Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, Duke of Rothsay,
Baron of Renfrew, Lord of the Isles, and Grand Steward
of Scotland,' expressed his opinion that his Royal High-
ness would be in every •respect an honour to this
country.

The-toast of His Royal Highness Prince Alfred, and
the rest of the Royal k araily " The Army, Navy, and
Volunteers' was then given by the Chairman, and
cordially received by the company.
The Chairman, in proposinf, the toast of the evening,
The Scottish Hospital, said that it was hardly neces-
sary for him to say much with respect to the history of
the hospital, which they knew was founded a short time
after the accession of King James I. for the purpose of
relng s fortunate individnas of the Scottish
nation resident in the metropolis and its immediate
neighbourhood, ,and who were not in the receipt of any
parochial relief in this country. Shortly after the hos-
pital had been established, its usefulness had been ex-
emplified in rather a peculiar,manner, for_ during the
-plague of 1665-6 upwards of three hundred natives of
Scotland were buried at the sole charge of the hospital,
while numbers more were nourished during their sick-
ness without subjecting the parishes in which they re-
sided to the smallest expense. (Hear, hear.) But the
purpose of the institution had been changed from what
it was at that time and it now contributed to the sup-
port of ten poor and infirm persons, exceeding 72 years
of age, to whom a pension of £l5 per annum was
allowed; for ninety, above 68 years, to whom £lO Was
allowed; and for ten, above 65 years, to whom £8 was
allowed. (Hear.) He might here observe that some mis-
take was frequently made by many Scotchmen in refe-
rence to the Caledonian Asylum and the Seottish Hospital,
which were supposed by the persons to whom he was
now referring as being one and the same society. This
was, as the gentlemen present that evening knew full
well, a great mistake. The Caledonian Asylum was
intended for the maintenance and education of the
children of Scotchmen; whereas the Scottish Hospital
was solely applicable to the purpose of affording relief
to aged 'Scotch persons resident in the metropolis.
(Hear, hear.) It would thus be seen that the two
institutions had different objects in view, and that both
were well deserving of the support of true Scotchmen,
and of all who desired
.to do good to the old and the
young. (Hear, hear.) With this explanation he
begged to urge the claims which the Scottish Hospital
had upon their sympathy and support. After a
further observations, the Chairman concluded by pro-
posing Success to the Scottish Hospital,' which was
responded to with enthusiasm.

kr. Moir, the secretary, then read a list of subscrip-
tions, amounting to between £6OO and £7OO. Of this
Sum her Majesty'sabscribed 100 guineas and tile Duke

faction, and the banquet passed off with great eclat.

articles.title: RED RIVER.
articles.text:
RED RIVER.

We have received an account of the plunder of a
convoy of goods on the road from Georgetown down to
Fort Garry. It appears that in consequence of the
Sioux massacres in Minnesota, and of a warning sent
from fort Abercrombie to prepare for the worst, Mr.
Kittson, who was in charge at Georgetown, determined
to remove the property at that station, and all the party
there, to Fort Garry, and started in September, sending
fifteen or twenty tons of cargo by barge, and taking
about the same quantity with him in waggons. At the
Grand Forks, where the Red Lake River empties itself
• into the Red River, about 2,000 Chippewas were en-
camped, waiting for the long-expected treatl with the
American Government respecting certain tracts of land;
and a number of half-breeds from the neighbourhood of
the boundary line were also assembled. When the
party from Georgetown approached they stopped for the
night three miles off; but a band of the Indians soon
arrived and demanded provisions, and after getting these
they coolly drove off all the cattle. Mr. Kittson fol-
lowed and appealed to the chiefs. The plea was that
they were starving, and he was obliged to be content
with getting back the cattle absolutely necessary for the
waggons. But a demand then arose for goods from the
waggons. Mr. Kittson explained that they were not
his to give, but belonged to Red River merchants, with
whom the Indians were wont year by year to do busi-
ness in the most friendly way. The chiefs complained
that they had been invited down by the American Go-
vernment and kept waiting with no result; their pro.
visions were gone, and they had lost time in which they
should have provided for the winter. Long harangues
were made of a characteristic description. Mr. Kittson
said he could not believe they would set themselves to
barefaced robbrry. The chiefs said they would not do
that; what they wanted was, that he should hand over
the goods to them, and their necessities compelled them
to insist upon it. He replied that he could not give
them the goods, but he was in their power, and it wns
useless for him to offer opposition. All this took place
in the presence of 2,000 excited Indians, who began
shouting that they were now at liberty to help them-
selves. The chiefs still restrained them, but represented
that if Mr. Kittson did not give, a general plunder
might be the result, which would leave him nothing,
and perhaps endanger life. At length, amidst the
general noise, wrangling, and confusion, Mr. Kittson,
seeing his helplessness, and anxious for his patty, which
included both sexes, bade the Indians go forward in
their work, Then tea, sugar, tobacco, carpets, blankets
were flung hither and thither among the crowd. silks
torn into pieces to tie over their heads, and the 'finest
scarlet cloths rent into pieces and tossed about. A few
half-breeds, being Roman Catholics, exclaimed against
taking some priests' robes and holy vestments, but the
Red Lakers cried, We don't care for priests, bring the
things here." When they had helped themselves, Mr.
Kittson found himself proceeding on his way, plundered
to the extent of above 20,000 dols.—a loss which will
fall heavily on the traders of Selkirk. Some of the
half-breeds were from parishes actually within the Red
River settlement. The barge was some distance in the
rear, and successfully stole past afterwards in the dead
ofthe night. It is said to be considered in the settle-
ment that Mr. Kittson, and the chief trader of the
Hudson's Bay Company who was with him, acted with
discretion, and that the loss could not have been averted
by any other course.

A JUMCIAL JOKE.—Judge Roosvelt was trying a
tedious lawsuit concerning patent medicines one day, in
which Mr. Dyett, of New York, appeared as counsel.
The judge remarked, 'Mr. Dyett, I wish you would
favour the court by postponing the motion until some
other justice is sitting at chambers. lam tired of being
dosed with pills.' Mr. Dyett: Well, if your honour
pleases. I would do anything in the world to oblige
the court, but my duty to my clients in this instance
forbids that I should longer delay this motion, the most
important that has ever been made in this case, and
which, if postponed, would greatly distress my clients.'
Judge: Mr. Dyett, if your clients are in great distress,
I would advise them in the first place to take some of
the pills; and if that does not bring relief, then I would
advise them to change their Dyett.'
