Government has determined to accomplish a reform in
the dwellings of the operative classes in Paris, and is
about to commence by the construction of a cite modele
on the Boulevard Mazas for unmarried workmen. The
situation is well chosen, being in the centre of the
manufacturing quarter of Paris. The proposed build-
ing is to be five storgs high, and each floor is to be
divided into small rooms completely separated, and to
be approached by a spacious staircase. The ground
floor is to be appropriated to a reception room, or
common hall, open to all the lodgers, to a restaurant or
dining-room, an office for the director, and an apartment
for the house-porter.--Paris Letter.
A correspondent of the Presse says thaf the canonisa-
tion of the Japanese martyrs, which recently took place
in Rome, cost the Papal government 100,000 f., and that
during the ceremonies, which lasted three days, 5,000 or
6,000 candles were burnt.
A translation into French of the Adventures of Baron
Munchausen ' has just been made by Theophile Gautier,
Ills. It is illustrated by Gustave Dore. A new edition,
in French, of Gulliver's Travels,' with illustrations by
Gavarni, and a preface by Jules Janin, has recently been ,
i,ssaed by a Paris publisher.

articles.title: CELEBRATION OF THE PRINCE 01 WALES'S BIRTHDAY ON THE ATLAIVTIC.
articles.text:
CELEBRATION OF THE PRINCE 01
WALES'S BIRTHDAY ON THE AT-
LAIVTIC.

(From the Boston Advertiser.)
The occurrence of the 21st birthday of the Prince of
Wales, during the late passage of the steamer Europa
from Liverpool to Boston, was made the occasion of an
interesting celebration by the passengers. Many of
the latter were English army and navy officers, on their
way to Canada or the West Indies, who would natu-
rally be unwilling to let such an anniversary pass unno-
ticed. Captain Moodie, of the Europa, presided, and
the close of the dinner on the 9th was chosen for the
celebration, which was opened, by request, with a sen-
timent in honour of Queen Victoria from the American
passengers. Mr. Samuel Bowles, of Springiteld, Mass.,
as their organ, said
The American ladies and gentlemen of this boat's
company claim the privilege, as they cherish the desire
most cordially, to participate in the festivities of this
interesting occasion—the majority birthday of the
future Sovereign of Great Britain. We do not forget__
it is too sad a fact ever to be forgotten—that the natural
and general good understanding of the two peoples is
now sadly and seriously interrupted. But we remember
also—and none of us who remember anything can fail
to remember this—that the kinship of 'England and
America is deeper than the interests of cotton, broader
than the conflicts of parties, and longer, thank God, than
the life of slavery. One in origin, one in language, one
in religious thought and action, one in the traditions of
the past and the hopes of the future, one in rioneership
in all thett is highest and noblest in modern civilisation,
in all that enlarges the comfort and liberty of man
as man, in all that elevates the social status and
protects the individuality of woman, and in all that
illuArates and advances the principle and practice
of self-government—these two nations and peoples
cannot long or widely be- separated in sympathy or in
action. But I recognise, also, personal. reasons for
American respect and honour for the Royal Family of
England. We should be false to our boast as the most
watlaaat people pf tk-wtnrld did we faiLalways to see and
to say; that whiletaueerk Victoria has occupied the most
conspicuous position before the world of any person of
her sex, she has also and always illustrated and honoured
every virtue of womankind—being at the same time the
most august of sovereigns and the most womanly of
women! Nor does our cause for honour here rest alone
on a sentiment. When the history of the politics of the
two countries for the last two years shall be written, it
will embrace a fact commanding the gratitude of every
American and the pride of every Englishman. I refer
to the circumstance that the despatch in which the
British ministry, in obedience to the popular feeling,
and as they thought to the national honour, pro-
posed to demand redress from the American Govern-
ment in the now famous and once alarming
affair of the Trent, was softened in its somewhat
curt and harsh tone by order of the Queen,
acting under the advice of her always wise and now
lamented husband, the late Prince Albert. Thus, it was
made easier for the American pride to yield, as it did
yield, to the demand, and rescue the world from a war
between its two most conspicuous and most intimately
associated nations, which, as it would have represented
no great principle, would have produced only disaster
Ind ruin to civilisation. England has many things for.
which ever to thank that modest and accomplished
personage, the late Prince Consort, but among them all
there is nothing so great, and noble, and useful as this.
And here at least America will ever vie with her in
doing h9nour to his name and family. Thus justifying
the sentiment as. no cold formality, we propose with
iordialgbod-will to herself, her family, her people, and
e!i.pecia'lly to you her loyal and right royal subjects here
present, 'The Health of Victoria, Queen of Great
Britain and Ireland.'

The speech and sentiment were received with much
enthusiasm, and the Queen's health drank with all the
honours. After this,
Rev. Dr. Leitch, President of the University of
Queen's College, at Kingston' Canada, rose and pro-
posed the health of President Lincoln. In the course
of his speech he said: It was not for him to anticipate
the issue of the present struggle between the two sec-
tions of that country. But this he would say, that he
had faith enough in the race to which th 3 Americans
belonged in the progress of humanity, and in
the Christian faith, to believe, that though they
might have to pass through a baptism of blood, they
would yet assert their place among the nations of the
world, and fulfil the high mission assigned to them by
Providence in advancing the best interests of humanity.
The Americans were taught to regard John Bull as a
disagreeable, surly, jealous, old gentleman, and the
English to look on Jonathan as a forward, pretentious
upstart. But meeting daily round that board, and
pacing the decks together, they discovered that their
American cousins were wonderfully like themselves,
and that national peculiarities formed but slight differ-
ences compared to the substantial sameness of character.
He would always remember with pleasure the delight-
ful intercourse with American citizens in sailing with
these ships. If Old John more frequently sailed with
Young Jonathan under the genial influence of Captain
Moodie, most of the present misunderstanding and
irritation would be removed.
Mr. Lincoln's health was then drunk with loud
cheering,

The toast of the occasion next followed from Captain
Kennedy, of the British navy, who, with a fervent prayer
for the long continuance of the life and reign of the
mother and for an equally honourable and successful
career for the son sovereign, proposed The health
of Albert Edward, Prince of Wales.'

The singing of God Save the Queen' by the whole
company concluded the exercises, which were through-
out of the most pleasant and gratifying character. So
far as it was an exchange of good feeling between
English and Americans it was a drop of oil upon a
troubled sea, but even such small contributions to inter-
national peace and good will may not be wholly without
usefulness. •

A mail steam packet communication has been esta-
blished between St. Thomas, in the West Indies, and
New York by four different routes, viz., via Havana,
Bermuda, Jamaica, and Colon. The communication is
six times monthly.

BOAT ACCIDENT AND Loss OF THREE LIVES.—
Three men have been drowned under melancholy cir-
cumstances at Blyth. With two other pilots they had
left the harbour in pursuit of their vocation on Friday
evening, and meeting with the Sancho, a vessel on the
eve of coming into the port, but which was nevertheless
sailing at a rapid rate, they at once put themselves in a
position to render the necessary- service. In the pro-
cess, however, the boat, by coming in contact with the
'quarter' of the ship, was unhappily upset, with the
whole of its crew. By the efforts of the men on board
the Sancho two of the poor fellows were rescued, but
the remaining three, whom no help could reach, perished
in the waves. Up to Sunday only one of the missing
bodies had been recovered.
THE CENTRAL RELIEF FUND.—A communication has
been received from Colonel Lang, of Batheaston, near
Bath, relative to an effort which is being made in his
parish towards the relief of distress in Lancashire. At
a meeting of the inhabitants of Batheaston the view was
strongly entertained that for some time to come there
should be assured monthly contributions from every
parish, in order that the central committee may be under
no apprehension of their funds falling short before the
period of distress is over. It was resolved that collections
should be made in the Batheaston parish church by the
weekly offertory, and also that the residents be asked to
contribute a certain sum monthly for the next four months.
By'these means upwards of £34 monthly will be collected,
and sent for the next four months to the c latral committe9.
Colonel Lang suggests that other parishes maybe disposed
to carry out the same simple, and, if generally adopted,
effectual method for raising funds.
A LAND'MONITOR. —Mr. Redstone, of Indianopolis,
offers to build for the Federal Government Land
Monitors,' or engines of war to weigh I,Boolbs. each,
25-horse engine and all, with coal, water, ammunition,
knives, &c.; each to be handled by two men; to dis-
charge from each 10,000 shots in half an hour ; to be
capable of running 20 miles an hour over any grade
less than 45 degrees, to be perfectly manageable in
turning, climbing, or descending; to clear more ob-
structions from artillery roads than 500 men; to reap
the rebels clear by divisions; to resist canister, grape,
and small shot. The inventor (Mr. Redeone) says, I
propose to engineer the advance car myself.' •

MELANCHOLY AND FATAL ACCIDENT AT ALDERLEY
EDGE.—On Thursday last a shocking and fatal occur-
rence took place at one of the mines belonging to the
Alderley Edge Company. At about one o'clock on that
day, James Mitchell, Esq., the chairman of the company,
was inspecting the mines with the cAptain, and whilst
stepping on to a ladder to go down a shaft at the ex-
treme end of the mine, missed his footing, and fell a
distance of forty feet on to a rock. Every assistance
was at once rendered to raise with ropes the unfortunate
gentleman, who was found to be living, but he expired
in a few minutes after he was brought up into the open
air. The general meeting of shareholders, called for
two o'clock on the same day, was adjourned in conse-
quence of the melancholy occurrence.—Manchester Ex-
aminer. -

The Hon. and Rev. W. J. Brodrick, canon of Wells
and chaplain in ordinary to her Majesty, has been ap -
pointed to the deanery of Exeter.
FATAL ENCOUNTER BETWEEN SICILIAN. SAILORS.—
CORK, Saturday.—This morning two Sicilian sailors,
from one of the foreign vessels lying in Passage, fought
a duel with long knives in a field adjacent to the town.
In a short time one was stabbed to the heart, and his
euccessful enemy fell on the ground covered with
wounds. The survivor is in custody, but another sailor,

The Austrian who sold the superfine chamois bags
at the Great Exhibition has netted a profit of £10,000!
A young lady ran away, last Tuesday, from her
school at Brighton with the music-master. She has
£5;000 of her own.-
A French paper represents the Chancellor of the Ex-
chequer as having delivered his well-known speech at
Newgate instead of Newcastle!
Engineers have been engaged in taking soundings at
Bray Head, with a view, it is stated, to the formation
of a harbour at that point. The charts and plans have
been in a great measure completed.
. Large quantities of a Canadian weed called asclepias
have been forwarded from Ottawa, in Canada, to Eng-
land, in ot der to have its qualities tested as a substitute
for cotton.
A fine old tapestry, reprecenting, in a suite of six
pieces, the story of the Roman hero Decius, has been
• recovered at Kilkenny Castle, and the Marchioness
of Ormond has made arrangements to have it pre-
served.
It is sajd that the pet name of the Princess Alexandra
among the Royal Family of England is Our Pearl,' a
term of endearment which the youthful lady, destined
for so high a mission, has earned by her many lovable
traits, and by her affectionate and amiable disposition.
It may, perhaps, in some degree, relieve the public
mind to learn that the total number of forged Bank of
England notes, printed on the genuine paper abstracted
from Messrs. Portal and Company's mills, still in circu-
lation is but seventy, and that in all probability these
will be traced in the course of a few weeks.
It is said that Miss CuShman recommended Mr.
Sothern to try his fortune on the metropolitan boards,
at the same time strongly urged him not to bind him-
self to any manager for more than three months. She
felt persuaded that he would make a great ' hit ' in Lord
Dundreary, and the result vindicates the soundness of
her judgment.
It is reported that the Sultan is about to make his
debut as a manufacturer, his Royal Highness having made
arrangements for establishing a paper manufactory at
Mogador, under the superintendence of an Englishman.
A meeting has been held in Tooley-street, Borough,
of the watermen, lightermen, and fellowship porters,
employed on the river Thames, and the most rigid reso-
lutions carried for lynching those garotters who attack
their fraternity.
The desire of all classes of the Greek people for Prince
Alfred as King continues to be universally expressed,
not only in the letters from that country, but among the
Greek merchants settled here. It is mentioned that
nearly every letter from Greece contains a request for a
photograph of the Prince.

AbOut-seventy individuals have been arrested by the
police of Constantinople for circulating false reports as
to the health of the Sultan. As a sharp look-out is
being kept for bAblers on this subject, critics of his Ma-
jesty's condition have to be guarded in their remarks.
A crowd of curious Parisians assembled the other
day at the Church of St. Elizabeth, in ,Rue du Temple,
to witness the marriage of a young French lady with a
handsome and fascinating young Chinese, with a
beautiful pigtail, the admiration and envy of all the
ladies!

The City authorities intend to introduce stringent
laws with regard to driving carts and heavily- laden
vehicles, the unloading of goods, &c., during the hours
of the great traffic of the day. It is hoped by this
means to unlock the dead-lock which occurs daily, and
it is certainly time something was done.
Considering that the Exhibition traffic is now entirely
ended, the railway receipts for the 'week ending Saturday
last were very satisfactory, sine() compared with the
same week of last year they show an increase of about
3a per cent., while the increase in the mileage daring
the twelve months has been not quite 31 per cent.
An important addition to the business institations, of
Cornwall has just been made by the opening of a Mining
Exchange at Cainborne.
A meeting was held on Wednesday at the board-room
of the Horticultural Society, for the purpose of pre.ent-
ing to Dr. Lindley an address from the colonial commis-
sioners, expressing their -thanks for the very valuable
services rendered by him during the course of the Ex-
hibition as superintendent of the colonial section.
•It is reported, though we heartily trust it is not the
case, that Redpolh, the model forger of a few years
since, has acquitted himself so well of his prison duties
that he is already at liberty, and in possession of the
money which he had acquired by crime, and which so
clever a fellow would not fail to dispose of safely before
his conviction. •
A female, tidily dressed, passes herself off at Arbroath
as the suffering widow of a Lancashire cotton-§pinuer.
The lady' appeals to the public in tears, and, taking an
apparently gold ring from off her finger, declares that
she parts with the last token of her happier clays, in order
to avoid starvation. In one case 7s. 6d. was obtained
from a gentleman. How much more she may have re-
ceived 'frcnn other benevolent persons we have not
learned. The rings, in value, did not exceed id. per
dozen.

New York papers received by the last mail contain •
an account of the trial trip of the Paissae turret battery,
built on the plan of the Monitor, carrying two guns in
her turret, one of 11 in. and the other of 15 in. bore, the
latter being the largest piece of ordnance that has yet
been mounted on board any vessel, The following are
the dimensions of the Paissae' s monster gun :—Maximurr
diameter, 48 in.; minimum ditto (rough), 38 in. ;
minimum ditto (finished). 261 ; bore, 15 in. Th
length:of the gun is 13 ft. iin. ; the weight of roue.
casting 68,000 lb. ; of the finished gun 42,000 lb.;
the solid shot 460 lb.; and of the shell 330 lb. T1';:
speed attained by the Puissae on her trial was only fiv
knots.

A curious fact transpired recently before the Court of
Exchequer. The proprietor of a theatre, at Boxton,
quarrelled with Mr. Wilde, the lessee of Leotard, thE;
trapezist,' as to a commission due to him. It came
out in evidence that Mr. Wilde paid Leotard £2OO per
week for his services at the Alhambra, and £2O a-night
for performances anywhere else. In other words, a
French acrobat receives a salary greater than the income
of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and three times that
of the Premier, for jumping from one rope to another
at the risk of his neck. There are, probably, not three
professional men in England who rna4e the sum earned
by a tumbler.
MISSING VESSELS.—AII the vessels that belong to or
sailed from this port previous to the late gales, and con-
cerning which fears were entertained, have now been
heard from, with the exception of three. The Maria,
Cormick, of this port, which left Sunderland With coals
for Dundee on the 16th nit.; the Venture, of Stone-
haven, Captain Lees, which left Wick with herrings
for Dantzic on the llth ult., and the Stemster, of this
port, which left Stettin on the 4th ult., are htill to be
accounted for.—John 0' Groat J:ournal.

before Queen Elizabeth, 1141558, tells her, 'lt may plelle
your Greco to understand that witches and sorcer.ers •
within the four last years, are marvellou-ly incretue(:.
within your Grace's realm. Your subj cts pine away
even to death—their colour fadeth, their speech is
benumbed, their tenses are bereft; I pray God they nover
practise farther than upon the subj, ct.' John Bell,
minister of the Gospel at Glaidsmuir, s.tys, 'Providently
two tests appeared to discover the crime: if the witch cries
out, "Lord have mercy upon me 1" when apprehended;
and the inability of shedding tears: because as a witch
could only shed three tears, and those with her left eye,
her stock was quickly exhausted; and that was the more
striking, as King James First shrewdly observes, "since
other women in general are like the crocodile, ready to
weep upon every slight occasion."
A new scientific discovery has been talked of this
week. It is a cheap method of manufacturing oxygen,
which will supply this material in an impure form, at a
if gold were as cheap as cork or glass, it
cost not greater than that of the ordinary coal gas. It is
, often said that,
would be used for even a greater number of scientific and
domestic purposes
than they are. A stream of oxygen
will produce, without time or trouble, all the effect,
brought about by the bellows in raising a fire to intenst.
heat. With a jet of the pure gas we may produce it.
any fire, and almost instantaneously, a heat in which an
iron bar may be burned like a bit of lath. As a substi-
tute for bellows, then, the gas, if cheap, might be of
great value, The brilliant light now so extensively
used for the magic-lantern, and which throws upon a
sheet or white wall the brilliant dissolving views which
have become a leading feature at London entertain-
ments, is produced by the use of oxygen. It is as difficult
to look with the naked eye at the light as to stare at
the sun in a clear summer day. The chief objection to
the use of this flame, as a means of illumination, has
been the great expense of the oxygen used in its pro-
auction. This, it is said, will no longer prove a difficulty.
The new process is immediately to be introduced at the
Polytechnic Institution, where there is an immense
consumption of gas for the magio_lanternS and dis-
solving views. The new material is impure.
less useful but, it is
said, not to an extent which will render it
than the pure gas for the purposes for which it is used
in the arts.
An influential meeting of the conservators of the Exe
was holden in Exeter on Friday, when it was deter-
mined to apply the act for the preservation of salmon
fisheries to that river, with the belief that it would,
before long, become again a salmon river.
Cochin China has scarcely been taken possession of
by the French, when it is traversed by electric lines.
One is at work regularly from Segon to Ton-Beon, and
another to Tran-bou. Letters state that as soon as the
dry season sets in, other lines are to be established be-
tween the principal towns.

AG.RICULTUBAL .PROSPECTS.

After a sharp white frost, the first day of the week was
fine and bright, with the wind frem the north-west.
Monday was also favourable after another slight frost.,
'with-the wind from the north-east.

The farmers had a good opportunity of progressing
with every descrip,ion of field-work. In Scotland, where
wheat sowing has been so very backward, °wino. to the
unfavourable state of the weather for finishing their
harvest, a-fair extent of work has been done. Fiirther
south we anticipate hearing that the farmers will have
well nigh finished their autumnal tillage at last in, very
good order;with prime seed corn for those who looked
out for the choicest qualities. We fancy More nursery'
*ill have been planted than in any previous year, while
generally, a greater quantity of red has been committed.
to the ground, and this soon will show itself this season.
Tuesday was a cohi day, after the third white frost,
and with a falling barometer • a change appeared to be
approaching'; the night was threatening—more with the
promise of snow than anything else. The weather thus
far this Week has been most favourable for thrashing
wheat, but .the farmers are not anxious to bring this to
market whilst trade is so far from encouraging, and
the deliveries have consequently fallen off. Prices no
worse, the improved condition causing the millers to
take more freely. From Lincolnshire- it has been re-
marked. The weather since our last has been cold and
frosty, with a few falls of snow and hail.'
Wednesday was raw and cold—wind N.N.W. ; but
there was no frost on the previous night, and slight rain
-during the day. Barometer down to 29.45 deg.; and
this was general thioughout the country.
On Thursday the atmosphere was thick and dense,
and son e rain fell for about an hour or two from 8 to 10
adn. Wind round to the W. and S.W.
The farmers are now pushing barley to market freely;
.and there was this week a great increase on the delivery.
Still fine malting samples have taken a turn upwards, as
the maltsters, who are determined to have this descrip-
tion, find there are more competitors for it than' for the
intermediate qualities. Some fancy as that sort com-
mands a good and remunerative price, it will be thrashed
in preference to any other, and will consequently be
<cleared out first; and that after Christmas there will not
be so much choice.

On Friday there had been. a slight return of frost;
but the wind being from the S.W., it did not appear
likely to continue ; and Saturday was a dull thick day.
Barometer rather higher—up to 29.60 deg. Wind N.E.
The sharp frosts at various periods of this month.have
done much good to the lands, pulverising it, and render-
ing it fit for anything; and when there is frost of im-
portance in November, it is often not so severe in
December. In the north of Europe the weather has
been very sharp, and many ports in the Baltic have
been closed by ice, which will at least stOp such large
importations thence, and give a turn in favour of agri-
cultural prospects.—Nov. 29.

amination before the Lord Mayor at the Guildhall,
when an immense number attended to hear the case.
,The prisoner was to-day defended by Mr. H. Breary.
! The witness Ann Clancy was recalled, and in addition to her former evidence about Mrs. Cooke (the
.prisoner) offering to give her a if she would put some-
;thing in the our bin in the proseenfOr's house, she
now.deposed that she remembered that the prisoner had
at the time the conversation referred to took place
asked her to go out and fetch some packets of rat
powder, observing also that if she could get shut' of
the old gentleman, Mr. Edwin (her husband) •Cvould
soon die of grief: She also added that they were a bad
family. Soen after this the witness -was discharged
from Mrs. Cooke's service.

Mr. Cooke, sen., was also called, and, after deposing
to some unimportant facts, he was cross-examined rela-
tive to .some domestic pecuniary matters. From this
evidence it would seem that the prisoner possessed some
money, the whole, or most part of which, had been in-
vested in the purchase of the prisoner's husband's busi-
ness in Coney-street. Money matters, therefore, it
seems has partaken largely in the family differences of
tie Cookes. He also stated that in consequence of the
former attempts to poison he had, for the sake of
precaution, ordered the servants to procure the flour
in small quantities of a dealer in the neighbourhood,
thus preventing the possibillity of too large a quan-
tity. of poisoned flour being made at once. The re-
mainder of the witnesses twelve in number, were then
,called, from whose evidence it appeared the prisoner,
on a recent visit to her father-in-law's house, was left
alone with the servant, when she took the opportunity
to ask several questions relative to the fastenings of
the back and office doors, between which places the flour
bin is said to have been placed. Mr. William Procter,
M.D., of York, had received a quantity of flour, bread,
and mince pies, which had been taken possession ot by
the police immediately after the last poisoning took place.
He subjected those articles to chemical analysis. In the
bread loaf he detected a very inconsiderable quantity of
arsenic; in the flour, however, there was a very large
quantity of that poison very unequally diffused, just as
the appearances would be presented if a person had placed
a quantity of arsenic in it, and then the portions of flour
had been aken out from time to time. In the mince pie
he discovered 223- grains of pure arsenic; and from the
piece of mince pie he obtained about 12 grains. He con-
sidered that between three and four grams were a fatal
dose. He had attended the family when they were ill,
and he was of opinion that they were all suffering from
poisoning by some mineral poison. The result of the
'case was not known.

Nice suffered considerably during the late storm in the
Mediterranean, but fortunately its finest promenade sus-
tained no injury.. _ _ _

The inauguration of the Boulevard Prince Eugene
promises to offer a day of fete to the Parisians, who
crowd daily to the Place du Trone to witness the archi-
tectural preparations, which are on a scale of great
magnitude. Curiosity seems much excited, and the
promenade of visitors during the day is somewhat re-
markable at this season of the year.
ALLEGED EXTENSIVE BANK FRAUDS. —One of our
Joint-stock banks is likely to figure in a court of law
as plaintiff in an action for the recovery of a sum of
money under a bond of guarantee for the fidelity of one
of its clerks accused of fraud and forgery to a large
amount. The surety tinder that bond—a private gentle-
man and a relative of the accused—is advised and re-
solved to defend the action, not being satisfied, after a
long and careful investigation, of the guilt of his re-
lative, who had been in the service of the bank for 14
years or longer, and left his employment with a first-rate
testimonial. The claim on his sureties was not made
till twenty months after he had resigned his appoint-
ment. •
A MONTGOLFIER BALLOON.—The new Montgolfier
balloon, invented by M. Godard, the aeronaut, has a
capacity of 4,300 metres. The car is provided with an
apparatus which enables the aeronaut to ascend without
either gas or ballast, and to descend or go higher up at
plessure. This apparatus consists of a kind of stove
formed by three c}linders separated from each other by
insulating substances, whereby all danger of fire is
averted. The flame is completely under the control of
the aerial traveller, and is prevented from rising too
high by a cap of wire-gauze, M. Godard asserts that
he can inflate his balloon in thirty minutes, and load it
with from 600 to 800 kilogrammes over and above the
weight of his person and his accessories; and, moreover,
that his balloon may be pierced with a bomb-shell with-
out endangering the aeronaut, who can himself cast
projectiles of any kind with impunity. Should this new
invention succeed, the balloon may be of considerable
service in time of war. —G all gnani.

articles.title: IMPERIALIST ATROCITIES IN
articles.text:
IMPERIALIST ATROCITIES IN

The Gazette of the 3rd contains a number of commu•
nications relating to China. In a circular da'ed
Sept. 2, Mr. Bruce informi British consuls in China that
in no case in which treaty rights are violated is force to
be resorted to, unless the security of British life or pro-
perty is threatened. A firm and temperate representa-
lion is to be made to the local authorities, and then a
full report of the case is to be sent to the British Minis-
ter at Pekin. The desirable object to be attained is that
of forcing the local officials to observe the treaty, and
protect her Majesty's subjects in the exercise of their
privileges, through the pressure brought to bear upon
them by the Pekin Government, and thus to escape from
the false position in which we have hitherto been
placed, of coercing the local authorities and pzople, and
thus doing the work of the Imperial Government. The
Government must be made to feel that the responsibility
of the acts of its officers falls. upon it. a a a

Earl Russell has signified his approval of this circular.
In a dispatch, dated June 16, Mr. Hammond directs
the attention of Consul Harvey at Ningpo to a state
went made in this country that the Taepings authorities
at Ningpo have established a regu:ar custom-house
there, and published a customs tariff. Mr. Harvey
reports, under date Sept. 10
I apprehend that the question relates solely to a
foreign custom-house, and to a foreign tariff, in which
case, I have the honour to inform you in reply, that no
foreign custom-house was ever established by the Taep-
lugs at this port, no. foreign customs was ever prosnul-
gated by them, add that, in short, Ningpo, was a free
port for foreign ships and cargoes from the 9th day of
December, 1861 (when the city- was captured by the
Taepings), until the return of the loreign customs
inspectorate, shortly after the expulsion a the rebels
from their occupation of this town.'
He goes on to state that a kind of Chinese office,'
which he elsewhere calls a pseudo-customs establish-
ment,' had been opened by the Taepings, and that
foreign merchants carry on there a trade which he de-
nounces as shameful :

Foreign guns and muskets, pistols and powder with
ammunition of every description, are likewise in great
demand by the Taepings; and these, it is painfully no-
torious, they contrived to obtain from the disreputable
foreigners here and at Shanghae (these anns &c., being
paid for by the rebels, at enormous rates, litth money,
silk, and other valuable produce) forcibly wrenched and
plundered from the murdered and oppressed inhabitants
of the interior), notwithstanding all the strenuois
efforts of Sir James Hope and the British author-
ities in these parts to check and put a stop to this
neferious and disgraceful traffic. • It is not to be won-
dered at, therefore, that those foreign merchants in
China, who are still engaged in these lucrative but
shameful dealings with the rebels, should lament over
the lesson given, in May last, to the Taepings at Ningpo,
and that the agents or constituents o'f these merchants,.
out of China, should join in those lamentations and
view with particular distaste any coercive action lamentations,
against their profi.table rebel clients. These foreiga
traders sagaciously conclude that it is not every year
that a Taeping horde will be permitted to occupy one of
our treaty ports, and consequently, that the easy terms
and exceptionally gainful days of Ningpo, under rebel
rule (without Imperial authorities, custom-house, or
tariff) are not likely to return and flourish once more
very quickly.
He imputes the complaints of the merchants against
the British functionaries who have acted against the
Taepiiags to the loss of large profits. He also deplores
the incredible bias' towards Taepingdom and its tenets
of a few others of a far different stamp and character,
and then in a strain of vivacity not common in official
reports, but which runs through his dispatch, he says
And because that secret leaning is suppressed and un-
avowed, let it not be supposed that it does not fully exist
in their inmost hearts, patiently waiting for its open
avowal and more patent vitality, when the times and
circumstances may seem less generally averse to the
Taepings and their cause. Let us earnestly hope, for the
honour of Christianity, that those times and circum-
stances may never be seen.
The last series of Chinese despatches relates to the
account, by an eye-witness, of atrocities perpetrated on
Taeping prisoners by the Imperialists at Shanghae. This
account, characterised by Earl Russell as so horrible as
to be almost incredible, originally appeared in the Over-
land Times of India, and attention was called to it at the
time by this and other journals. Earl Russell asks
Consuls Medhurst and Harvey to report immediately
whether there is any foundation for it. Consul Harvey
writes :

The statement from the Overland Times of India is
the first intimation I have received of these atrociles.
It seems to me very strange that, living so near Shang-
hae, I should not, before now, have heard of them, con-
sidering that at the period of their alleged occurrence
there were two newspapers published in Shanghae.
He states that great humanity, moderation and sober-
ness marked the recaptures of Ningpo, Chinhai, and
Yuyaou.

articles.title: GAROTTE ADVENTURES.
articles.text:
GAROTTE ADVENTURES.

Permit me,' writes to the Times, a Mr. Redl, music
teacher and late bandmaster of the R. G. Y. Hussars,
to describe an encounter I had some time ago with
street robbers, to show the necessity of having more of
the police force in private clothes, also for the purpose
of putting persons on their guard who happen to be out
after dark, and not to neglect to provide themselves with
the means of defence, as it is almost absurd to expect a
policeman in uniform to be near at the time of attack,
as, of course, he is watched out of the way, as in the
case I refer to. Two powerful ruffians came behind me;
the one nearest, armed with a life preserver in his right
• hand, and his left arm raised partly to conceal his face,
bored upon me, the other fellow close behind him. I
repeatedly, in a loud voice, warned them off, demanding
what they wanted of me, I walking backwards some 30
yards; neither of them would answer. The fellow
nearest me was on the point of rushing on me, but I
was too quick for him and severely wounded him, when,
to my surprise, he called out, Oh, 'my God! police,
police !" and staggered away. His calling "police" pre-
vented my doing so. I made the best of my way home,
and stated the particulars at Scotland-yard next morn-
ing, also at the police-statiol near the locality. This is
not the only time' I have been attacked (my profes-
sional duties occasion my being often out late), and I
owe my safety only to having a tolerable knowledge of
the sword exercise, self-defence, and always keeping a
good look out.'
Another successful defeat of garotters is described in
the following letter On Friday last I had occasion to
be out rather late on business in the neighbourhood of
Orme-square, Bayswater-road. On returning to ray
residence about ten o'clock, •and when about 100 yards
from the square, a suspicious-looking fellow, dressed in
an Inverness cape and wide-awake hat, wearing dark
moustachios, and having the appearance of an Italian,
passedme ; on doing sohe looked full in my face. Notliking
his appearance, I turned round and saw that he was looking
after me. I passed hurriedly on, and in a few seconds I saw
that he was following me, though at a distance. In a second
or two more I looked round again, and found that he
was close upon me. He mast have run stealthily, as I
did not hear his footsteps. When I saw that he was
making towards me I stopped, as if hesitating whether
I should proceed or not, when he passed me, and then
returned, and asked me in r gruff manner what time it
was. I looked at him, put my hand on my revolver,
which is now my constant companion, and another on
my watch, and answered, I cannot see, but perhaps
you can (pulling out watch and revolver at the same
time) ; you seem a sharp fellow, and possibly by the flash
of this article you may be assisted." I need scarcely add
he was off in a jiffy. I followed some distance„ but he
was lost in one of the turnings of the locality. Nothing
like being prepared for such " roughs." '

•
SAVE Us PROM OUR FRIENDSe—A ridiculous story,
apropos of garotters, is now being told in London. A
very timid man, resident in the suburbs, always carries
a loaded stick, and is constantly on the look-out. The
other night, as he was walking home near his house a
man push& rudely against him. The timid gentleman,
presence of mind, immediately struck him a
with
gtererbelaow with the loaded stick, and the man ran off,
leaving his hat behind him. The timid man, greatly
elated, picked up the hat, and read on the lining the
name of one of his intimate friends. Dreadfully shocked,
he at once hastened to his friend's house to explain
matters. •He was received at the door by his friend's
wife, who, in a voice inarticulate with sobs, said, Oh,
I'm so glad to see you! oor Edward !—in bed up-
stairs !—covered with blood !—he's been garotted !'—
Express.

_
TEMPERANCE IN THE ARMY.—The temperance cause
is progressing rapidly in the army. At Woolwich, since
the Garrison Temperance Society was formed last year
519 non-commissioned officers and men have signed the
pledge; and at Warley Barracks, within little more than
a year, upwards of 700 have become teetotallers. A
missionary of the National Temperance League, who has
laboured upwards of five years amongst the military is
of opinion that in the portion of the army with which he
has lately come in contact 16 per cent. of the soldiers are
teetotallers. When 3,000 men recently embarked at
Woolwich and Gravesend for India the National Temper-
ance League presented a packet of temperance publica-
tions to each man; and the commandant-general, Sir
Richard Dacres, issued an order expressing his high
gratification that every man was forthcoming at the
time, and that not a drunken man was to be seen—
quite a new feature in the embarkation of soldiers for
foreign service.

articles.title: HURRICANES IN 2IIE GULF 01 A LYONS. FRENCH AUDIENCE IfISSING M MARIO.
articles.text:
THE HURRICANES IN 2IIE GULF 01 A
LYONS. FRENCH AUDIENCE IfISSING M
MARIO.

Letters from Marseilles and Toulon are filled with
accounts of the disasters caused by the second huiricane
which burst over the Gulf of Lyons. The storm was
experienced at Marseilles on Tuesday morning, and its
first effect was to level a new house which had been
raised to the fourth story, and two men who were sleep-
ing in an adjoining house were buried in the ruins. The
firemen immediately repaired to the spot, but after
incessant labour for two hours they extricated only two
dead bodies. Several :other houses were thrown down
during the day. The disasters at sea were still more
serious. The coast was covered with wreck, and six
merchantmen were totally lost in the port of Frioul.
Two of these vessels were Spanish, from the Havannah,
laden with sugar. Fortunately all the crews were saved.
There was a ship of war in the Frioul at the time, but she
was unable to afford any assistance. The same hurri-
cane caused more serious injury in the port of Cette.
The Fortuna, a fine three-masted Norwegian laden
• with salt and wine' whiCh sailed the preceding day,
attempted to return during the storm, having five feet
of water in her hold; the violence of the waves, how-
ever, prevented the helmsman from steering, and she
was knocked to pieces under Fort St. Pierre in less
than ten minutes. Four only out of her crew of 15
were saved. Among the drowned are the captain and
his son, and the ton of the owner. Two seamen of
the port of Cette, who exerted themselves to save the
crew, are dangerously wounded. At the same time a
French brig, the Dieuville, was lost with all her crew
on the jetty of Frontignan, under the Pilotes. The
sea made a breach in the railway from Cette to Fron-
i tignan 300 yards n length. The train from Cette to
Montpellier ran off the rails, which were loosened by
the force of tho waves, and fell over on its side, but
fortunately none of the passengers were injured. A
locomotive was sent to their assistance, and conveyed
them back to Cette.

Further accounts have also been received from Toulon
of the hurricane which prevailed there during four days.
Ships continued to fly before the storm to take shelter
at the islands of the Ilyeres, or to enter the roads of
Toulon. The violence of the wind was so great that
it drove the waves over the high cliffs on which the
batteries of Cape Brun are built—a fact never before
observed. A number of fishing and pleasure boats,
which had been drawn up 90 feet above high-water
mark, were swept away and dashed to pieces against
the rocks. All the rivulets in the neighbourhood
of Toulon had overflowed and covered the bridges. The
isthmus of the Sablettas, which connects the peninsula
of St. Madrier with the mainland, was covered with
water to the depth of three feet, and a boat might float
on a place where the waves never reached during any
previous storm. The French brig Jenne Therese, frem
Genoa to Marseilles, laden with •.wheat and bears was
lost on the morning of the 24th at the islands of the
Hyeres. Several newly built houses continued to fall
at Marseilles in consequence of the violence of the
storm. Since the preceding accounts three had fallen
on the Boulevard Vauban, and six at the Villa Paradis.
Twenty men were employed at the Frioul in collecting
the wreck of the six merchantmen lost there. At every
moment casks and articles of merchandise ,were being
thrown on the coast.

Galignans thus describes the disgraceful scene at the
Grand Opera, Paris, on Monday night
The great event looked forward to for. the last few
weeks—tile reappearance of Mario—came off on
Monday night, and we regret to have to state that the
engagement from which so much pleasure was anti-
cipated came prematurely to a conclusion the same
night. After several changes and delays, arising from
accidental circumstances, Meyerbeer's Tfuguenots was
finally selected for his first appearance, and this
capacious theatre was crowded to its uttermost extremity
to witness the return of the favourite tenor to the scene
of his earliest triumphs, nearly every seat in the salle
having been engaged for weeks in advance. Oa his
entracein the character of Raoul, there was evidently
a mischievous intention abroad, for the s +lutation of his
friends was met with cries of "Silence I" Mario wasin
fair voice, and the first act passed off tolerably well,
though the hostile manifestations of a party among the
spectators were always apparent. This unusual treat-
ment evidently disconcerted the artiste very much, and
soon began to act upon his voice. Upon the first sign
of weakness the opposition showed their &termination
to put him down without reserve. Every point in the
play, every expression that gave the least opening for
ridicule, was seized on without mercy, and received
with laughter. , and boisterous interruptions. It is
scarcely necessary to say that this unhandsome proceed-
ing was met by the majority of the audience by decided
efforts to put it down' but these well-intended endea-
vours only increased the tumult and confusion, and as
is always the case a persevering and noisy minority were
enabled to triumph over twenty times their number.
The result was that M. Mario at once cancelled his
engagement by an amicable arrangement with the
director, who in common-with many of his friends,
wished him a remain and try at least by another essiy
to test the real feeling of the public at large towards
him, instead of thus giving way to the opposition of an
evidently small minority.'
M. Mario, however, is re-engaged at the Italiens,
and will appear at that theatre, on Sunday night, in
II Barbiere de Siviglia, with Mdlle. Patti as Rosina.

articles.title: MEXICO.
articles.text:
MEXICO.

As the Mexican news which has been received re-
cently has flowed through French channels, it is inte-
resting to read a letter from a correspondent of the
Times, dated from the city of Mexico, October the 27th.
lie writes :

Contrary to the expectations of every one, Comonfort
has accepted the invitation sent him by Juarez. He is
now within a few leagues of the city, and is said to be
accompanied by 4,000 men. What part he intends to
play at the approaching crisis nobody seems able to
divine. His presence in the city will, at all events,
afford us some little guarantee; he is a man arespecta-
bility, and not likely to s)nction any very extreme mea-
sures. Doblado sticks to his government of Guanaxuato,
and does not seem at all disposed to come to the rescue
of his quon.dam friends.

Ross, a Liberal General, who has for some time past
been committing the most unheard-of atrocities in the
neighbourhood of Tepic, is expected with his corps,
numbering some 600 men, in the course of a few days;
so that what with him, Cuella, Buitron, Caravajal, and
a few others of that stamp, we shall have a nice set in
the capital. What will take place when all is uproar
and confusion, and these men are about to retreat to
the interior, none can predicate, but the very worst is to
be apprehended. -
_ _

Yesierday the Government are said to have received
intelligence that the French are in full march. General
Bazin, with 6,000 men, is reported to be at Las Vogas,
about seven leagues on this side of Jalapa, and General
lorencez with the forces from Orizaba, at Tehuacan.
Should this news prove correct, we may very shortly
hear of Puebla being attacked. The French are said to
number about 25,000 men, and they are accompanied by
Marquez, who is at the head of 4,000 reactionary troops.
If a stand. is made in Puebla, I believe that little or no
resistance will be offered here. That city once in the
possession of the French, the Government will lose no
time in making its way to the interior. We know for
certain that Ortega has abandoned the positions he had
taken up on this side of the Cumbres and retreated on
Puebla. This would seem to corroborate the statement
that the French are on the march. We may, therefore,
expect to welcome them in the city of Mexico in about a
month from the present time. The forces at the disposal
of the Government cannot possibly exceed 25,000 men,
and these are in a sad state of disorganisation. We have
heard of the safe arrival of the expelled Frenchmen at
Guanaxuato, where they are to await the further orders
of the Government.

The Admiralty have published a large blue book con-
taining the detailed accounts of the cost of the various
articles produced in the workshops of her Majesty's
dockyards and steam-factories. This is the first time
such accounts have been printed for the information or
the public.
PRESIDENT JETFERSON DATis.---"-The Richmond. corre-
spondent of the Times has sent a second letter which was
published Dec. 1. In alluding to the Southern President
he makes the following remarks In a former letter
from the North I expressed the opinion that Mr. Davis
was the ablest living American; that impression is more
than confirmed byintereourse with him. The President
is one of those calm, firm, undemonstrative men, inclining
to reticence, but if interested, easily led on to animated
conversation, who belong to a type which, strange to say,
seems to abound in the South, and is at variance with
the imputed impulsiveness of these children of the sun.
In many interviews with Northern men of mark it has
never been my fortune to encounter one whose mind
was not made in the same mould with that of his fellows,
who had not travelled along the same macadamised road
of learning along which, though pursuing it to different
lengths, the 20,000,000 of the North undeviatingly
advance. An interview with President Davis reveals to
you an American with striking originality, whose mind
has made its own road as it journeyed, who has thought-
fully profited by his own experiences, and got beyond
the set phrases and the primers which circumscribe
vigour and reach of thought. Each word is slow,
weighty, and luminous, the countenance and voice
agreeable and convincing, the mouth one of the firmest
that ever were set in mortal head. The President looks
spare and worn, but speaks cheerfully of his health.
There is nothing to justify the repeated allegations of
Northern papers, that he is physically at his last gasp.'
RECEIn WILLS.—The will of Miss Sarah Clay, of
Great Warley, Essex, who died on the 11th ult., was
proved in London under £45,000 personalty. There
are several devises and legacies to her relatives, friends,
and also to her servants, and the following charitable
bequests :—..C1,000 to the Religious Tract Society,
£l,OOO to the British and Foreign Bible Society, £l,OOO
to the Church Missionary Society, and £5OO to the
London City Mission; also, £l,OOO towards the en-
dowment of Christ Church, Warley Common, together
with the gift of land adjoining the parsonage.—The
will of Sir Martin Hyde Crawley Boevey,Bart., of
Flexley Abbey, Gloucestershire, was proved in Lon-
don by two of the executors—namely, Lady Crawley-
Boevey, the relict, and Sir Thomas Hyde Crawley-
Boevey, Bart., the son; power to prove hereafter being
reserved to the other executors, the Rev. John Daubeny
and the Rev. Thomas May. The testator, who was
highly connected both by descent and marriage, in-
herited considerable landed property, and by the will
of his father had the power to charge the estate of
Flaxley for the benefit of his widow and younger
children, which he has done to the extent of 500
a-year for his relict for her life with a like annuity to
her from his own estate, and £4,000 for his two
daughters. To his relict he also directs very liberal
annuities, to be paid during the minority of his
younger sons, of which there are six surviving, and to
each is left a legacy on attaining the age of twenty-
one. His eldest son, the present baronet, is in hie
twenty-fifth year, to whom the testator has bequeathed
his hunters, and whom he has appointed residuary
legatee of his real and personal estate. The deceased
Baronet died at the age of fifty, and executed his will
only the week before his death.
F. M. Sir E. BLAKENEY.—The United Service
Gazette states that the officers who have served on the
personal staff of Field Marshal Sir Edward Blakeney
have subscribed to present him with a miniature model
in gold of the baton which is the insignia of the rank of
field marshal. The miniature baton is expected to be
ready in about ihreeweeks, when it will be presented to
Sir Edward at Chelsea Hospital, together with it short
address illuminated on vellum, and signed by the officers
who are included in the prcsentation.

articles.title: BOARD OF TRADE RETURNS.
articles.text:
BOARD OF TRADE RETURNS.

he Board of Trade returns for the past month have
been issued, and show a satisfactory condition of the
general export business of the country with the excep-
tion of that in cotton yarn and manufactures, the ship-
ments of which have amounted to little more than half
their total for the corresponding month of last year.
The aggregate value of our exports show a falling off of
£1,838,075, or 15f per cent., from October, 1861, and
more than the whole of this deficiency is repre-
sented by the diminution in the cotton trade, which
has been £1,874,972. The linen, silk, and woollen
trades all show continued activity. Last month
there was a singular falling off under the head
of ‘unenumerated articles,' and the same feature
is observable on the present occasion, although
not to the same extent. Possibly it may have
been consequent on the International Exhibition having
caused an increased home demand for miscellaneous
articles, which has temporarily reduced the supply of
such articles available for exportation. The following
table exhibits the exports of the month in detail, and
the increase or decrease in each case. It is to be re-
marked that he month of October last year, notwith-
standing the progress of the American war, was
characterised by large commercial transactions, and that
even the cotton shipments at that period were of fully
their usual magnitude, so that the present figures are
intrinsically less unfavourable than they would at first
sight appear. Contrasted with the same month of 1860,
they show a falling off only 121 per cent.
The total exports of the first ten months of the year
have been £103,519,269, against £105,480,242 in the
corresponding months of 1861, showing a decrease of
only £1,960,973, or less than 1 per cent. The changes
have been as ibllows

Compared with the corresponding ten months of 1860
a decrease is shown of L 9,437,258, so that our aggregate
trade this year has been but about 81 per cent. below
that of the most inflated year on record.
With regard to imported produce, the chief feature is
that the arrivals of wheat and flour have slightly ex-
ceeded the unprecedented totals of last month, and were
nearly three times as great as in the month of October,
1861.

Arr AMUSING IIisTARE.—A gentleman of Douai was
going out, in his carriage to make some calls with his
wife, when he discovered that he had left his visiting
cards. He ordered his footman, recently come into his
service, to go to the mantelpiece in the sitting-room and
bring the cards he should see there. The servant did as
he was ordered, retained the articles to be used as he was
directed, and off started the gentleman, sending in the
footman with cards whenever the not at home' oc-
curred. As these were very numerous, he turned to the
servant with the.que,stion, How many cards have you
left?' Well, sir,' says the footman, very innocently,
there's the king of spades, the six of hearts, and the
ace of clubs " The deuce 1' exclaimed his master.
That's gone,' said John.

BALLOON ASCENT AT COMPIEGNE.—A letter from
Compiegne says The stag hunt which was to have
taken place in the forest of Compiegne on Saturday was
countermanded in the morning, owing to the frost, the
ground having become dangerous both for riders and
horses. In consequence of that disappointment, a
message was sent to M. Godard to prepare for an ascent
in his balloon, and it being market-day a crowd speedily
assembled before the palace to witness it. The
Emperor, the Empress, and the Prince Imperial were
present at the filling of the balloon, which was effected
on a plan peculiar to M. Godard, who makes use of a
boiler placed below the balloon, and which he takes up
with him, so that he can at will modify the aseensional
po ger. After remaining in the air for about three-
quarters of an hour, in which time he went over a
distance of about 15 miles, he descended at Marival, a
hamlet about six miles from Villers Cotterets.'

STRANDING OF A WHALE.—The Beluga, one of the
monsters of the deep, was left on the beach by the
ebbing tide, on Saturday, at Robin Hood's Bay. It is
supposed to have been dead ten or twelve days. It
measured in length 17 feet,. and 12 feet 10 inches in
circumference at the thickest part. The blubber was
taken off by the fishermen the following morning. The
Beluga, or white whale, is a native of the high
northern latitudes, and is one of the most beautiful and
active of its rue. Its colour is pure milk white,
sometimes tinged with a rose colour, or a slight wash
of yellow, and the skin is very soft, smooth, and
slippery. The flesh of this animal is eaten by the
Greenlanders and other people of the Arctic regions.
It is as red as beef, and of somewhat similar flavour.
The female produces one or two at a birth, towards
which she displays the strongest attachment.
FATAL ACCIDENT.—John Dawson, mule spinner,
aged 29, employed in Scar Mill, near Huddersfield,
was on Monday afternoon, while passing through the
room immediately below that in which he worked,
called by a piecer to assist him in repairing the side
chain of his machine, which had broken. He at once
went towards the piecing machine in question, and
in proceeding to take hold of the broken chains that
the other might link them, he threw his arm around
the tin mains of an upright revolving shaft which stood
within two inches of the machine, at the end where
the deceased was standing. The next moment he was
pulled off his feet and taken round by the shaft, the
tin case also going round with him at the rate of 108
revolutions a minute. He knocked down the person in
charge of the machine, and was dashed with great
rapidity against the adjacent fixtures, and soon re-
duced to a mass oi horrible mutilation, owing to the
narrowness of the space he was dragged through. The
engine was stopped immediately, and the unfortunate
man was released, but expired four hours afterwards.
THE BREADALBANE TITLE AND ESTATES.—The fol-
hr.ving caveat has been lodged with the sheriff-clerk of
Perthshire relative to the title and estates of the late
Marquis of Breadalbane Should a petition be pre-
sented by John Alexander Gavin Campbell, Esq., of
Glenfalloch, or by any other party,. praying to be
served nearest and lawful heir of tail= and provision,
or in any other character, to the Most Noble the
Marquis of Breadalbane, who died on or about the Bth
day of November current, the subscriber claims to be
heard on behalf of Lieut. Donald Campbell, late of the
37th Regiment, residing in Port Glasgow, the nearest
lawful heir to the title and estates of Breadalbane.—
ALEXANDER WILSON, solicitor, Perth.—Perth, Nov.
26th, 1862. Lodged Nov. 26th, 1862.' •
It is proposed to contribute the £BO,OOO balance of the
Indian Famine Relief Fund, now lying at Calcutta
doing nothing, to the relief of the English famine in
Lancashire. The presence of this sum rather checks
generosity in India, and would be a welcome addition to
our resources. There are certain other funds' such as
the India Mutinyohe Patriotic, and the Tinzes'Crimean
Funds, of which a balance remains in hand, and which,
it is said, should be devoted to the same purpose. With
less wisdom, one of the chief committees proposes to
oink £40..000 in the Three per Cents.

gittrarg Stitrtium.

Pittsburg is the Merthyr-Tydvil of Pennsylvania; or,
perhaps, I should better describe it as an amalgamation
of Swansea, Merthyr-Tydvil, and South Shields. It is,
. without exception' the blackest place which I ever saw.
The three English towns which I have named are very
dirty, but all their combined soot and grease, earl dingi-
ness do not equal that of Pittsburg. As regards scenery,
it is beautifully situated. . . I was never more in
love with smoke and dirt than when I stood here (on a
hill outside the city) and watched the dari.ness of night
close in upon the floating soot which hovered on he
housetops of the city. I cannot say that I saw thJ sun
set, for there was no sun. I should say that the sun never
shone at Pittsburg—as foreigners who visit London in
November declare that the sun never shines there.
Everything in the hotel was black; not black to the eye
—for the eye teaches itself to discriminate colours' ev(n
when loaded with dirt—but black to the touch. On
coming out of a tub of water my foot took an impress
from the carpet exactly as it would have done had I trod
barefooted on a path laid with soot. I thought that I
was turning negro upwards, till I put my wet hand upon
the carpet, and found that the result was the same; and
yet the carpet was green to the eye—a dull, dingy green,
but still green. You shouldn't damp your feet,' a man
said to me, to whom I mentioned the catastrophe.
Certainly, Pittsburg is the dirtiest place I ever saw, but
it, is, as I said before, very picturesque in its dirt, when
looked at from above.—Trollope's North America.
STEPHENSON'S DOG.—George still found time to
attend to his favourite animals while working at the
Water-row Pit. Like his father, he used to tempt the
robin red-breasts to hop and fly about him at the engine
fire, by the bait of bread-crumbs saved from his dinner.
But his favourite animal was his dog—so saBacious that
he performed the office of a servant, in almost daily
carrying his dinner to him at the pit. The tin contain-
ing the meal was suspended from the dog's neck, and,
thus laden he proudly walked the road from Jelly's
Close to Water-row Pit, quite through the village of
Newburn. He turned neither to left nor right nor
minded for the time the barking of curs at his heel. But
his course was not unattended with perils. One day
the big strange dog of a passing butcher espied the en 7
gineman's messenger' ran after him, and fell upon him
with the tin can about his neck. There was a terrible
tussle and worrying between 'the dogs, which lasted for
a brief while, and, shortly after, the dog's master,
anxious for his dinner, saw his faithful servant approach-
ing, bleeding, but triumphant. The tin can was still
round his neck, but the dinner had escaped in the
struggle. Though George went without his dinner that
day, when the: circumstances of the combat were related
to him by the villagers who had seen it, he was prouder
of his dog than ever.—Lives of the Engineers. By
Samug smiles.

NEGRO SONGS.—A Philadelphia lady has been endea-
vouring to give a specimen of the songs in vogue among
the negroes about Port Royal, but says it is difficult to
express the entire character of these negro ballads by
mere musical notes and signs. The odd turns made in
the throat, and the curious rythmic effect produced by
single voices chiming in at different irregular intervals,
seem almost as impossible to place on score as the sing-
ing of birds or the tones ef an Alolien harp. The airs,
however, can be reached. They are too decided not to
be easily understood, aid their striking originality would
catch the air of any masician. Besides this, they are
valuable as an expression of the character and life of
the race which is playing such a conspicuous part in
history. A complaint might be made against the songs
on the score of monotomy. It is true there is a great
deal of repetition of the music,but that is to accommodate
the leader, who, if km be a good one, is always an im-
provisator. For instance, on one occasion the name of
each of this lady's party was dexterously introduced. As
the same songs are sung at every sort of work, of course
the tempo is not always alike. On the water the oars
dip Poor Rosy' ,to an even andante; a stout boy and
girl at the hominy mill will make the same Poor Rosy'
fly, to keep up with the whirling stone; and in the even-
ing, after the day's work is done Heab'n shall abe my
home' peals up slowly and mournfully from the distant
quarters. One w oman—a respectable house servant,
who had lost all but one of her twenty-two children—
said to the lady, I likes "Poor Rosy" better dun all
de songs, but it can't be sung widout a full heart and a
troubled sperrit !" Perhaps,' added the lady, the
grandest singing we heard was at the Baptist Church on
St. Helen's Island, when a congregation of 300 men and
women joined in a hymn—
" Roll, Jordan, roll, Jordan!
"Roll, Jordan, roll ! "
It swelled forth like a triumphant anthem. That same
hymn was sung by thousands of negroes on the 4th of
July last, when they marched in procession under the
Stars and Stripes. A friend writing from there says that
the chorus was indescribably grand—" that the whole
woods and world seemed joining in that rolling sound."'
A DEvou'r WORIMAN.—A shipwright, at work upon
the timber platform, stepping from the permanent to
the temporary work,. set his foot upon a loose plank,
which canted over. Accidentally, however, a huge nail
had been driven—no one knew why—into the end of a
cross-bearer on which the temporary platform rested;
and this nail-head catching the leg of the man's futian
trowsers near the lower end, where he fell, held him
suspended. head downwards, swinging to and fro,
gazing at the river a hundred feet beneath him. The
man's comrades ran to his assistance, and, placing a
ladder from the lower bridge, they with difficulty
rescued him from his perilous position. Being a devout
Methodist, the shipwright attributed his preservation to
the direct interposition of Providence in his behalf. In
the course of about a week, however, a tailor's adver-
tisement appeared in the local papers, containing a letter
from the rescued workman, in which he gave the sole
credit to the trowsers by which he had been suspended.
On another tailor publishing his claim to the merit of
having made them, a controversy between the tailors en-
sued, which may possibly remain unsettled to this day.
—Lives of Engineers. By Samuel Smiles.

Horse:wedain,rs were formerly much in vogue in
Wales, and, about ten years ago, the practice was carried
on at Devynnock, in Breeonshire, when the well-
mounted bride was pursued by pretty nigh all the parish,
in the vain attempt to steal her away, somewhat after
the fashion of the Tartar tribes. Of course she was
caught only by her own intended, to whom she yielded
a willing captive, and it *q to be hoped that man and
wife lived a happy life together. Did they not do so,
the episode of the cefyl pren' became an unpleasant
feature in their married career. Perhaps the misde-
meanour was of a class which, in high life, would have
involved the calling in the aid of Sir Cresswell to solve
the difficulty; or perhaps it was only a simple case of
scevitia upon the part of the lady, who, in the attempt to
prove the grey mare was the better horse, had
dared to lay hands on her lord. In either case,
an effigy of the principal offender was paraded about to
the accompaniment of cleavers, whistles, and other
hideous noises, and finally halted at the house of the
guilty parties, when it was pelted, ducked, or otherwise
maltreated. Indeed, in gross cases, a sort of lynch-law
was inflicted on the persons of the unfortunates, who,
however, frequently deemed it most prudent to abscond
before the vox populi made itself heard.—Once a Week.
_

„
If men may dare to idolize any sublunary thing,
it is a sinless and smiling child. 'Suffer,' says Jesus
Christ, 'little children to come unto me, and forbid
them not, for of such is , kingdom of heaven.' The
author of these beautiful words was once an infant him-
self, and oh, ineffable glory! the pure light that encircled
the child, still shone around the man! It is a touching,
and I hope not an irreverent reflection, that he whose man-
hood, surpassed all human conceptions—he whom men
believe to have been the Deity himself—did not, in his
earlier years, exhibit to earthly eyes more innocence and
beauty than are easily conceivable in a human child.
Could we but preserve our first purity with the pro-
gress of our intellectual powers, we should in deed be
little lower than the angels. The description of our first
parents in Paradise is like a radiant vision, but I cannot
help regarding it, beautial as it is, as in some degree
deficient in one great source of poetical and human
interest, when I remember that they knew not the
charms of childhood, but came abruptly, I had almost
said unnaturally, into mature existence, unaccompanied
by thoFe earlier associations which like the shadows in
the golden light of evening, grow more and more lovely
as our day declines, and reflect their lingering hues
upon our latest path. Methinks that even Paradise
itself would have looked more divine, had little human
cherubim flitted gaily over the green velvet slopes, and
passed from flower to flower, their light laughs breaking
like celestial music on the air, and their golden locks
glittering in the sun.—Essay on Children, by D. L.
Richardson.

THE TURF SCANDAL.—The court of inquiry upon the
officers of the Grenadier Guards implicated in the turf
scandals has made its report, but it is neither as clear in
its conclusions or in any way as satisfactory as could be
wished. Virtually, it leaves the whole decision of the
fate of Colonel Burnaby in. the hands of his Royal High-
ness the Field-Marshal Commanding-in-Chief; and upon
the charge of sharping at Mamhead a kind of question-
able verdict is pronounced, leaving matters in much the
same state as the stewards of the Jockey Club left the
Tarragona affair at Newmarket This can scarcely be
considered satisfactory to Colonel Burnaby or the regi•
ment whose honour is more or less mixed up with his
name. We hope that the Duke of Cambridge will act
not only with justice but with fearless firmness in the
matter, and take care of the fair fame of the service.—
Army and Navy Gazette.

articles.title: VISIT TO THE CITY FLOUR .111 ILLS
articles.text:
VISIT TO THE CITY FLOUR .111 ILLS

(From the Baker's Free Press.)
Of the many thousand passengers by the river
iteamboats plying daily between London and West-
ninster bridges there is scarcely one who has not
30me time or other been attracted by an enormous
block of building standing almost midway between
St. Paul's wharf and. Blackfriar's-bridge. For some
time our curiosity has been excited as to the internal

economy of these monster millsl, and having con-
sulted another member of the literary craft, in
course of time we obtained permission from
the proprietors to visit the establishment.
Arriving with some friends at the mills,
we were received most courteously by
.the pro-
prietors, the Messrs. Hadley, and, without losing
any time, the first step in our proceedings was to
put on a special coat and hat which is lent to every
visitor who purposes going over the establishment.
The first significant source of work is on the ground
floor, an apartment about 70 feet by 50, in which
are two engMes of 250 horse power each, which may
be considered the motive power for the varied.
operations whieh are seen throughout the build-
ing. Everything here is in first rate condition,
and being the primary power given to milling
attracted some time of our inspection. There are
high and low power cylinders. The low pressure iss 6,
feet stroke, 4 feet 6 inches in diameter; high,
pressure, 6 feet stroke, 30 inches in diameter.

The next apartment contained the boilers, of

which, if we recollect correctly, there are seven,
each 30 feet long, and 7 feet 6 inches in diameter,
worked at a pressure of 35 pounds, having patent•
fire bars, and an apparatus for consuming their own
smoke. Moreover, there is a double set of furnaco.
bars, one up and one down. A portion of the
brickwork at the west side of the mill, just above
the creek, indicates the work there must have been
to get in one of these boilers recently. Adjacent
Ito this there is accommodation for 700 or 800 tons
of coals, a considerable convenience if one takes into
account that Old Father Thames does sometimes
experience the disadvantages of a very severe
'black' frost. There is little chance of a supply of
water being deficient,, there being three feed pumps
for the engine- room provided by the river. The
contingency of fire is provided for so far as the
building is concerned, everything being of iron,
stone, or brick. We were informed that the
proprietors have duplicates of most of the appliance;
and also that the new fire bars were first introduced
by them, and, government having sent to in-
spect them, appreciated their value and utility,
ordered them extensively for some of the large
yards, &e. Having ascended a stone staircase we
arrived at the first floor, and went into the room
where all the meal is ground, which is thence, by
machinery, carried up higher for other processes.'
It may be remarked here that nothing is touched by
hand from the time the wheat is put in until it is
turned out flour: In this department there are 32
pairs of stones in ordinary work, and, one
of our party, who has an inkling of science, in-
timated, that one pair of these stones was equal'
to any three of the ordinary stones. The stones
of the City flour mills grind at the rate of
twelve bushels an hour: The driving riggers
for the stones .are of a very, fine construction.
In the next compartment -on this floor may be found
the beauty of the engines in their construction, for,
if an accident were to occur in one half the building
the process of. grinding could still be carried on in
the other. Sixteen driving riggers could be worked
in No. 2 mom on this floor if the sixteen in No. 1
room were affected. Proceeding on our way again
we ascended to No. 3 floor. Amongst other opera-
tions carried on here the stones are dressed.
Eight pairs of stones are taken up every morning
to be dressed, and put down every night. The con-
trivance for slinging the stones is of a very effective
character. The cold air blast may be experienced
here by any person who has a desire for being
cooled. It occurred to us as we placed our hands at
the bottom of the blast that it would be a fine thing
to operate upon gentlemen who might be subject
to ungovernable fits of passion and rage. There
are also on this floor and the one above two
pastry rooms, where the flour is placed after
it has been dressed, capable of holding 7,000
sacks of flour. We also observed here the first
part of the process for unbranning wheat. This
is done by the firm on an American principle.'
They have worked it for some time now, and have,
after the most careful calculation, arrived at the
conclusion that by this invention there is an in-
crease of upwards of 10 per cent. upon the quantity
of wheat converted into flour for the purpose of
bread over any other process known. Passing by
the screening room; the sack room, and the work-
shop, we arrived at the 4th floor, where may be
seen another portion of the American machine at
work. There is no doubt that the best means are
adopted here for thoroughly cleansing and purify-
ing the wheat. This appeared to us to be a locality
that, taken altogether, would be very attractive to
the inquisitorial devotee of science and mechanism.
There are four machines for separating the bran,
pollard, and offal. Our party now proceeded to No.
5 floor, where the first thing that attracted our
attention were the enormons shoots to take the
flour into the pastry rooms down stairs. Here also
may be seen the wheat when unbranned. The
stive ' room is also here. There are also seve-
ral Mins, each being :the purveyor to one pair of
stones. We were much attracted towards the scrub-
bing machines: These are composed of large hollow
cylinders, moved round by steam, with brushes
inside working a contrary way, the cylinders being
made of iron ribs, about three inches apart, and the
intermediate spaces being made of wire gauze.

Proceeding on our. way we arrived at No. 6 floor,
which is almost exclusively devoted to the dressing of
flour. There are altogether 32 silks, each one being
about 45 feet long, encased. Passing No. 7 floor,
from which one of the finest views of St. Paul's can
be had, we at last reached the summit of the
magnificent establishment, No. 8 floor. Here, by
means of a double action tackle, the sacks are raised
from the barges up to any floor requisite, and one of
the prettiest sights here is to stand over the trap door
and, looking down into the barge below—you
see a sack tied to the chain, and come up with.
machinery precision through trap doors on each
floor until it arrives at its destination, when, being
wheeled off, it takes .its place in an array of other
sacks to await its turn for undergoing the various
processes we have before referred to for converting
the contents into our 'daily bread.'
What the amount of wheat and flour in sacks
in the City Mills may be it is impossible for us to
say. But when we state that there are eight floors,
each 300 feet long, by 76 feet wide, and that if
the space occupied by the machinery be allowed
for, there is nothing but wheat, wheat flour, flour,
packed close together. We cannot be surprised
that Mr. Tremenheere, of the Home Office, has left
on record that the Messrs. Hadley are the largest
millers in the world.

A REMAIUCABLE LEAP.—On Tuesday week last a
numerous party of ladies and gentlemen assembled at
Hincbinbrook House, the residence of the Right Hon.
the Earl of Sandwich, for the purpose of joining in a
fox-hunt. The sport commenced shortly after ten
o'clock, when two foxes were started, one of which,
after a smart chase, was run down. The other, how-
ever, took 'home,' and reached the wall of Hinchin.-
brook House without being captured. The wall, at
this point, is about ten feet high, apd Reynard, behrg
pressed by the hounds, and sorely puzzled how to make
his escape, took a leap, and actually succeeded
reaching the top of the wall, whence he fell exhaus'
on the other side, having received some severs a...
*les in the performance of this extraordinary feat.
