SATURDAY, DECEHBER 6, 1862.

articles.title: SUMMARY. FOREIGN.
articles.text:
SUMMARY.
FOREIGN.

The Greeks continue firm in their resolution
to elect Prince Alfred as their future King,
but the young gentleman is in demand,
and the authorities of Saxe-Cobourg G-otha
have intimated their determination not to part
with their.heir apparent to the dukedom.
The Italians are delivered from the Ratazzi
Cabinet, and have got in their place a new
government, who are not a ministry of not-
ables; as their leader is unknown to fame;
but the new people may do better than their
predecessors, and nobody seems to know any
evil of them.

The inundations of Italy and the south of
France continue, and have been attended by
very great losses. This extraordinary fall of
rain in the regions named was predicted on
scientific grounds.

Rumours of plots in France, to assassinate
the Emperor, occupy the police, and great
precautions are
.taken against the employment
of infernal machines to-morrow; the day chosen
by the Government for a• ceremonial opening
of some new street in Paris.

The French expedition into
.Mexico expe-
riences the sharp opposition of disease and bad
roads, and has lost many men; but its orders
are onward to Mexico, although the French
Chancellor of the Exchequer dislikes the
threatening prospects of the drafts on the
French treasury.

The French- and Russian papers agree in
considering the proposal to place Prince Alfred
on the Greek throne as "preposterous," and
its success a thing not to be thought of.
The constitutional disagreements in Prussia
between the King and his Commons continue
without any prospect of a solution, and the
Danish and German squabble on Schleswig

Holstein produces new rolls of correspondt,nte,
wherein our Foreign Secretary distingtitieires
himself, but not in a favourable manne.

Intelligence from America is to the 22nd
November. At that date the Confederates and
Federals were drawn together at Fredericks-
burgh, a small town on the south bank of the
river Ra:pahannock—at a point where it seems
to be navigable for small craft. The Federal
programme of the campaign under General
Burnside involves a basis at Acquia Creek,
which is lower on the Potomac, and as the,
river flows to the south east, is nearer to.
Richmond than Washington. Fredericksburgh
is ten miles or thereby south of the Potomac at
this point, and is only sixty miles from Rich-
mond. A battle has probably occurred for the
possession of Fredericksburgh, as the Federal
General Sumner threatened to shell the
town. It is probable, on the other hand,
that the Confederates will allow the
Federals to advance nearer Richmond before
offering a decisive resistance, and just as pro-
bable that the Federals will consider Frederics-
burgh good winter quarters, which they may
fortify as the basis of their operations in the
spring.
No intelligence has been received of any
proceedings in the South, although rumours of
skirmishes are published in the press of New
York.

Gold commands a premium of 30 to 31, and
the strikes for more nominal wages, to be paid
in depreciated paper are still prosecuted.

COLONIAL.

The Queensland colonists have vote d
£lOO,OOO to aid emigration to that colony;
and a number of the Manchester overseers
propose to proceed there. The Queensland
Cotton Company offer to defray the passage of
the men; and from the large sum offered by
the colony we presume that little difficulty
will exist in providing passages for their
families.

The success of some miners in British
Columbia is shown by the fact that a quarter
of a million sterling in gold is now invoiced by
two steamers for this country.

The West India steamer brings among
other freight 250 bales of 'cotton, picked up
among the islands—not a great matter—but a
symptom of a future trade. The papers still
refer to the proceedings of the negroes in St.
Vincent, incited originally, we presume, by
the immigrationof Portuguese labourers, who
are more successful than the negroes; and the
white population sleep, according to one letter,
With revolvers beneath their pillows. The
Jamaica Legislature offer a home to free
negroes from the States.
_

The Indian intelligence is favourable, with
the exception of the appearance of cholera in a
fatal form at Peshawur, the north western city
of the empire. Cotton had &Hen slightly at
Bombay.

articles.title: DOMESTIC.
articles.text:
DOMESTIC.

Cotton and corn are rather dearer. Consols
and money present no change. Six new bank-
ing companies have been projected this week.
With the exception of cottons, the Board of
Trade returns show a- good export trade for
October.

Another ten thousand are added to the
recipients of relief in the cotton districts,
according to the returns for last week. In
London the mortality of the week has been
greater than in any other week for the last
four years. London also suffers from an un-
usual prevalence of robberie3 with violence;
and the precautions taken to prevent them.
One person was accidentally killed while learn,
ing to fence; and another has nearly shot
away his own hand while firing a pieta at an
aggressor in the public street. Are our morals
following our streets into a condition of mud
and barbarism?

The Saturday Review recommends its readers
to take lessons from Jem Mace and Tom King,
with the view of defending themselves. In
this article, contributed by Young Lead, who,
finding no rival in the ring, has gone on the
staff of the Review, the topic is discussed in his
usual masterly style.

LESSONS IN POLITICAL ECONOMY.
THE COTTON TRADE.
SOME time ago we proposed to publish some
papers under the title of lessons on polit-
ical economy, and carried out the intention so
far as to write a few. We got through the
explanation that every person had -some idea
on political economy; that no set were entitled
to usurp the name; and that the persons who
railed at the political economists had their own
opinions on the subject, and were "political
economists" themselves. The term in,!luded,
as was then stated, the science of providing for
the prosperity and wants of a nation, exactly
as the kindred phrase, "domestic economy"
included the means of providing for the main-
tenance and success of a family. Our papers
only illustrated these truths; but we found
then that nearly all our correspondents were
political economists, and that as their contri-
butions were chiefly connected with that
science, our columns would be entirely occupied,
if we inserted their favours and our lessons,
regularly on one subject. We allowed prece-
dence to our friends, and now that they have
completed their statements, we revert to the
subject.
The cotton famine affords materials. It rages
in the land, because too many cotton goods
had been produced and were in stock when
suddenly the supply of material failed, in
consequence of a quarrel among the people
who had been enriched by the trade. The
danger of leaving the nation dependent on one
country for the supply of material and of food
had been enforced during the agitation against
the corn laws. It was the chief argument
employed by the Manchester men in that dis-
cussion; although the danger was confined in
that case, to the risk of climate, and excluded
the risk of hostilities between the consumers
and the producers. It is now: it always was a
good argument; although in our case, it is
greatly neutralised by the extent of our
colonies and possessions, if our dependence
were restricted to them. In the cotton trade,
Lancashire was dependent on a foreign
nation, with whom hostilities might have oc-
curred, but who were producing cotton in a
partly unfavourable climate, subjected to the
probability of floods and frosts; and by slave
labour.. The climatic influences might have
interfered with the crop of a. season; and
the misery now encountered in Lancashire
might have been caused at any time by a ser-
vile war.

The emancipation of the slaves, which all
parties in this country profess to seek, must
at once have added fifty per cent to the price of
cotton, and produced a difficulty in Lancashire, ,
not much less severe than the trial of the pre-
sent year. The risk under which the trade
existed, and as it was said flourished, could not
be concealed from any intelligent person,
and entreaty preceded warning--and warning
re-produced entreaty, addressed to "the
cottonocracy " and to the government by disin-
terested writers, in vain, for more than twenty
years.

Let us remember that no ,a4l,,range or unfore-
seen event has occurred toiie cotton operatiVes.
We hear at public inedtaugs invariably the
same fiction that tans 'calamity originates in
causes that were tentitmly unforeseen; but the
character of the'ass‘ation as a "fiction" is not
in any dregree improved by its frequent repe-
tition. The dilemma was foreseen, although
the -exact manner of its occurrence is unex-
pected. A fbw politicians have stated their
opinion in past times that the American
federation would separate into different parts;
but a separation, accompanied by desolating
and fierce hostilities, was not anticipated,
at least during the present century.
No fact has been more frequently pressed
on the minds of persons interested respecting
it than the dangers, to this country, from the
interruption by any cause of the cotton trade;
and the prudence of adopting measures to ex-
tend the cultivation of the plant in our own
possessions. No fact has been more cruelly or
more obviously disregarded by the capitalists
concerned in the business and by the Govern-
ments. The Manchester manufacturers say
for themselves that their business is to pro-
duce goods, and not to grow material. We
are not at present concerned with this excuse,
although in passing it we remark its " down "
look. It does not seem an honest course for a
man to collect together many operatives
entirely for his own advantage, without
providing for the maintenance and regularity,
as far as that may be possible, of his trade.
Waiving that point for the time as being more
a matter of Commercial than of political
economy, we notice that the "Manchester
School," often described as "the political
economists" also deny the right of the Govern-
ment to interfere in this class of matters.
There is one point where two schools of
"political economy" diverge. We hold that
the Government of a nation is not confined to
the duties of hangman and jailor in its internal
arrangements; that it is not only to be a terror
to evil doers, but "a praise to that which is
good." The Government is we consider bound
to provide by every possible means for the
secular prosperity of the nation and their well-
being. On this principle the Factory Act, the
Navigation bills, the Bleachers bill, the mea-
sures relating to mimes and all sanatory
statutes—to the police enactments regarding
municipalities—are justified, anditheir propriety
could not be maintained on any other ground;
but the "political economists" resisted all these
reforms, with the exception of the muncipal
acts, proceeding consistently with their views.
According to them the commercial duty of an
Executive Government is to enforce contracts;
and the duty of aLegislativeAssembly is to con-
fer on the Executive the powers essential to this
restricted position. According to this theory
the executive Government, as they had not
the power, certainly had not the right to take
any precaution against a cotton famine or any
other famine, but in distress are reduced to
the dreary duty of helpless watchers by the
way to the tomb. They may knock a garrotter
on the head, when he does evil, but they can-
not provide him with employment if he be
inclined to do right. They may imprison a
child for stealing a turnip, or a pennyworth
of wood—as, was one on their authority a few
days ago—but they can do nothing. to train
up a negleteted child to industry; Such is the
theory._ We'rej ect it as inhumane,and therefore,

wrong.

No rule is without an exception, and
accordingly some of the political economists
have recently made an exception of India,
justifying this departure from their principles
in the fact that the Government is in reality
the original landlord of India, or its owner, and
is bound to discharge the duties appertaining
to property while it receives the rents, forming
the chief part of its revenue. Property has its
duties, as it has its rights, they say, and invite
the Government to make .roads and improve
rivers in India. They are right, according to
our general principles, and by their own special
case on the Indian question and we put it
aside at present. although, While referring to
cotton, it is difficul to thrust India out of the
way.

he Government of this country, according
to our political economy, should have foreseen
and provided against this cotton calamity in
self-defence, and in the interest of the people
committed to their charge. The interest of
the money sunk in our cotton business ; in
buildings, plant, and ships: with the profits
commonly derived, and the wages earned in

the trade, may average a half million sterling,
weekly, or twenty six millions in each year.
Mr. COBDEN calculates the mere wages lost in
1862, or being now lost monthly in the course
of 1862, at the rate of seven millions sterling for
each year; but that is a poor representation
of the loss to the nation; for each shilling
brought into the country circulates almost
beyond the power of reckoning, and operatives
who earn little can pay little; if they are
badly employed, they cannot be good em-
ployers.

- this great interest involving twenty-six
millions annually of profit or wages, might
have, and should have .occupied the attention
of the Government, not at the moment of suf-
fering, but to prevent suffering. Successive
Governments knew that twelve years ago fair
common cotton was offered at Natal for two-
pence per lb., if any company or individual
would secure a regular cash market. They also
knew twenty years ago that cotton might be
freely grown in Queensland, for the experi-
ment had been tried, and a country as large as
England, fertile and well watered, was open to
our often suffering people, where from the
salubrity of the climate they could cultivate
cotton and other tropical produce. The
Govenment knew the broad distinction between
the character of our fellow countrymen in Upper
Canada, and the population in the Western
States: they knew that the Canadians allowed to
to the fugitive negroes from the South a fair
field for their industry: permitting them every
right of citizenship and equality: and the Home
Government might have known that a negro
population of nearly "forty thousand" had
been collected in Upper Canada, but might have
been more advantageously employed in growing
cotton in Jamaica, and our other islands of the
West. Our Goverment knew that Guiana con-

tains capable waste land sufficient to grow more
cotton than all Europe requires; and only
needs men to cultivate the idle soil, and money
to pay them. They knew that Western Africa
is at their disposal, and that the millions paid
annually to watch slave dealers, would have,
been more efficiently expended in encouraging
the cultivation of cotton in that district, as the
slave trade exists only because men are cheap.
All these circumstances were better known
to the Government than to any of their sub-
jects, but they were not spurred on by public
opinion. The nation favoured "the do- nothing
and know nothing" system. Year after year
cotton cost more for growing, and yielded less
for spinning, but the Government or the nation
. _

left i-he trade to grapple with the difficulties as
they pleased; and the only grappling was
elicited in grumbling, and in some strikes to
prevent a reduction of wages. The Govern-

ment and the people are now at school. They
-are compulsory scholars; learning a hard
lesson in political economy which involves the
" unlearning " of a bad system. If our political
economy had been followed, the nation must
have felt the consequences of this sad war in
America, but Lancashire would not have been
ruined; its population would not have been
starved by cold and hunger, or demoralised by
idleness and dependence, treated too often as
if it were real pauperism; and the nation
would not have sustained this great loss which
must affect all interests in the three kingdoms.
Political economy is the most important
branch of science connected with time and the
interests of time.

THE BIRMINGHAM DAILY POST AND
THE BEE-HIVE.

The Birmingham Daily Post of last Saturday
has an article on the recent correspondence
respecting the Padiham committee, and the
relief of distress in Lancashire, which appeared
in our columns. The Padiham committee
had sought some assistance from the Birming-
ham committee, and this correspondence arose
out of the application; with which we
are entirely unconnected. The secretary of
the Padiham committee, and the secretary of
the Birmingham committee did not concur in
the course which should be pursued; and while
both parties were allowed to make their state-
ment in our columns, we are not responsible
for the opinions of either of the two. The
Birmingham Daily Post states that two dele-
gates from Padiham visited Birmingham, and
offered to insert in the BEE-HIVE, a "with-
drawal of all offensive imputations," made by
their secretary on his Birmingham correspon-
dent. We shall gladly insert any statement
they may have to make as an advertisement;
but no delegates from any town can undertake
to insert communications in our columns;
except on their general knowledge of our in-
tention to do anything calculated to make
peace among these committees; or any other

persons.
The Birmingham Daily Post apparently en-
tertains some animosity to the BEE-IlivE, as
to any other paper connected with industrial
interests; although as apparently we are not
favoured by the addition of its editor to our
other readers. The Post says :

The BEEHIVE, after many weeks of solicitation on
behalf of the Padiham clique, has only succeeded in
raising from the working classes of Enaland an amount
of some .L5O or go, while the Daily Teleyraph, having
started a subscription about a week ago with the avowed
purpose of transmitting its proceeds to the Central com-
mittee at Manchester for distribution, has already
received, chiefly from working men, a sum of seven or
eight hundred pounds, in addition to the five hundred
with which it headed the list. Does not this show that
general opinion is unmistakeably in favour of the Man-
c'ester Executive, and that isolated bodies, such as the
one at Padiham, obtain, as they probably deserve, but a
trilling amount of public confidence?
The writer must suppose that the BEE-HIVE
has only advocated the transmission of snb-
scriptions through its office to one fund. We
have not limited our advocacy to this isolated
case. At a recent period we noticed the pur-
pose to create one national committee at Man-
chester, and the absorption of all other com-
mittees in this "great central," and we opposed
the plan; believing that the Mansion-house
Committee had been extremely useful, and
commanded the confidence both of the donors
and the recipients, while the Manchester Com-
mittee might be suspected, even, perhaps, most
unjustly suspected, of local favouritism; and
complaints were made by the committees of
other towns near Manchester, and requests
forwarded from them to the Mansion-honsp,,
committee that the ,latter would continue their
labours. We in no other manner indicated a
preference, believing that all the committees
are actuated by a sincere desire to relieve the
present and urgent distress; but we were
requested to receive subscriptions for the East
Lancashire Committee, and we have received
and transmitted the amounts to the rector of
Habergham, who is connected with and resident
at Padiham.

If we had urged our readers to send their
subscriptions through this office in preference
to any other channel, we believe that more of
them would have taken our advice; but we
only referred to the East Lancashire Com-
mittee, as a body who engaged to supplement
ordinary relief; in a quarter where .‘ members
of co-operative and of trade societies" were not
regarded with much favour by some of the
persons engaged in the administration of the
local or the general funds....

Old animo-sities may still rankle in many
minds, for the country contains a great multi-
tude of men, not connected with the Binning-
&int Daily Post, of very narrow minds; but
it is creditable to find comparatively few
examples of these feelings re-appearing in these
days of great trouble; although if we had
not desired to avoid any excuse fbr reviving
past rancours, we could have ' quoted
examples of a discreditable character from the
correspondence of journals, unconnected with
the opinions which we represent. We rejoice
that the proprietors of the Daily Telegraph
were able and willing to give a liberal subscrip-
tion from their own business; but the Daily
Post is mistaken in supposing that they had
collected and transmitted the money stated, in
addition, as it says, to their own subscriptions;
while we had sent, not £5O or £6O merely,
but £llB. The BEE-HIVE has not the circu-
lation claimed by the Daily Telegraph: if we
had, we could promise one, two, or three
thousand pounds to the Lancashire fund;
while we publish, not daily, but weekly, so that
if the Daily Post will multiply £llB by six,
and remember that its "many weeks of solicita-
tion" are only its own imaginings—and no
more substantial or valuable than these things
are in general—it will see that to a local and
supplementary fund the result was not
contemptible.
The business is now left by us to the London
Working Men's Committee, who represent the
different trades, and will distribute the funds,
collected by them in our office, to different
places. They have adopted the means neces-
sary to acquaint themselves with the condition
of the different localities; and our connection
with the fund only involves the subordinate

duty, or labour of receiving and paying over
as the committee may direct,
The Daily Post informs its readers in Bir-
mingham, that the secretary of the Padih am
committee "published in the BEE-HIVE news-
paper (a journal edited by Mr. GEORGE POTTER,
of strike notoriety), a letter "—which the Post

_
describes, and our readers may have seen.
The animus of attacks against Mr. POTTER are
obvious. If a, - man declines to follow

the course marked out by professed Liberal
politicians who manage matters in Birming-
ham and elsewhere, they mark him. The Daily
Post is acquainted with the circumstance that
Mr. POTTER is the publisher, and is not the
editor of this journal. It is not necessary, it
is not usual, and at one time it was

altogether opposed to the usage of the press
to mention an editor by name. He was sup-
posed to be a mysterious personage—nearly
invisible. All the details of our office are,
however, well known ;- and while we concur in

Mr. POTTERS opinions, excepting the misre-
presentations most unjustly ascribed to him,
yet he is not responsible for our views. We
are not fitvourable to strikes, we always regret
them, as every intelligent man must regret all
quarrels, especially between partios who have
common interests; but strikes are calamities,
and not crimes, and each case must be tried on
its own merits. The animosity exhibited
towards Mr. POTTER by such portions of the
press as the Post represents, is discreditable.
Last week, when the Times inserted a brief
report of the proceedings at the meeting for
the formation of the London Working Men's
Committee, it ascribed in the report opinions
to him which be does not hold. The error
might easily have occurred in the haste of
reducing a long address to the limits of a brief
paragraph; but the Times declined, or failed
to insert the correction sent in the following
terms :

Snt,—ln reference to your notice of the Trades'
Delegate Meeting concerning the distress in Lancashire,
while I am not surprised that an error may have fallen
into an abstract of report of its proceedings, be pleatied
to let me express my gratitude to the Mansion-house and
other committees for the efforts they are making for the
alleviating of this distress, and further, to add that my
object in moving for a London Working Men's Cen-
tral Committee was with the hope that the trades may
imitate -the churches, and other sections of society, in
bringing a little supplementary aid to those who surely
stand so much in need of it, and show in addition how
much they appreciate the generous assistance given by
men of all ciasses at this time. G. POTTER. j
. .

The original error might have occurred with-
out a bad intention, but the omission of any
reference to the correction, in a case of this
nature, indicates a determination to misrepre-
sent, and to keep misrepresented, any man who
has the audacitr to oppose the Times; and
against a general imitation of its characteris-
tics we need not to warn the Birmingham
Daily Post, which is, however, quite capable
of following this bad example.

articles.title: MASONS OF EDINBURGH.
articles.text:
THE MASONS OF EDINBURGH.

IN November of 1860 the masons of Edin-
burgh informed their employers that in
March, 1861, they would adopt the nine hours
system instead of the ten hours system pre-
viously pursued; and they accompanied the
intimation with notice that they would accept
a reduction of on-tenth in their earnings, to
compensate for the proposed reduction of time,
until the experiment could have a fair trial.
One half, or thereby, of the employers refused
to adopt the proposal, and in March of 1861
they closed their works. As no good or even
plausible reason could be given for this course, '
they urged their suspicions that the men would
on the establishment of the new system,ask ten
hours' wages for nine hours' work. They
resisted short time, therefore, on suspicion.
To obviate this fear, the men resolved to
accept the reduction of one-tenth in money
as compensation for one tithe of time, for
twelve months. After the adoption and publi-
cation of this resolution, the resisting employers
fell back on the Roman resolution, sic volo sic
jubeo, or a master mason may do what he likes
with his own men and mortar. They were
defeated, as they deserved to be, and the nine
hours system was established. It appeared to
work well; for although the men earned three
shillings per week less than before, yet they
had less broken time, and had received, per-
haps, the same amount by the nine hours as
by the ten hours' scheme before the close of
the year.

In last November a portion of the employers
obeying the injunctions of their secret society,
resolved to reduce the wages payable under the
new agreement,by- a penny per hour, nine-pence
per day, four shillings and sixpence per week.
They did not adopt this course in consequence
of defective employment, for in that city there
is considerable activity in the building trade.
They did not seek the reduction because their
contracts were shifted, or shifting, for they
had been made on the common rate of wages.
They cannot allege any loss by these contracts,
arising from a civil war among the quarriers,
which has enhanced the price and reduced
the supply of stones, and they cannot plead a
famine of timber. They have only selected an
opportunity to obtain revenge sweetened with
profit, by seizing on a moment of deep
distress in other quarters, when they
know that the funds of the trades
societies, and the means of tradesmen,
are strained almost to breaking; and on it
these masters seize, in order to accomplish a
grea:-, wrong. They do not agitate in the
interest of their customers, for they will not
even divide with them, by a reduction from
their contracts, the gains of this greed; if it
be successful greed. As the larger of' the con-
tracts now under completion in Edinburgh are
for national buildings, the public should claim
their share of the spoil, if the employers esta-
blish the reduced scale of wages.
The effort made to save this money
originates no doubt in revenge. The greater
part of the members of the master builder's
secret union of Edinburgh would probably
confess themselves bound by the fifth petition
in the Lords's prayer to forgive all sins com-
mitted against themselves; but these people,
read very literally, and would be sharp enough,
if they were wicked enough, to say that the
petition does not bind them to forgive
men who have done them no wrong.
In that manner the masters in ques-
tion may deceive themselves into the
opinion that they can take their pleasant
revenge righteously. We do not recollect any
proceeding more uncalled for, more unfeeling,
or more likely to excite and maintain that
rancour between different classes which all
men should endeavour to smooth down; but
the Edinburgh trades have their remedy. A
good demand exists among them for the de-
scription of houses hitherto built by their
Company. The experiment has been, we
understand, successful in regard to demand, to
price, and therefore to returns. The capital of
the company may, therefore, now be safely
increased. It has an expansive field, for it will
not soon supply the demand for houses to the
working classes; and it can enter gradually on
other departments of its trade, while no
sympathy would be felt at present by persons
who have given contracts, towards contractors
who, during the currency of their engagements,
endeavour to reduce the data on which these
engagements were founded. Indulgence in
time will not be conceded to speculators who
are not resisting a demand for more money, but
are only engaged in endeavouring to abstract
four shillings and sixpence weekly from every
mason in their employment over and above the
profit which, at the date of the contracts, they
deemed necessary, and were entitled to receive.

THE FORDINGBRIDGE MURDEX.—On Monday last,
as a man named Parker was engaged in removing a
portion of the thatch from the root of the cottage of
George Jacob Gilbert, who was executed a few
months since for the murder in June last of Miss
Mary Ann Susan Hall, of Midgham Farm, near
Fordingbridge, he discovered, hidden in the thatch,
the trinkets worn by the unfortunate young lady on
the day she was $o brutally murdered. These melan-
choly memorials of the murdered girl were taken to
Midgharn Farm by Parker, the finder, who Was libe-
rally rewarded by Mrs. Hall, the step-mother of the
deceased. Her father, Mr. Hall, it will be remem-
bered, died a short time after the perpetration of the
crime.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

THIRD EDITION.-SATURDAY EVENING.

PRINCE ALFRED AND THE GREEK THRONE.

PARIS, THURSDAY EVENING.
Letters from London, says the Paris Patrie, autho-
rise us to believe that the situation of affairs has been
materially modified. The Queen taking into consider-
ation the serious interests which the accession of Prince
Alfred to the throne of Greece would undoubtedly
interfere with, has manifested her intention to decline,
in the name of her son, the succession of King Otho.
It is stated that a sovereign who has, under various
circumstances, given proof of a remarkable spirit of
political prudence, and who is united by ties of rela-
tionship to the English Royal family, has by his dis-
interested counsels in a certain degree led to this
result,

ATHENS, Dec. 1.
The Russian Minister has communicated to M.
Bulgaris the opinion of his Government, that the
principles of the protocol signed by the protecting
Powers in 1830 should be upheld.

articles.title: LANCASHIRE DISTRESS.
articles.text:
THE LANCASHIRE DISTRESS.

The weekly meeting of the Mansion-house Corn-
mitte for the Relief of the Distress in Lancashire took
place ye sterday. The receipts during the week have
been £32,374 58. id. Grants were made to the dis-
tressed distticts to the extent of £14,550. The total'
received by the committee up to Thursday last has
been £251,837 28. 2d.

At the meeting of the collecting committee of the
Central Relief Fund at Manchester, held on Thurs-
day, it was stated that the balance of the fund now in
the bankers' hands was £210,000. Large as this
amount is, it was stated that much more would be re--
quired, as the distress is daily increasing.

articles.title: 11ORRIBLE IiVRDER IN Ba..
articles.text:
11ORRIBLE IiVRDER IN Ba..

HINGHAIII.

Lite on Thursday night an atrocious murder was
committed in Bissel-street, Birmingham. The victim
is a girl named Alice Insley, aged 17, who lived with
her parents and was employed in a jewellery ware-
house, and the murderer is Henry Carter, alias Nobby
Hall, a brass founder:4i He has been keeping company
with deceased, who did not :look upon him with as
much favour as he wished. On Thursday evening
Carter spent the evening with her at the house of
her parents, and when he rose to leave the house the
girl went with him to the end of the entry leading
into the sreet. A woman, who was standing ouside
the entry, heard Carter say .to-the deceased, Do you
mean it, Alice?' and heard her reply, I do.' A_
moment later she heard a pistol shot, and Carter im-
inediately rushed past her into the street. She then
went up the entry, and at that end of it nearest the-
court-yard she found deceaSed lying on the ground
quite dead. It was found that she was shot
through the back, apparently with a pistol bul-
let. About one o'clock on Friday morning,
when a large crowd had collected on the spot
where the murder was committed, Carter walked uj.
hurriedly and was going up the entry, when some one-
cried "flat's him, and police-constable Maconochie
arrested him. At the moment he was arrested priso-
ner was saying 'Where is she ? • I must see her,' and
tried to brake away from the officer and get into the
house where the body was lying, but made no resis-
tance to the apprehension. When charged with hav-
ing murdered the girl he admitted that it was him who
had fired the pistol.
At the Birmingham Police-court yesterday, Carter
was brought up charged with murder, and was-
remanded to await the result of the inquest.

articles.title: TWO MURDERS IN LIVERPOOL.
articles.text:
TWO MURDERS IN LIVERPOOL.

On Thursday morning a shocking murder was per-
petrated in this town, the victim being the wife of a.
tinker named Read, residing at No. 7, Lower Myrtle-
sti eet, off St. Anne-street. From the facts which are •
at present known, it appears that Read, his wife, and.
a son about eleven years of age, resided in the cellar of.
the house in Myrtle-street, and in the morning a.
police-officer WaS informed that a woman had been
stabbed there. The constable at once went to the,
house, where he found the deceased, Ann Read, lying.
on the floor, bleeding from a wound under the left
arm. Medical aid was obtained, and every effort made
to revive the poor woman, but without avail, and she
died immediately after the arrival of the doctors. Read.
and his son have absconded.
The victim of the second murder is
a_l3o. a woman.
Her name was Isabella Tongue, and she cohabited with/
a man named Thomas Edward, a butcher, and sup-
ported himself on the earnings of her prostitution. On
Thursday morning, about four o'clock, while Edwards.,.
the deceased, Jane Wilson, and a man named Thomas
Sullivan, were sitting round the fire in a house in
Norbury-street, Edwards seized a butcher's knife and
rushed at Tongue, whom he stabbed in nineteen places..
He also stabbed Wilson and Sullivan, but not very
seriously. The woman Tongue never rallied, but died
in a few hours. An inquest has been held, and a,
verdict of wilful murder returned against Edwards.

articles.title: TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

THE LONDON BOOKBINDERS.
A serious dispute has broken out in this trade be-
tween Mr. Bone, the binder, of Fieet•street, and his
" 'workmen. Mr. Bone has for some months past been
gradually introducing boys and porters to undertake
the lower branches of the work usually performed by
the skilled workmen, contending for the principle pro-
mulgated by all employers when they desire to reduce
wages, that they have a right to employ whom they
please. These gentlemen have no idea of the give
and take' principles—they only think of the taking'
portion. These repeated innovations of Mr. Bone are
subversive of the rules and customs of the trade, and
the manifest tendency of which was, to effect an
immediate reduction in the wages of the skilled
workmen, has at last reached such a height that
the workmen remonstrated with him upon the subject.
Mr. Bone, however, stated that he should persevere in
the course he was pursuing, and that his was not a
binders' shop' but a binders' factory '—(remember
that, ye who send in your fine work.) The men
(about forty in number) at once gave notice to leave
48 employ. The Bookbinders' eSociety have in con-
equence issued the following notice :
LONEON CONSOLIDATED LODGE OF JOURNEYMAN
BOOKBINDERS.

5, Raquet-court, Fleet-street, E.C.
Stn.,—l am directed by the Committee of the above
society to inform you that there is a dispute now
Pxisting between Mr. Bone, of Fleet-street, and his
Men, and they rely on your good feeling to take such
measures—in the event of an application from him for
men (whether by advertisement or otherwise) in your
locality—as will prevent such application being suc-
cessful. The dispute is occasioned by the unlimited
employment of Boy and Porter Labour on the work sot
the trade, which the men are determined to resist.—l
am yours, most truly,
December sth, 1862. T. J. DUNNING.

THE BLACKBURN COTTON SPINNERS.

The following appeal to the Building Trades of
London, has been forwarded to us by the Black-
burn Operative Cotton Spinners' Association :
Fellow men, can you help us a bit? In prosperous
times the Spinners' Society in the Blackburn District
numbered over 1,100 members; at the present time
there are over 600 members entirely out of employ-
ment, the remainder are working front two to four
days per week, and their average earnings is not more
than 9s. for four days' labour; this is owing to the bad
material they have to work. We are now entering
upon a second winter of severe distress. The rules of
our society guarantee to all payable members when
out of work, the small pittance of 6s. each, as card
money, and to deceased members, the sum of £3, and'
to member's wife, £2. These items, though they ap-
pear very small, have amounted to over £3OO during
the distress. We have a few members leaving off
work almost daily, and an account of cur funds being
quite exhausted—those that should be recipients now
are deprived of those little privileges which others have
received. The reason why we make an appeal to you
is, that all the cotton trade societies are in the deepest
of distress, and we may also state that when any other
trade society has been in difficulties, and made an ap-
peal to us, we have never on any occasion sent them
away empty handed. For instance, we have given
over £3,000 to other trades during the last five years,
which gives us encouragement to hope that our appeal
to you at the present time will not be made in vain.
Any assistance you may please to forward to us will be
thankfully received. We are your humble servants,
the committee of the Spinners Society :—John Holt,
William Lanthworth, Thomas Slater, Patrick Mulling,
Robert Bennett, and George Nightingale; Richard
Greenwood, secretary, 35, Duckworth-street, Whalley
Banks, Blackburn.
Blackburn, Nov. 26, 1862. - - _ - -

,
N.B.—All Post-office orders to be addressed to John
Walsh Walmsley, Britannia Inn, Penny-street, Black-
burn, on behalf of the Spinners' Society.

STIRLING BUILDING TRADES' ASSOCIATION. The
first annual dinner of this association was held in the
Golden Lion Hotel, Stirling, on the afternoon of Fri-

Mr. Thomas Turnbull, mason, croupier. There were
about seventy gentlemen present, including delegates
from Edinburgh, Perth, Dundee, and Alloa. After

articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
GENCE.

EDINBURGH CO-OPERATIVE BUILDIN G COMPAN Y.
On Tuesday night, at a meeting of the Association in
the Masons' Hall, High-street, the usual preliminary-
formula of business was gone through, and the quar-
terly report was submitted to the meeting. The
number of shares disposed of during the quarter was
60, bringing up the total to 1082—the paid up capital
of the society amounting to £1,062, leaving a balancel
due to the company of £2O. The report submitted to
the last meeting showed that the third block of eight
houses would be ready for occupancy by the Martinmas
term. The houses are now completed and disposed of,
with the exception of one dwelling. The fourth and
fifth blocks of buildings are so far completed that they '
will be ready for occupation by Whit-Sunday, 1863
three of which are sold. Mr. David Rintoul, chairman
of the meeting, addressed the members and in the
course of his remarks, said that he deprecated the con-
duct of the working classes in not assisting the move-
ment as they should have done. It waa well known,
he said, that houses in Edinburgh were charged at a
most enormous rental, but he believed that, by com-
bination, the working classes could get cheaper houses,
and that the Edinburgh Co-operative Building Com-
pany was no myth, but calculated to raise the masses
in the social scale. A vote of thanks to the chairman
terminated the proceedings.
HOWDEN AND PERCY MAIN CO- OPEitATIVE SOCIETY.
—The secretary of this society writes --‘ We have just
finished our fifth quarter's accounts, and paid a divi-
dend of 2s. 3d. in the pound, and a resolution was
adopted unanimously at the quarterly meeting to pay
the odd threepence to the Lancashire fund—not as an
act orcharity, but as a slight recognition of the great
debt Of gratitude we, in common with all co-operators
—more especially in the north—owe to the Lancashire
men for the noble way in which the true principle and
Make of co-operation have been developed and made
one of the greatest blessings to the working man; and
,
as ousands of co-operators are now reaping the
benefits of this mighty system I think the present the
most approPriate time to testify in deeds by regularly
8 It portion of their dividends to those poor
fellows who, but a short time ago, were as proud and
as prosperous as ourselves.'
Ma. COBDEN, M.P., ox CO-OPERATION.—At a meeting
-
the following letter was read from Mr. Cobden,
operative Society, held on Tuesday
of the Prestwich Co
evening,
M.P., addressed to the chairman, Mr. Henry Pitman:
—t andhurst, Nov. 28, RA
—2.—Dear Sir,—It is not in
ray power to accept your invitation to be present at
the meeting of the Prestwich Co-operative Society; but
I will not omit the opportunity of assuring you of my
unabated interest in the movement. I am delighted to
hear that the distress in which the industry of the
cotton districts is unhapPilY involved has not yet had
he effect of closing one of the co-operative stores ; and
earnestly hope they may all be enabled to ride out
the storm. But they cannot expect to escape from a
share of tie loss and suffering which must be the
common fate of all classes in Lancashire; and I think
lean perceive the salutary influence of your movement
in the calm and reasonable demeanour of the popula-
tion during this trying season of adversity, which may
be largely attributable to the fact that numbers of the
working-class have, by co-operation, been added to the
ranks of capitalists, and have thus become participators
in both the firmefits an 4 the reverses to which the

possessors of property are liable. This, I have reason
to know, is the view of the largest and most intelligent
capitalists in your district, among whom I believe the
co-operative effort has now scarcely an opponent,
whilst many of them are its warmest friends. Sincerely
wishing that the horizon may soon clear, so that the
sun of prosperity may again shine on your efforts, I
remain, truly yours, RICHARD COBDEN. Henry Pitman,
Esq.' Sympathetic letters had also been received from
Mr. Bright, M.P., the Mayor of Manchester, &c.

articles.title: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

FORESTERS.

BRISTOL.—On Monday the anniversary dinner of
Court Perseverance, No. 1,726, was held at Allen's
Angel Inn, High-street, when a large and respectable
company of brethren sat down to the festive board.
HULL—The Court Friendship,' No. 765, Keying-
ham, Holderness, of the above order, has contributed
the sum of five pounds to the Executive Council, now
assembled at Portsmouth, for the relief of their dis-
tressed brethren, at present suffering great privation
through the want of employment in the cotton dis-
tricts.

ANCIENT 0 ItD ER OF SIIEPH EROS. —Sanctuary 3,143
of the above order, having removed their court house
from the Old Castle Tavern, Castle-street, to the Robin
Hood, St. James's, was opened there for the first time
on Monday last, when several new members were
initiated.

ODD FELLOWS (M. U.)
LONDON.—Ou Monday evening last the members and
friends of the St. Bride's Lodge, South London Dis-
trict, held their anniversary dinner at their lodge
house, the White Hart, corner of Lambeth Hill,
Upper Thames-street, when about forty membcrs and
friends sat down to an excellent repast provided for
them by Host Lowen. The chair was taken by P. G.
A. F. Harris, and the vice-chair by P. G. Marshall,
treasurer of the lodge. After the usual loyal and pa-
triotic toasts had been given, and drank, the Chairman
gave The Manchester Unity, and South London Dis-
trict,' which was duly acknowledged by P. G. Sewell,
who gave an account of the progress of the district
during the year. After drinking success to the St
Bride's Lodge very cordially, P. G. and Sec. Shepherd
gave a short glance at the progress of the lodge, and
informed the company that after paying all demands
for the year they had saved upwards of £5O, and the
total capital of the lodge is over £520. The health of
the oldest member of the lodge, P. G. James Bark-
worth, was then drunk and duly acknowledged by him;
likewise the stewards, the host and hostess, and the
proceedings terminated after having spent a very com-
fortable evening.
NEWCASTLE.—On Monday the members of the Bro-
therly Love Lodge held their annual dinner at the
house of Mr. James Anderson, Half Moon Inn, Mosley-
street, Mr. Shipley, N.G., presiding, and there were
about s.xty members present. Mr. W. Moran proposed
The Newcastle District and the Officers.' Mr. W.
Moffat, in responding, stated that there were now
nearly 1,500 members in the district, that they received
an accession of nearly 100 membersiduring the past year,
and that they had something like £B,OOO invested
capital. (Cheers.) Mr. Dent gave the Brotherly
Love Lodge.' Mr. Moran, the Secretary, responded.
From January to November in the present year the
income of the lodge was £69 4s. 2d. ; the expenditure,
£36 17s. 6d. ; and the number of members is 91.

HuLL.—England's Temperance Lodge, No. 453, of
this flourishing order, held its annual tea meeting at
England's Temperance Hotel, Salthouse-lane, last
Tuesday night, November 25. About 140 ladies and
gentlemen—friends and members of the lodge—sat
down to a splendid tea, provided by the host, Mr. John
England. Among the friends we noticed Mr. Thomas
Westoby, the kind advocate of the temperance cause.
—The Secretary, Brother A. Anholm, briefly stated
the prosperous state of the lodge, and read letters from
Mr. Wade and Mr. Councillor Moseley, which stated
unavoidable engagements prevented them attending,
but he felt sure that ere long the lodge would be
honoured with the presence of these two gentlemen as
honorary members, the latter of whom had enclosed a
donation of £1 Is. We may state that this is the only
,lodge whose business is transacted at a temperance
house, its object being, whilst providing against sick-
ness and death, to keep working men from lodges held
at public-houses.

DISHONEST FRIENDLY SOCIETY'S OFFICER. —At the
Manchester court, on Tuesday last, Giles Sanderson,
secretary and treasurer of an Odd Fellows' Lodge, was
charged with fraud. The case had been adjourned on
a point of law, but the magistrate now ordered the
accused to pay £lO5, or he must go to prison for a
month.

SAVAGE TREATMENT OF A WlFE.—Jchn Boyle, hack-
ney carriage driver, badge 15,112, was charged at
Clerkenwell Police Court with brutally assaulting
Ilary Ann, his wife, at the Red Lion public house,
St. John's-street-road, Clerkenwell. He was sen-
tenced to six months' imprisonment, with hard labour.

A MONKEY FOR A JUDGE.—At the Stafford assizes
yesterday, John Martin, a notorious burglar, was con-
victed. He had been six times previously convietod,
and in 1859 to four years' penal servitude. His lord-
ship sentenced him to twenty years' penal servitude.
'The prisoner, addressing his lordship: I hope you
will sit there until I come back again, and I'll bring
you a monkey.' He then left the dock laughing.
THE ROYDON HALL GAME CASE.—Alfred Burr
Luck, Thomas Stevens, George Allahan, Joseph Obey,
Stephen Burgess, John Catt, and Joseph Clipson, the
,seven men who were
.tried on Wednesday for the
manslaughter of the gamekeeper and acquitted, and
who afterwards pleaded guilty to a charge of night
poaching arising out of the same transaction, were
then placed at the bar to receive judgment—The
learned judge sentenced Luck and Burgess, who, he
said, appeared to have been the original projectors of
the expedition to be imprisoned and kept to hard
labour for twelve, and the others for four months each.
As the prisoner Luck left the dock he declared with
great earnestness that he was not the man who shot
the deceased.
FATAL OCCURRENCE AT THE LONDON DOCKS.—The
investigation into the circumstances attending the
death of Mr. George Wood, a Custom-house officer,
who lost his life by falling into the water of the
London Docks, was resumed on Wednesday before Mr.
IL R. Walthew, at the George and Vulture Tavern,
St. George's-in. the-East. The proceedings excited
more than ordinary interest, as the question arose
whether dock companies were liable for accidents
which occurred through the want of barriers or other
protection along the quays of docks. Mr. Nicholls,
solicitor, represented the London Dock Company; and
Mr. Humphreys, of Newgate-street, attended on behalf
of the friends of Mr. Wood. It having been proved
that there were no chains or other barriers around
some of the quays of the London Docks on the Thurs-
day when the accident occurred, but that the next
day the company placed ropes around the basins, the
following evidence was taken :—Jean Baptiste Fichte,
mate of the Albert steam vessel, said that he resided
at Dunkirk. The steamer arrived on Sunday, the 9th
of November, in the docks. The following Thursday
evening there was a dense fog. The Custom-house
officer went on shore at five o'clock. At that time it
was perhaps sufficiently clear to enable Mr. Wood to
see to walk on the quay. Witness did not see de-
ceased fall into the water. He knew of two or three
persons who fell into the docks that night. Mr. Jones,
an inspecting engineer, lost his life by falling into the
water about the same time. Witness left the vessel
before six o'clock, and immediately afterwards there
were loud groans. Witness found him much injured
in a boat moored some feet from the quay. He was
insensible. Other evidence having been offered, the
coroner summed up. The room was then cleared,
and, after a long deliberation, the jury returned a
verdict, That the deceased, George Wood, fell into
the water from it certain unguarded part of the quays
of the London Dock, and was thus drowned, and that
if proper precautions had been taken by the dock
company the sad accident might have been avoided.'
THE NORTH AND THE SOUTH.— On Monday evening,
at Surrey Chapel, the Rev. Newman Hall, in a lecture
to upwards of 2,000 working men and others, On
Passing Events,' said that the recent election suc-
cesses of the democrats in America revealed a formid-
able opposition to the emancipation or republican
party. The democrats were for carrying on the war
as much as the others, only they would preserve the
domestic institution' of the South. Those who sym-
pathised with the democratic party sympathised with
those who fought for the Union and slavery, as opposed
to those who fought for the Union and freedom. The
whole of the North were resolved on war, but the
Southerners were the authors of that war. They
began it, and while claiming the right of maintaining
slavery and extending it wherever they pleased, war
seemed as inevitable as with a band of determined
brigands. If they were our own near neighbours and
demanded as the price of peace the right to bring 'their
slaves over the border, and retain them as slaves, we
must be always at war until they withdrew that claim;
but they, not we, should
,be responsible for the evils
such a war would entail. The inconsistencies of those
who urged us to sympathise with the South were con-
stant and glaring. Let Englishmen wash their hands
of all participation in slavery, and let all friends of
freedom throughout the country, whatever their dif-
ferences cf opinion in regard to the war, resolve never
to purchase another yard of cotton branded with the
mark stolen goods,' stained with blood, and crying to
God against those who keep back the bite .of the
labourer.'

articles.title: AGGREGATE MEETING OF CAB DIUVERS AND PROPRIETORS.
articles.text:
AGGREGATE MEETING OF CAB
DIUVERS AND PROPRIETORS.

A public meeting of the metropolitan cab proprietors
and drivers was held, on Wednesday evening, at the
Whittington Club, Arundel-street, Strand, for the pur-
posa of receiving a report from the delegates appointed
to prepare a revision of the Hackney Carriage Act, and
to consider other measures for obtaining a redress of
grievances. Lord H. Cholrnondeley occupied the chair,
and was supported on the platform by Captain Fish
bourne, R.N., Mr. Edwards, Mr. Smith, Mr. Bennett,
and several other gentlemen, who take an interest in
the movement, and in the cabmen's clubs. There were
also present a large number of influential proprietors,
who evinccd great interest in the proceedings. The
admission to the meeting was obtainable by tickets,
charged 6d. each.
The noble Chairman said, having been requested to
preside over the meeting, he felt bound to comply with
that request, being, in common with many friends
around him, always anxious to do anything in his
power to promote either the spiritual or temporal wel-
fare of the hard-worked and persecuted cab-driver.
The object of the meeting was to hear and adopt, if
they deemed proper, the resolutions agreed to by their
delegates which it was desired to incorporate into an
amended Hackney Carriage Act. He was not at
present prepared to express any opinion upon the
resolutions, but he understood they had been carefully
considered by the delegates before adoption, and
if adopted, they would have the effect desired. He
would now call upon one of the delegates to read the
report.
Mr. Goodwin (a proprietor and driver) read the re-
port of the delegates, which, after detailing their pro-
ceedings at some length, went on to enumerate the
various amended clauses it was considered advisable to
introduce into a new act, the principal of which may
be thus summarised :—The present 6d. hiring to be
abolished, and no driver to be compelled to let his cab
for less than is., but to be bound to go two miles for
that
,13um if required. The metal badge now worn by
drivers to be abolished, it being no proof that the
driver wearing it is the person duly licensed, and that
in its place a certificate containing the description of
the person licensed be given to every driver on re- '
ceiving his licence, which he shall produce when called
upon to do so. No driver to be deemed plying for hire
unless standing upon some place authorised by the
Police Commissioner. That all, special agreements
between hirers and drivers be binding on both parties.
That the distance of four miles from Charing-cross be
measured by the road, instead of the radius. That
children be charged for, as upon railways. That all
packages be charged 2d. each. That all dogs carried in
or outside a cab be charged at the rate of 6d. That
any driver proving his case before a magistrate shall
receive compensation for himself and witnesses. That
every driver shall receive notice of the unfitness of his
cab or horse for public work before becoming liable to
prosecution. That none but hirers be empowered to
prosecute in any dispute between themselves tnd
drivers. That a cheap power of appeal be granted
from magisterial decisions. That when any hirer
refuses to pay his fare, or make compensation for any
damage to a cab, the driver to have the power to
compel him to go to the nearest station house, where
he shall deposit the amount of such fare, or give secu-
rity, previous to going before the magistrate.'
Mr. Wise (a driver) then moved the following reso-
lution :—‘ As the present Hackney Carriage Act is
considered tyrannical and unjust towards the drivers,
and so often misconstrued by the magistrates in their
decisions, who often decide differently at different
police courts resolved, that the amendments to the
present Hackney Carriage Act, as read by Mr. Godwin,
be adopted.' He contended the Act under which they
were now working was all one-sided, and required a
revision. He believed the clauses prepared by the
delegates would act fairly to all parties, the proprietor,
the driver, and the public. He was not there to deny
that there were bad men amongst cabmen; there were
bad men in all classes of society, but the cabmen were
not, as a body, worse than any other class. The
speaker then detailed at great length the manifest
grievances under which he contended cabmen were
labouring, arising from the persecutions of the police,
and contrary magisterial decisions. He mentioned
many cases of injustice to the Men caused by
police officiousness during the period of the Ex-
hibition; and cabmen have had great obloquy
thrown upon them in connection with that Exhibition.
What was the fact? There were from 4,000 to 5,000
cabmen daily attending to their duty at the Exhi-
bition, and yet out of this number the complaints after
all brought forward by the police against cabmen did
not average more than one per day. Cabmen more
than any other class were free from serious charges,
such as felony; and, though they made their appear-
ance so often at the police courts, that was due to the
unjust and vexatious law under which they carried on
their business. After referring to the lost property
question, he concluded by moving the resolution.
Mr. W. Towell (a driver), seconded the motion,
with some few remarks on the lost property question.
Mr. Case (a proprietor), did not agree with all the
propositions brought forward by the delegates. He
had heard nothing about the district meetings held to
discuss them.

The Chairman said, though for the sake of con-
venience the clause proposed by the delegates were
moved as a whole, it was not intended, he was informed
by the delegates, that any one voting for them should
be bound to every word they contained.
Mr. Case having expressed himself satisfied with this
explanation, the resolution was unanimously adopted.
Mr. Wakelin (a driver), moved the adoption of a pe-
tition to the House of Commons, praying for an inves-
tigation into the grievances of cabmen. The speaker
went at some length into the manifold grievances
under which cabmen were labouring, and advocated
union amongst the body as the only means by which
they could hope to be successful in removing those
grievances.
Mr. Miles (a driver) in seconding the motion, said at
the commencement of the agitation there was a great
deal said of a strike, and that the cabmen were goin; to
adopt that means of gaining their object. They were
going to work in a more business-like manner by
bringing the case before the Legislature. He thought
free trade in cabs would 1..3 injurious.
Mr. Powell (a proprietbr) advocated free trade in
cabs.

Mr. Bennett, the secretary, having read the petition
it was unanimously adopted by the meeting.
Mr. Bates (a driver) then moved a resolution
declaring the necessity of a deputation waiting upon
members of Parliament, and upon the Home Secretary,
with the view of obtaining their support to a Parlia.•
mentary inquiry into the present Hackney Carriage
Act, with a view to the introduction of an amended
act.

Mr. Earle (a driver), seconded the resolution, which
was agreed to.
Mr. Smith (Secretary of the Sogth London Cab-
men's Club), moved a resolution for the appointment
of a general committee, to sit permanently until the
object of the movement was successful. In the course
of his remarks Mr. Smith strongly advocated free
trade, which he felt convinced would ultimately become
the rule of the trade.

Several other delegates having spoken,
Mr. Case rose, and, in a long speech, advocated the
union of the proprietors and drivers as the only means
by which they could hope to obtain any permanent
benefit. He trusted the resolutions would be amended
to allow of an equal number of proprietors sitting on
the committee with the drivers.
After some discussion this course was assented to,
and the resolution, as amended, was adopted by the
meeting.
A vote of thanks having been proposed and carried
to the Chairman,
The Chairman, in his reply, said he felt bound to
congratulate them on the orderly and business-like
way in which they had conducted their meeting. They
must not be too sanguine, and not expect too much at
once. He had no doubt the present act required amend-
ment, and if they could obtain a Parliamentary com-
mittee of inquiry, and could give evidence of any bona
fide pressure under which they were suffering, they would
obtain redress. He should feel it his duty, while they
acted with their present moderation, to render them all
the assistance in his power.
Votes of thanks were also given to Captain Fish.
borne, R.N., the delegates, and to the BEEHIVE news-
paper, for the support it had rendered to the move-
ment, Mr. Miles urging on all cabmen to support and
purchase that paper.
The meeting, which had been one of a most enthu-
siastic and satisfactory character, then concluded.
The secrets:ry having, previous to the meeting, corn-
municated with Sir R. Mayne, that functionary had
instructed the inspector of the F division, to allow
cabs to stand at the bottom of Arundel-street, while
their drivers were attending the meeting.
At the conclusion of the public meeting, a meeting
of the delegates was held in the committee -room, when
it was determined that the delegates should meet on
Tuesday evening, the 16th inst., at the BEEHIVE
Office, at nine o'cloA, and that the secretary should
I write to the Central Association of Proprietors, inviting
them to send representatives to the meeting.

In our report of the Cabmen's Midnight Meeting,
held last week, it was stated that the number present
was 3,000. This was a misprint, it should have
been 300.

articles.title: MORE GAROTTE ROBBERIES.
articles.text:
MORE GAROTTE ROBBERIES.

On Monday evening, about nine o'clock, a man
named Lewis, in the employ of Messrs. Newman, job-
masters, of Regent-street, and residing in Golden-
place, Golden-square, while passing through the square
was attacked by two men, one on eaili side. One of
the fellows put his arm round his neck, while the other
put something moist to his mouth. Lewis immediately
became insensible and fell, and while doing so received
two or three kicks in his ribs, and then lost all recol-
lection. On recovering himself Lewis found himself
in the gutter, with his purse, which had contained
nearly £3, lying by his side. Lewis was taken to
Charing-cross Hospital, and attended by the officers,
and shortly afterwards taken home.
On Tuesday morning, as Mr. John Matthews, for
many years employ-,d as a compositor on the _Daily
News, was proceeding to his residence in the Camber-
well yew-road, at four o'clock a.m., he was garotted
close to the Police-station by two of the artistic Thugs
of London. Mr. Matthews, with praiseworthy pre-
caution, had left his watch and other valuables at home,
so that his audacious assailants were not only foiled
and frustrated, but disappointed in their diabolical
design. His screams for assistance was heard by his
wife, but apparently not by the police at the station.
The sufferer is still disabled and unfit to attend to his
duties, a certificate of which has been given by his
medical adviser, who states that he would not be able
to resume his duties for some days to come.

At Westminster Police Court, Johß Hurley and
Alfred Lee, two young men, were charged before Mr.
Paynter with an attempted garotte robbery. Hannah
Miller, a young woman living at 8, Roberts-buildings,
Chelsea, said that she was seeing a female friend home
at a little before twelve on the previous night, and had
arrived at the corner of Turk's-row, Chelsea, when she
was suddenly seized by the throat by Hurley, who was
accompanied by Lee and another man. She im-
mediately told Hurley that if he wanted to rob her she
had got nothing, when he replied, Haven't you ?
well, we'll see.' She called 'Police!' and at the
moment two constables came up, and Hurley, who had
his arms round her neck, and the others left her
without injuring her, and endeavoured to escape. The
police said that they had not only been convicted of
felony, but Lee was a ticket-of-leave man, who had
had three months' imprisonment since he had obtained
it. Prisoners were committed for trial.

George Lines was brought up at Mary lebone, charged
with a murderous garotte assault and robbery upon
Mr. Woodward, on the night of the 12th ult., in
Maitland Park Villas' Haverstock hill, Hampstead.
Mr. Yardley committed the prisoner for tial, and re-
fused to take bail.

At Worship-street, Mark Archer and William Hay-
cock, young men unfavourably known to the police,
were charged as follows :—Mr. Edward Morley, resi-
dent at Bethnal-green, said: About twelve o'clock on
the previous night I and three friends left a public
how e in Suffolk-street, Bethnal-green. We were
perfectly sober, and walked away in pairs, Mr. Higgs
and myself being about a hundred yards in advance.
suddenly I heard a cry for help and of Police.' We
ran back, and I found both prisoners confronting my
other friends, Archer striking one of them with a short
stick. I instantly rushed up and endeavoured to get
hold of him, but he dealt me heavy blow on the head
with the weapon, which caused me to stagger against
the wall. I bled freely from the wound, and was laid
upon a door step, where I became insensible. Subse-
quently I was taken to the station house, where I saw
the prisoners, and preferred a charge against them. I
yet feel very weak. Ai cher struck Mr. Bull on the
head.—Remanded.

At the Woolwich Police-court on Wednesday, a man
named James Collins, and two women, named Eliza-
beth Ross and Catherine 'Watson, all old offenders,
were charged with violently assaulting John Forbes,
a timekeeper employed at the Royal Arsenal, and
stealing from his person a watch and 6s. The evi-
dence proved that about 9 o'clock on the previous
night the prosecutor was passing near a dangerous
locality, known as Ropeyard Rails, at Woolwich,
when he was suddenly seized by the throat by the
male prisoner, and robbed by the women. From
information received the prisoners were subsequently
apprehended, and were now identified by the prose-
cutor.—The prisoners were fully committed for trial.
On Thursday morning, between 12 and 1 o'clock,
Mr. George Leader, a theatrical employe, was proceed-
ing home to his residence at Paddington, when, in
passing through a narrow throughfare called Manor-
lane, he was accosted by a female, who importuned
him for drink. Mr. Leader passed on, the woman fol-
lowing up behind, when, on reaching the end of the
lane he was suddenly confronted by a man wearing a
white smock frock. lie was at. the same time seized
round the throat from behind and thrown to the
ground, the woman kneeling upon his throat while
the man rifled his pockets. They then gave him a
blow on the head, which stunned him. On recovering
he managed to get to the police station, and several
officers went in pursuit of his assailants. It was near
the same spot that Mr. Shalders, the comedian, was
garotted, dying subsequently from the effects.
On Thursday morning, Michael Garretty, residing
in Webber-street, Lambeth, expired from the effects
of injuries inflicted upon him by garotters in the St.
George's-road, Southwark, on Saturday night. The
men now attack females; and a young woman, named
Jane Stokes, living in Belvedere-road, has, it is said,
just expired from injuries thus sustained in passing
through Stamford-street.
In the neighbourhoods of Battersea, Wandsworth,
and Wimbledon, numerous persons have been garotted
and plundered, and great alarm prevails in those
localities.

On Wednesday the police were made acquainted with
the death of a gentleman unknown, having taken place
on the Lightptevious, by garotting, at Tooting, Surrey.
The deceased's studs had been forced out of his shirt-
front, his pockets rifled, and, apparently, rings forced
from his fingers. The Croydon constabulary were also
informed of no less than four garotte robberies, with
dreadful violence, which took place on Tuesday last
and yesterday.

DEATH.—Died, on Tuesday, December 2nd, at the
residence of his son James, Mr. John Murray. of 34,
Great Russell-street, Bloomsbury, late of Gerrard.
street, Soho, and formerly of Newport, Isle of Wight,
in the 88th year of his age.

GALE AT GIBRALTAR.—A violent gale from the south-
west visited Gibraltar and its neighbourhood on the night
of the 23rd ultimo, accompanied by driving sleet and one
or two heavy showers. Two vessels went on shore. The
British bark Mary Catherine, W. Ward, master, from
Fiume, with staves for Bordeaux, parted both anchors,
and stranded under the line wall early on the morning
of the 24th. A little cutter yacht, the Doris, which was
anchored off the Devil's Tongue, went on shore at the
North Front. The barometer was lower during the night
than it had been for many years. On the 24th ult., at
8 a.m., it stood at 29, but it afterwards rose one-tenth.
The ordinary range in Gibraltar is from 29.50 to 30.50.

articles.title: LAW INTELLIGENCE,
articles.text:
LAW INTELLIGENCE,

COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH.
(Before the Lord Chief Justice.)
MR. DIGBY SEYMOUR, M.P., V. BUTTEILWORTH.

. .
This was an action for libel, brought by Mr. Sey-
mour, M.P. for Southampton, against Mr. Butter-
worth, a bookseller of Fleet-street, and publisher of
the Law -Ifagazine, arising out of an inquiry made some
months since, by the Benchers of the Inner Temple,
into some alleged mal-practices.of Mr. Seymour in his
capacity as a barrister. The trial lasted the whole of
Monday, Tuesday, and Welneeday, but was of no
public interest. The jury returned a verdict for the
plaintiff with 40s. costs.

articles.title: COURT OF BANKRUPTCY. (Before Mr. Commissioner Goulburn.) IN RE GEORGE STIFF.
articles.text:
COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.
(Before Mr. Commissioner Goulburn.)
IN RE GEORGE STIFF.

The bankrupt was late the proprietor of the London
Journal, Morning Chronicle, and other journals. This
was the sitting for order of discharge. The accounts
have already appeared in detail; the unsecured debts
are £34,000; as yet there has been no dividend, but
one is expected next month, when the accounts of Mr.
Hart, the manager, will be submitted, and the amount
then in hand will be divided.

Mr. Linklater said the assignees did not oppose the
granting of the order. The only circumstance that
could have been urged against it was the personal ex-
penditure, but considering the sanguine tempera-
ment of the bankrupt, and the character of the pro-
perty, they did not think that he could be charged
with extravagance. The bankrupt had now been nine
months before the court.
The Commissioner: Let me understand; are the
assignees, for whom you appear, friendly assignees?
Mr. Linklater: Oh, no. In fact they have opposed
the bankrupt—l might say violently, at former stages.
Mr. Lawrence said that the creditors for whom he
appeared also consented to the bankrupt having his
order.

Mr. Lewis: Under those circumstances my duties are
very light.

Tne bommitsioner : Then let him take his order of
discharge.

SOUTHWARK COUNTY COURT.

THE AAIALGAAIATED CARPENTERS'
SOCIETY.
JUNIPER AND OTHERS T. JkIIVS LEA.

This case was reported last week, when the judge
finished the hcaring in his private room, reserving his
judgment. ,This judgment was sent on Wednesday to
the parties concerned as follows
This was an application by certain members of the
Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners, for an
order of the court under the provisions of the statute 18
and 19 Viet. c. 63. I made an effort by mediation to
arrive at some settlement which would reconcile the
differences of the two parties, but I did not succeed.
Each stood upon his supposed rights, and I am called
upon to decide the real question between them, viz.,
who is the rightful secretary of their society. The
differences that have arisen spring from the usual
source, viz., the ambiguity of the rules, and their in-
sufficiency to meet the contingencies that have occurred.
The powers of the executive council are ill-defined; so
are the occasions when the general council must be re-
sorted to; so also the method of electing its members, and
their qualifications. On these and other matters
brought before me an amendment of the rules is highly
desirable. In whom should reside the power of dismissing
the secretary, is a point upon which the rules of the
society are silent, but which should certainly be made
clear. What right of appeal theofficer, when dismissed,
should enjoy is another. Both these questions were
mooted in the present case; but the opinion I have
formed is independent of them. I have come to the
conclusion that upon the election of secretary, which
took place in August, the present defendant had not a
majority of votes, and that his competitor (Applegarth)
is the member duly elected. It follows, that the latter
is entitled to the books, papers, &c., belonging to the
I office and claimed in this action, and they ought to be
delivered up to him forthwith. In coming to the
above conclusion as to the result of the election of
secretary, I have been guided by the necessary die.
tinction between those things which are essential to
the validity of an election, and those which are not.
Something in the nature of a scrutiny was entered
into, and 1 have satisfied myself as to the objections on
either side which are or are not legally sustainable.
The plaint will stand adjourned for the present, to give
the parties the opportunity of carrying my opinion in to
effect without the compulsion of an order of the
court. J. WHITMORE, Judge, &c.
