articles.text:
ASSIZE INTELLIGENCE.

HOME CIRCUIT.—MAIDSTONII.
(Before Mr. Justice Byles.)

MANSLAUGHTER OF A WlFE.—Major Murton, 52,
a respectable-looking man, who has been for a
great many years engaged in extensive business
as a fanner, near Chatham, was charged upon the
coroner's inquisition with the manslaughter of his
wife, Lena Murton. The facts of this case have been
recently reported. The jury returned a verdict of
guilty. Sentence was deferred.
THE POACHING AFFRAY AT ROYDON HALL.—Alfred
Burr Lusk, 29; Thomas Stevens, 29; George Allchin,
28; Joseph Obey, 48; John Clapson, 26; Stephen
Burgess, 25; John Catt, 31; and Stephen Everslield,
56; who had been admitted to bail, who were all
described as labourers, were charged with the man-
slaughter of James Gray. There was another prisoner
named John Hawkes included in the indictment, but
he was admitted as evidence for the Crown. There was
also an indictment against the prisoners for night
poaching arising out of the same circumstances. The
evidence was lengthy and confused, and alternately
the jury gave a verdict of not guilty as regarded the
whole of the prisoners. The prisoners then (with the
exception of Eversfield, against whom the charge was
abandoned, and who was ordered to be discharged
from custody) pleaded guilty to the misdemeanour of
being in pursuit of game illegally in the night-time.
Mr. Ribton urged, on behalf of Lusk, tbat he had
served for eleven months in the trenches before Sebas-
topol, and had received a Crimean medal, and left the
army with a very good character. He had already
been eight months in prison upon these charges. His
lordship said he should consider what sentence should
be pronounced.
THE CHATHAM MUUDER.—Upon the application of
Mr. Rtbton, who appeared for the prisoner, the trial of
Robert Alexander Thurton for the murder of a lad at
Chatham, was postponed to the summer assizes, when,
it is understood, the defence of insanity wi!l be set up.

OXFORD CIRCUIT.—STAFFORD.
(Before Mr. Justice Mellor.)

TILE S BEGLEY MURDER—Jesse Watts, William
Henshaw, Hannah Simms, and Mary Downing, were
indicted for the wilful murder of Henry Swinnerton,
on the 4th November last, at Sedgley.—lt appears
that on the 4th of November the deceased was out
drinking at saveral public-houses. At one of these
public-houses—the Three Horseshoes—he treated the
female prisoners to drink, and he was there joined by
the two male prisoners. He accompanied one of the
female prisoners out of the house, and was shortly
afterwards followed by the other prisoners, who beat
him with a life-preserver, and robbed him, and from
the effect of the injuries received he died on the 10th
of November in a frightful state of suffering. Several
witnesses were examined, but, the particulars of the
case having so recently been before the public in the
evidence given in the police court previous to the com-
mittal of the prisoners, it is unnecessary to repeat rt.—
The jury found all the prisoners guilty of manslaughter
—Sentence deferred.

NORTHERN CIRCUIT.—NEWCASTLE,
(Before Mr. Justice Keating.)
THE MURDER AT HIGH CRANB.—John Dixon, 21,
boatman, and Thomas Miller, 22, labourer, were
charged with the wilful murder of Patrick Rogers,
on the 16th August, 1862. The murdered man
was well known throughout the counties of North-
umberland and Durham, gaining a living by selling
needles, pins, and other small matters from house
to house, and generally went by the cognomen of
' Needle Jack.' He was an inoffensive creature of
weak intellect, aad was often made the butt of the
mischievous. The prisoner had previously borne a
very bad character. It appeared from the evidence
that on Saturday afterroon, the 16th August, about
two o'clock, persons on High Crane-wharf, and adjoin-
ing the Tyne-bridge, saw the deceased come into the
privy. The deceased entered a public privy on the
High Crane-wharf, adjoining the old Tyne-bridge. The
prisoner Miller had entered previously, and Dixon came
in shortly after Needle Jack.' He was shoved
against the wall by Dixon. On the deceased making a
move as if he were about to leave, Miller said to him,
You —, if you stir from there until we are ready
to let you go kill you.' Millerthen said to Dixon and
two other men who were present, Have either o' you
a bit o' paper ' Dickson answered, No.' Miller then
struck a match, and set fire to Jack's hair. Both pri-
soners then seized hold of the unfortunate man, and
in spite of his struggles thrust him down the hole of
the privy. The floor of the privy hole is made with a
great descent into the river, and, as it is a deep water
berth, there is at all times of tide several feet of water
immediately beneath the outlet from the privy. The
deceased, on reaching the bottom of the hole, slid
rapidly down into the river. The prisoners imme-
diately ran away as hard as they could. A witness
said there were two feat of water over the outlet of the

hole at the time. He looked over the quay and saw
the arm of the deceased once before he was carried by
the ebb tide beneath the bottom of a ship lying in the
tier a few yards off, and was drowned. The ship had
to be moved from her berth before the body could be
recovered. The jury returned a verdict of man-
slaughter. His lordship commented on the enormity
of the offence the prisoners had committed, and sen-
tenced them to ten years' penal servitude.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

GUILDHALL.

A CAB BILK.9—Ed ward Sandell, a respectably-
dressed, tall, thin, and cadaverous-looking young fellow,
was brought Hp before Alderman Copeland on a war-
rant, charged with neglecting to pay a cabman his
lawful fare. William Bray, a cab-driver, said the
prisoner employed him on a Friday in August last, and
after driving him about for some time he left him with-
out paying him his fare. His master, who was one of
the best masters in London, did not believe his story,
and directed him to make up the deficiency on the
following day, but unfortunately he met with the
prisoner and drove him again, and was again deceived
by him, and not having any money for his master at
night he was discharged. The prisoner did not dispute
the cabman's claim. Alderman Copeland ordered the
prisoner to pay 17s. and 6d. for the fare, 6s. for two
summonses, 4s. 6d. for the warrant, and Hs. for the
cabman's loss of time, or 21 days' imprisonment in de-
fault. The amount was paid. •

articles.title: BOW-STREET.
articles.text:
BOW-STREET.

THE LATE CHARGE OP STABBING A CONSTABLE AT
THE LYCEUM.—Francis Bartlett Graham was brought
up on remand on the charge of stabbing Police-con-
stable Brown, of the A division, who, it was stated,
was still too ill to attend. Mr. Lewis, of Ely-place,
solicitor for the defendant, requested the magistrate
to admit the prisoner to bail, on the ground that his
health, physical and mental, was suffering from the
confinement. Mr. Henry could not do that. The
constable was still in a bad state. of health—worse,
indeed, than the day alter he received the injuries.
Mr. Lewis said he believed that the constable was not
suffering so much from the injury as from general ill
health. Mr. Henry : Still I cannot admit prisoner
to bail. He must be remanded till the constable is
able to attend. The prisoner was accordingly re-
manded.
SOUTHWARK.

GAROTTERS AND BaRGLARS ON THE LOOK•OUT.—
Daniel Green, a young fellow of determined appearance,
was placed at the bar for final examination, charged
with loitering about the streets with two others at two
o'clock in the morning, and having in his possession a
house-breaking implement called a jemmy,' for the
purpose of committing a felony. The magistrate was
informed that there was no evidence to show that the
prisoner had ever been convicted of felony; although he
was known to be a companion of very bad characters.
The prisoner, electing to be tried by the magistrate,
pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to three months'
hard labour under the Vagrant Act.

articles.title: LAMBETH.
articles.text:
LAMBETH.

THE ESCAPED CONVlCT.—Frederick Layton Cleft, a
convict, sentenced to ten years' transportation on a
charge of arson, but who, with two others, succeeded
in effecting their escape from Milbank Prison, on the
26th of May last, was brought up on remand on two
other charges besides that of breaking out of prison,
namely, that of forging acheque for £34 and obtaining
articles of jewellery to that amount by fraud, from
Mr. Kellsworth, a jeweller at New Cross.—Mr.
Elliott, having ascertained that there was, no person
present from Millbank Prison, inquired if any commu-
nication had been made to the governor on the subject
of the prisoner's apprehension.—lnspector Frost replied
that he had himself waited on the Governor of Mill-
bank twice—once before and once after the prisoner's
examination—and had particularly mentioned the fact
of the prisoner's examination on that day.—Mr.
Elliott: I shall now commit the prisoner for trial on
the charges of forgery and fraud, but shall remand
him to a future day to learn from the authorities at
Millbank whether it is their intention to prosecute
upon the third charge of breaking out of gaol, and
must request you, Mr. Frost, to call at the prison and
obtain this information. •

THAMES.
A CURIOUS BIGAMY CASE. -An Irish sailor, ,
named Bei tholomew 31'Grarry, was brought be-
fore Mr. Woolrych charged with feloniously inter-
marrying with Mary Halloran, while his first and.
lawful wife was alive. Both wives were in court._
The first an old woman, very poor, and meanly ,
clad, and many years the senior of the prisoner—
the second, a younger woman than the prisoner,
and well dressed. The first marriage was solemnised
in Ireland in October, 1833. They had been living,
apart many years, and, in the month of February, ,
1861, he was married to Mary Halloran at the Roman
Catholic church of St. Mary and St. Michael, in the -
Commercial-road East. The second wife said that
when she became acquainted with the prisoner he
said his first wife had been dead and buried 14 years..
The first wife here groaned aloud, and exclaimed,
M‘Garry, now did you toll her that lie of me?'—
The second wife then produced the certificate of the
second marriage, and said: My husband told me the
week before Fast that he was married to this old
woman.—The first wife: Och ! may the Lord save
you, M‘Garry, was there iver such a bad man !
The prisoner, after receiving the usual caution, said:
I know 1 have done wrong; I have been married
to both women. lam a most unfortunate man; I
must put up with it —Mr. Woolrych committed the
prisoner for trial.—The latter then asked the magis-
trate to allow the money, n 165., taken from him
by Barrett, the police constable, to be given to his
first wife. The second can work for her living, the
old woman can't.—The first wife (clapping her hands) :
God bless you, M‘Garry.—The prisoner then left the
dock.

MARLBOROOUGH-STREET.

A CAB PROPRIETOR CHARGED WITH RECEIVING STOLEN
CORN.—Robert Smith, in the employ of Mr. Gilbert
Charles Northcote, a City gentleman, was charged
with stealing some corn, the property of Mr. Henry
South, livery-stable keeper, of Queen-street, Cheap-
side; and Wm. Newton, a cab proprietor, of Pimlico,
was charged with receiving the same with a guilty
knowledge. The prisoners ware watched on two or
three occasions by Dawson, 301 A, and Butcher, 137
C, and Newton was seen buying corn of Smith which
had been given him to supply the horse belonging to
Mr. Nor thcote. Mr. Knox said it was a class of theft
of a very serious nature, horses being starved in order
that the persons stealing the corn might get some
paltry gain out of it. In this case the proper food WAS
supplied, and the horse deprived of it, and the well-
being of an animal of considerable value concerned.
He should commit both prisoners for trial. Mr. Smyth
applied that bail might be taken for Newton, but Mr..
Knox refused.

SALE OP THE SUN' NEWSPAPER.—Yesterday at
the Auction Mart, the copyright and goodwill of the
Sun newspaper were sold by Mr. E. Lumley, pursuant
to a decree in Chancery, to Mr. Fearer, for the sum ot
£l,OOO. The purchaser has also to take at the sum of
£1,420, the machinery and plant.

THE MELANCHOLY CASE OF STABBING IN TR E
Sritarin.—On Wednesday Mr. Payne held an investi-
gation at George's Hotel, Strand, respecting the death
of Mr. Edward Leigh, agcd 21, which was caused by ei
wound in the abdomen, inflicted with a cheese-knife, at
the Somerset Hotel. After hearing the evidence the
jury returned a verdict of Accidental death.'

MAzzist.—The Nova Europa of Florence publishes
a letter from Mazzini, in which he complains that
every word the moderate journals publish respecting • •
him is a falsehood, that they are labouring to sow
mistrust between him and Garibaldi—between the men.
who followed the latter to the battle-field, and those
who had prepared the campaign by their apostolate, • -
that is, by preaching Mazzinian doctrines. He con-
cludes with declaring that he has one thing in common
with Garibaldi; and that is the recollection of their -
youthful days, when they both swore together to be
faithful to Italy.

SERIOUS Films- .—On Thursday morning, about three
o'clock, a fire broke out in the principal part of the'
High-street, Homerten. The premises in which the
disaster commenced formed three houses, and were •
numbered 3,4, and 5, and were in the tenure of Mr.
J. Hayward, a wholesale and retail grocer and cheese-
monger. The inmates of all made for the back windows, -
and fortunately, with assistance, managed to reach the
street without receiving any serious injury. At one
time it was feared that not only .the entire range of •
premises belonging to Mr. Hayward were doomed to be
destroyed, but also that those on the other side would
be levelled. The firemen succeeded in partially saving
the premises of Mr. Cressy and those of Mr. Crowther,
but were unable to get the flames extinguished until
the three houses belonging to Mr. J. Hayward were
totally destroyed, and the contents, including stock in
trade, fixtures, and other effects were consumed. A fire
also happened in the premises of Mr. Thomas Hill, a
confectioner, No. 24, Baker's-row, Whitechapel, but.
owing to the timely arrival of assistance, the damage.
was confined to that part of the premises in which the.
fire commenced. Another, fire took place in the premises
of Mr. J. Graguy, No. 2, Roman-road, Old Ford. Con—
siderable damage we done. The loss will fall upon
the General and.,lWal Exchange fire offices. A flip_
likewise broke out in the premises of Mr. J. Squires, a.
carpenter and joiner, No. 11, High-street, Stoke New-
ington, and was net extingaishect:until considerable
damage wae dam .

In answer to this insinuation, I would say, no portbn of
the ship has yet received more than two coats of paint

6th. F. B. says : But how can he account for the
rain water going through where the two new plates
were put under the bottom, after it was all finished
and painted, &c.? _

At no time did the rain water come through
more than would, have damped a lady's handkerchief,
had,it.been used; but the foreman, on the customary

public. should-know that Government inspectors in
contract yards have often to order rivets to be driven
out for the above or other reasons, and if this were the
place I could say a great deal en that subject, but for-
bear. But is it not A trange that boilermakers should,
expeotsuch perfection from m n confessedly new at the
work as they themselves, with all their experience,
have never been able to arrive at ? I will inform
F. B. that san one occasion not long since, the attention
of one-of theboilermakees was drawn to a leak in the
bottom of an iron ship lying in dock at Keyham, and
although the water ran down the side of the keel in a
stream as broad as a quill, he said, 0, we think
nothing of that.'
7th. -Regarding the difficult (?) matter of levelling
the plates, F. B. says :—Companies of shipwrights
are clay after day hammering these large plates, some
with wooden mallets and some with sledge hammers,
until they have exhausted both strength and patience,
and all thia without accomplishing their ends.
7th. The end is accomplished, and any person curious
in these matters may certify this to his own mind by
paying a visit to H.M.S. Ocean. This reminds me of
a story to this effect :—A poor fellow, for some mis-
deed, had been put in the stocks. A comrade happen-
ing to pass' cried out, How is this? How came you
there? What have you done?' Upon being informed,
he said with indignation, They can't put you in the
stocks for that." Bat,' says the prisoner, what is
the good of your saying that. lam here.' The in-
fatuation of some men is amusing in the extreme.
They won't believe their own eyes. All the time they
are saying the shipwrights can't do this or that in
connection with iron-plating the work is being done.
When Fulton was about to get up steam for the trial
trip on board of his little ship (which some old fogieshad
taken the liberty to christen 'Fulton's folly,') the
unbelievers on the quay, to which the vessel was
moored, said she would never move, but by and by
she did move. Then they said she would not go far,
but she did go out of sight. And then they said she
would never come back, but she did, and BO became
'the Little Grandsire ' of a mighty family that now
covers the ocean. I am afraid that, like Nelson at
Copenhagen, not wanting to see the signalehat would
defeat their own purpose, they turn toward the object
the blind eye of prejudice.
The public should know that since the discharge of
the two boil r makers for refusing to level the plates
for the shipwrights, the plates have been levelled
entirely by labourers alone, who no doubt feel quite sur-
prised at the ease with which they are able to accom-
plish this very arduous (?) undertaking. Moreover,
the plates referred to as being so badly manipulated
by the shipwrights, so as to exhaust both strength and
patience, have not only been levelled, but are now
forming part of the bulkheads and wind passages of
H.M.S. Ocean, the whole of which has been built by
shipwrights alone. Here I would in passing mention
a well known fact, namely, that nearly all the great
undertakings of modern times have been accomplished
by men acting independent of routine and custom.
Read lives of the engineers—Stephenson, Brindley,
Smeaton, or Brunel.
F. B. may therefore rest enured that in this as in
most other things the old adage applies there is more
ways of killing a dog besides hanging him.'
The shipwrights who have been employed on the
bulkheads and wing paseages referred to are most
anxious that the work done by them should be com-
pared with a similar job performed by the boilermakers
on beard H. M. Ship Liverpool, now lying in dock at
this doekyard, and to the most superficial observer the
superiority of the work performed by the former will
be quite evident. And if this be true, if shipwrights
already can beat the boilermakers on what they have
so long considered their own grcund, what.might we
reasonably expect would be the progress of the iron-
plating business in the hands of such men?
And now, Sir, I will give a few figures illustrative
of the comparative cost of iron-plating as performed
by boilermakers and shipwrights. And taking what
appears to me the fairest method of calculation possi-
ble, the results are as follows
By BOILERMAKERS. By SHIPWRIGHTS.

plating taken off and re- plating 1,344 square feet,

nine days to complete, £496 Be. or 7s. 41d. per
reckoning 4s. 6d. as the, square foot.

Leaving a balance of is. 41d- per square foot in
favour of the shipwrights, although the difference in the
thickness of the plates on the two ships, vie:, Princess
Alice inch, Triton I, and some even inch have not
been taken into account. Nor will we say a -word
about the extra work done in the same period by the
same men, such as the drawing out of defective rivets
by the hundred, and putting in new, removing defec-
live butt
pieces and fitting new pieces to stenson, re-
pairing sternpost, refitting pintles and braces, and
shipping !udder. Nor will we lay any stress on the
fact of thousands of feet of ceiling having been removed
by the same men in order to come at the defective
plating and effect the necessary repairs.
There remains still the statement made by F. B. re-
specting the smith who refused (ria F. B. says) to do ihe
work of setting to rights the alleged defects of the
shipwrights' work. If the shipwrights weie allowed to
interfere—on this assertion let ma ask any thinking
man if such a refusal was likely seeing the fate of

imiMiko&koit

the two boperniakers who had just been discharged
for the same offence? No, I now inform the public
that the smith in question gives the-statement of F. B.
'an unqualified denial, whilst theconversatioia said to
have taken place between him and a foreman of ship-
wrights regarding the efficacy of red lead to form a
joint between two plates, according to the smith's own
showing resolves into so simple a matter that it reminds
me of another old saying, which I here repeat for the
consideration of other eaves-dropping boilermakers,
viz., what. you watch for that you will catch.' Bat
is it manly on the part of F. B. to make statements
likely to prove injurious to a deserving fellow work-
man? Should
.not considerations of truth and sober-
ness beweigly the promptings of class selfishness ?
The whole of the statements of F. B. as far as they are
capable of being laid before the public eye, must by
this time appear, but one tissue of misrepresentation
and slander.

A few words on his concluding remarks. His state-
ments but confirms my first impression—he is a member
of the boilermaker's society, and from the prominence
which he has given himself, I should judge a leading
oriel but it would have been better for F.B. and his
advisers if they had acted upon the truth, that dis-
cretion is the better part of valour.' In defending the
fortress of his own domain he should not have unwarily
disclosed its secret weaknesses, nor in throwing missiles
into the camp of the enemy should he furnish those
that in the hands of a dexterous foe may be returned
with tenfold force and power. He should also beware
that in the attempt to dislodge an enemy from a strong '
position he does.not cut off his own retreat. He thinks
it right to unite for mutual protection and advan-
tages,' and upon this principle (?) seeks to maintain a
right hold upon a trade that does not rightfully belong
to a boilermaker, whilst he danounces the attempt on
the part ot the shipbuilder to maintain a right which
unquestionably belongs to him. Let the cobbler stick
to his last, let the boilermaker stick to his boilers, and
make them well too. At any rate, if the boilers for
the future turn out so unsound as the statements of
F. 8., somebody else will have to take them in hand.

F. B. seems to have made a very valuable discovery,
at which I heartily rejoice. He says that, having a
common nature and long endowed. with intellectual
and moral faculties, whose exercise is essential to their
full development, and improvement they (that is the
boilermakers) have a natural and inalienable right to
their exercise.' I rejoice at this discovery, because I
have some hope now that passion will give place to
principle, and that a knowledge of the laws that
regulate trade will enable them to see that no combi-
nation can ever permanently retard the natural pro-
gress of events, nor circumscribe the lawful efforts of
men.

Here, as far as I am concerned, this correspondence
will cease, nor should I have deigned to notice F. B.'s
last effusion did it not contain statements likely to
mislead the public upon a question of great national
importance. A. J.

articles.title: OLD MR. FLEMING TWICE MOBBED
articles.text:
OLD MR. FLEMING TWICE MOBBED

AT GREENOCK.

The Greenock Advertiser says—' On Tuesday after-
noon, about half-past four o'clock, old Mr. lleming
landed at the Steamboat Quay, and being recognised
instantly, was followed up East Quay-lane by a mob of
blackguards, who jostled him and used most offensive
language. A number -followed him to the railway
platform, but the officials prevented the entrance of
others by keeping all out who had no tickets. They
took Mr. Fleming under their protection until the
departure of the 4.40 train in which he left amid the
boutings of the despicable Characters who had managed
to reach the platform. Yesterday, we regret for the
credit of tl.e town to say, the scene was repeated. Mr.
Fleming, on his way to Dunoon, arrived here at ten
o'clock, and proceeded to the Steamboat Quay. He was
again recognised, and obliged to seek refuge in the pas-
sengers' waiting-room, which was soon surrounded by a
large and infuriated mob. The quay policemen sent for
assistance, and the inspector, two sergeants, and a dozen.
constables proceeded to the spot, and kept guard on the.
waiting-room until the arrival of the steamer Alma at
noon. A lane was then formed for his exit, but a rush,
was made, ani the police and Mr. Fleming were jostled=
so much that the latter was got on board with great.
difficulty. It is mid that during the crush the police
were obliged to use their batons, and that after Mr.
Fleming got on board the steamer pieces of coal were
thrown at him. He, however, received no injury, the
only parties hurt being some women and children, who
were severely crushed by the crowd.

FUNERAL or Dn. BERNARD.—The funeral of Dr.
Simon Bernard, the French democrat, who died in Lon-
don on Wednesday last, took place on the 30th ult.
Shortly before two &clock in the afternoon a large
number of person; assembled in. Percy-street, Bedford-
square where Dr. Pernard had resided,. with the inten-
tion of following his remains to the place of interment.
At two o'clock, all being in readiness, the mournful pro-
cession stari ed, some of the immediate friends of the
deceased following the hearse in mourning coaches, while
about a thousand persons, two-thirds of whom were
foreigners, accompanied it on foot, walking four abreast.
The procession proceeded along Oxford-street and
Edgware-road to the Paddington Cemetery at Kilburn,
which had been selected as the last resting-place of the
exile. The coffin having being lowered into the grave,
orations were delivered by MM. Darante, Schroder,
and Pierre, on behalf of the French refugees, and by
Messrs. Bradlaugh and Holyoake on bthalf of the Eng-
lish Soeialist body. The proceedings were brought to
a close by cries of 'Vivo in Republique,. Democratique
et Sociale.'

INTERNATIONALEXHIBITION AND HUNGARIAN WINES
—lnternational exhibitions unquestionably do good not
only to trade but to morals and religion. They bring
men together from all parts of the world, and, by the.
interchange of ideas, the well-being of man is promoted.
The improvements as well as the products of distant
countries bt come through them suddenly known to all
the world. As an instance, we may mention the subject
of Hungarian wines. Until very recently they were
comparatively unknown—and, when better known, they
are sure to command a very extensive sale. Hungary
produces almost as much as France, and, with judgment
and care in the selection, these wines would soon be-
come popular in England—for fresh supplies of deli-
cious,, light, unadulterated, and cheap wines can be
procured from Hungary equal to the best French Clarets
and Souternes. The quality of these wines, including
the famous Tokay, as supplied by Mr. Philip Bonfort,
of 31, Bush-lane, Cannon-street, London, cannot, in
our opinion, be surpassed in this country.
OVERLAND TO BRITISH COLUMIA. The Canadian
(not the Engli-h) party arrived at the mouth of the
Queanelle, in British Columbia, in 134 days from their
departure ft om Toronto. They reached Fort Garry at
the end of May, the train consisting of 146 men, one
woman, and tht ee children, with 100 waggons, 20 horses,
arid 80 oxen. The route was .by Minnesota and the
Red River settlement, and through the Yellow- head, or
Leather Pass of the Rock \fountains, to Cariboo. The
party did not reach their destination without much
sufft ring. Travelling was for the greater part of the
way very disagreeable; in many places they had to
wade up to the waist in Ayr er. Provisions ran short,
and the travellers were put scant allowance. A horse
was killed and eaten in the 1 sof the Rocky Mountains;
a skunk and muskrat, when they were to be had, were
likewise served Twe deaths occurred in the course of
the journey; Mr. A. Robertson' a Canadian, was
drowned at one of the rapids on the Fraser - and Mr. E,
Patterson, a young Englishman, died of malignant sore
throat. A small section of 'he party remained on the
east side of the mountains to explore for gold In the
Saskatchewan River and its tributary streams. Ac-
counts from Cariboo state that the miners were being
literally starved out of the diggings provisions being so
scarce that they were hardly to be Obtained at any price.
CHARGE OF MURDER.-031 Friday the magistrates
sitting at East Dereham; Norfolk, were engaged in in-
ve,tigating the circumstances attending the death of
John Greengrass, a laboure It appeared that on the
night of Monday, the 24th ult., the deceased and two
other men, named Benjamin Newall and Samuel
Edwards, were drinking at the Horseshoe public-house
at Great Dunham. On leaving the house they began to
fight in the road, and the deceased knocked Newall and
Edwards down, taking a stick away from the former,
who exclaimed, 'I have got something for a like
you,' and stretched forward as if with the intention of
st tbing his opponent. There is little doubt that he
did so, for the deceased almost instantly fell, calling out
that he was stabbed. He was then taken to his house,
which was only about 100 yards off, and a medical man
was sent for, but it was found that he was so seriously
injured that it was considered advisable to take his
deposition in the presence of a magistrate with as little
delay as possible. This was done b/ Mr. A. C. Spurgeon,
Neu all and Edwards, who had been apprehended, being
also brought into the presence of the dying man .who
stat( d positively that Newall stabbed him, and that he
saw the knife with which he was assailed. On Thursday
Greengrass, who had never rallied, expired, and on
Friday the 'prisoners Newell and Edwards, who had
been remanded to Swaffham Gaol, were brought before
the magistrates at East Derehana. The beech con-
sidered the evidence conchisive against Newall and com-
mitted him for trial on a charge of wilful murder.
Edwards was discharged.

articles.title: TEE GROWTH OF COTTON IN
articles.text:
TEE GROWTH OF COTTON IN

JAMAICA.

A public meeting, convened by the Chamber of Com-
merce, which was influentially attended, was held last
wi ek at the Ath oamum, Bristol, on the subject of the
growth of cotton in the West India Islands with
reference to the present position of the cotton manufac-
tures in this country, and the means of averting in
future a recurrence of the distress now consequent on
their nmdition. Mr. Herbert Thomw, chairman of
the Chamber of Commerce, presided, and Mr. Stephen
Bourne, secretary to. the Jamaica Cotton Company,
attended to give explanations of the working of that
company. There were upon the table several pieces- of
goods manufactured from cotton grown by the company,
as well as some specimens of raw cotton, and some
coloured paper manufactured from cocoa fibre.
The Chairman having opened the proceedings,
Mr. Stephen Bourne, atter some brief introductory
observations, read letters from• Lord Brougham and
others. The speaker then said: The small bag of cotton
on the table before you is one of 36 we have received.
from Jamaica. It has not been opened, but was grown
from Egyptian seed, sent out from this country since our
meeting at Messrs. Barnard, Thomas, and Co.'s, 1 think
in August last year. We tried in vain to obtain Sea
Island or New Orleans seed, and as the next best, sent
out the Egyptian. In about four months after planting
it began to bear cotton, and of this kind, and indigenous
cotton, we have received about 10 bales of 3001 b. each,
in bags averaging 1121 b. each. We have since been
able to obtain Sea Island seed, and have
,planted, of all
kinds, between 300 and 400 acres. All the expenses of
cultivation will not exceed ..-C7 per acre. We expect
the first year's crop to be at least 3001 b. per acre,
which at 6d. a pound would cover the expenses; at 9d.
'would yield a profit of 50 per cent.; at is., 100 per
cent.; and at its present value, Is. 6d. to 25., 150 to 200
per cent on the cost of cultivation. The proprietors of
the Great Western Cotton Works have been kind
enough to make up for us about 1,500 yards into twill
and stout calico, a piece of which is on the table for in-
spection. A few pieces of this have been dressed and
dyed, and specimens of this also are on the table. Lord
Brougham, Earl Fortescue, the Marquis of Normanby,
Mr. J B. Smith, M.P., Mr. Gurney, M.P., and many
other of our friends have had waistcoats made of the
same, and wear them to show that far better cotton may
be grown in Jamaica, and sold in this country as cheap
as well as good as that heretofore purchased from
slave owners in America. We have also sold some
cotton of a longer staple and finer texture, and one
of our friends, Mr. Charles Ogden, of Manchester, has
had the kindness to send us a little Jamaica doubled
150's for inspection. You will see from it that Jamaica
cotton is capable of being spun to great lengths. We
hope in the spring of the year to have much better
cotton, from better seed and better land. The question
now is, could not enough of this cotton be grown and
imported to supply the cotton manufactories of this city
with the kind of cotton they require and also a large
quantity of Sea Island cotton for the fine spinners of
Lancashire. It is not a question of land, and we do not
think it is much that of labour, for we find an abundance
of labourers ready to work at cotton planting, weeding,
and picking for a very moderate remuneration. To
show what the facts really are we have had the
original pay-lists sent home, and they are open to
your inspection. You will find the number of labourers
constantly increasing, and the pay for four and
five days' labour in each week from 6d. to ls., and
for or overlookers only is. 3d. per day. On our present
limited scale we do not want more capital, for we have
paid for our estates, buildings and machinery,, and have
a handsome balance at the bankers to meet the purclo at
of another estate, and tae monthly expenses of cultiva-
tion. We can make another call of nearly £4,000, and
in four or five months shall be receiving a return for
our past outlay. But why not grow 10,000 acres of
cotton instead of 2,000? Your cotton mills require it..
The labourers look to you for support, whether employed,.
or not. The freed peasantry of the West Indies equally
need suitable and profitable labour for the women and
children as well as the men- Employ all and they will
increase the demand for implements and manufactured,
goods. Bristol was once classed as the second commer-
cial city of the empire. Most of its wealth and com—
merce were derived from the West India trade.. Let
its merchants, manufacturers, and traders help on the
movement of free labour and, free trade in Aunaica and
the other free labour colonies,, and it may yet take its
original standing.
Mr. Bourne said they could not, in the first year cal-
culate on more than 3001bs. per acre, but that would
gradually increase-until an average of 6001b5,.. per acre
was attained.

Mr. A. Vickers said there was upon the tables por-
tion of about 1,500 yards whieh. he had wozked upt
piece of material being printed, The cotton which he
had seen from Jamaica was of. a really good and
viceable quality; it was better than American.cottot
(hear, hear)—it was better than,ordinary,
good American cotton; in fact it was better than
zuerican cotton, save and except the Sea Island. The
Jamaica cotton had.a longer fibre, and was finer and
stronger; and every practical man would know that
they. were indispensable and very valuable attributes.
He wished that he had.plenty of it, for he should be
very,g,lad to use it to the exclusion of American cotton.
(Applause.)
The Rev. J. Hollins could. not but think. that good
would arise to the nation at large from the present
struggle in Americ?,a. The subject they had had under
discussion was ono of immense importance, and he con-
sidered that they were indebted to the Bristol Cotton
Works for having,shown them,. the adaptability of the
cotton grown. in. Jamaica by. working some of it into
cloth.

of extensive importations of cotton from the West Indies,
and thanking the proprietors of the Great Western

ing the Jamaica cotton.

WicK HERRING TROADR.—Our local herring trade is
at a stand, and may be said to be nearly over for the.
season. There are only two or three holders, and they
will not sell at the late quotations of 245. and 19s. The
quantity to ship in the spring will be much the same as
last, viz. :-3,000 to 4,000 barnals.—John 0' Groat

PUNISHMENT AND REFORMATION OF CRIMINALS._
Miss Emily Faithful has just issued from the Victoria
Press, in anticipation of the publication of the Transac-
tions of the National Association for Promoting Social
Science the papers on Punishment and Reformation. of
Criminals, read at the last congress of that body. The

A CYPRESS TREE UONTERTED INTO A DORMITORY.—
Lady Mary W. Montague,, in her interesting travels,
mentions a cypress tree in a garden at Kujek Checkmedji,
that was converted into, this rather singular use. The
house and garden whcih she visited belonged to the
hogia,' or schoolmaster. I asked hitai' she says, to
show me his own, apartment, and was surprised to see him
point to a tall cypress tree in his garden, on the top of
which was a place for a bed for himself, and a little lower
one for his wife and two children, who slept there every
night. I was so much diverted with the fancy,' says her
ladyship, that I resolved to visit his nest nearer. But
going up fifty steps, I found I had still fifty to go up, and
then I must climb from branch to branch with some
hazard of my neck. I thought it therefore the best way
to come down again.'
THE BULLET FOUND AT LAST.—So long a period
has elapsed since the carpenter named Bourn discharged
a pistol at his forehead in the Cause is Altered,'
Dover, that the circumstince was wellnigh forgotten.
At the time•Bourn was removed in a state of insensibi-
lity to the Dover Hospital, where opinion was divided
as to the presence of the bullet in the wound • and in
due course the man recovered sufficiently to be placed
on his trial for attempted self-destruction, and he was
acquitted. Subsequently, while sojourning in Canter-
bury, he casually drew the attention of M 7. W. Wall
(of Dover) to the wound, complaining 'that a pressure
of some weighty substance near the eye incapacitated
him from work. Mr. Wall examined the wound, and
detected the presence of a dark substance, which Bourn
believed to be the mysterious bullet, and begged his
friend to cut it out. Instead of complying with this
request, Mr. Wall suggested the employment of a sur-
geon, in which Bourn acquiesced, and Mr. Holttum
was called in. The issue was the extraction of the
bullet; but it was so embedded and flattened against
the skull as to afford considerable resistance to its
removal, and when cleansed was found to be about the
size and substance of a shilling. We understand the
bullet is to be forwarded to the museum of the Royal
College of Surgeons.
THE ACCIDENT NEAR ALNWICX.—Two MOTS deaths
have occurred at Rock, near Alnwick, through the ex-
plosion of the boiler of a thrashing-machine engine upon
Rock-moor-farm, on Wednesday last, making ten who
have fallen victims to this sad accident. Their names
are David Richardson, 16, and Robert John Pallister,
the son of the steward, a little boy, aged seven, who was
hurled against a hayrick and had one of his legs broken.
Some others of the young people who were injured are
so severely niutilated that bat slight hopes are entertained
of their recovery.

articles.title: ADDRESS BY 711 E ARCIIBISHOP DESIONATE OF CANTERIJURI.'.
articles.text:
ADDRESS BY 711 E ARCIIBISHOP DE-
SIONATE OF CANTERIJURI.'.

The subjoined address to the Dean wad Canons of
York, and to the Archdeacons and clergy of the several
archdeaconries in the diocese of York, has just been
issued by the Archbishop Designate of Canterbury :
My Rev. and Dear Brethren—l accept with cordial
thankfulness the expressions of affectionate and re-
spectful regret with which you have addressed me on
my-approaching departure from among you; and -I
desire to scicnowledge those tokens of your regard in
return for the efforts I have made to advance the cause
of religion in the diocese of York with a deep sense of
gratitude to Him with whom are the preparations of the
•heart in man; who quickens the wills and prompts
the actions of His servants. Your indulgent an-
ticipations of future advantage to the Church
of Christ through my translation to the see of
Canterbury, while they strongly impress me .with the
consciousness of the arduous character of the functions
tam-about to undertake, are such marks of your con-
fidence as will prove second only to the divine blessing
on my labours, my chief support and encouragement
under every coming trial; and I trust that your pro-
mised prayers will never cease to be offered, though I
may be prospered from above in the discharge of those
solemn duties which now await me. Though no
longer your chief pastor, I can foresee ways in which
I may still be able to serve you; mid it will be a lasting
pleasure to me to avail myself of such opportunities, in
grateful memory of a connection of too short duration
indeed, but which leaves upon my mind the abiding
impression of much valued aid and harmonious co-ope-
ration; of prompt and cheerful compliance with
wishes expressed, and of much earnest devotion to the
cause of our adored Master, in furtherance of His great
purposes of mercy to man—recollections which serve to
enhance the regret, I feel at the prospect of the speedy
dissolution of the ties which bound us together. Nor
will the prayers which I have offered for you in times
past be forgotten in days to come, that you may be
ealightened more and more with the true understand-
ing of the Divine Word; that you may illustrate it by
the doctrines you preach, and show forth its fruits in
the lives you lead; that you may so abound in the
grace of our Lord Jesus Christ as to save both your-
selves and those who hear you, and may at length,
through His merits, obtain that crown of righteousness
which He will give to all them that love His appearing
and final advent.—l
C. T. I.:BOB and CANTERBURY ELECT.'

articles.title: PROFESSOR KINGSLEY ON EDUCA-
articles.text:
PROFESSOR KINGSLEY ON EDUCA-

TION.

On Sunday the Rev. Charles Kingsley, Professor of
Modern History in the University of Cambridge,
preached in the parish church of St. Andrew, Holborn,
on behalf of the parochial schools. He selected his text
from the first few verses of the 15th chapter of St. Paul's
First Epistle to the Corinthians, and remarked that the
schools were established in 1696, one of the good old
foundations of those times in which he §ometimes fancied
the real meaning of the Church of England was better
understood, than now, but not nearly so well as it would
be understood in the times of our children and grand-
children. The text, he argued, set, forth clearly and
explicitly the doctrine of the Church of- England as it
was understood and taught in 1696, and as it ought to,
be preached now—a comfort to human hearts for ever.
He pointed out that the catechism which the children of
the Church of England were required to learn did not
darken their minds with such doctrines as the darkness
and the pains of hell, for, like a young plant, the human
mind wanted the sunshine in order that it might grow.
He pleaded, he said, for these schools, which afforded
that genial, loving education which the Church of Eng-
land commanded in the name of Him who never said a
cruel or harsh thing to any human beine, except the
Scribes and Pharisees, who wanted to make the world
as dark as themselves.

On the motion of the Earl of Zeltand, the Grand
Lodge of Freemasons have subscribed £l,OOO towards
the fund for therelief of the distress in Lancashire.
FREEMASONRY AND LANCASHIRE DISTMESS.—Mr.
Haig has addressed the following letter to Lord Zet-
land :—‘ Union Club, London Nov. 27th, 1861 To
the Earl of Zetlanc4 Right Worshipful Grand Master of
Masons.—Right Worshipful,—l beg to enclose for the
benefit of our Masonic brethren in Lancashire who are
poor and distressed Masons a cheque for £5O; but I
wish this to be applied merely to the relief of distressed
Masons, not to the outer world, who are not Masons.
I think that if you were to appeal to the Masons of
England you would obtain many subscriptions to a
Mason Fund, to be distributed by the Masonic body
in,the distressed counties, from those who, like myself,
would otherwise decline to give to an ordinary fund.—l
am, Right Worshipful Grand Master, yours fraternally,
3. It• HAIG, P.M., 23.'

RAILWAY ACCIDENTS IN GERMANY--Railway acci-
dents are rare in Germany compared to some other
countries, and this may probably be attributed, at least
in part, to the very moderate paca of the trains, the
frequent stoppages even of the expresses' and the general
deliberateness of the whole system. On Saturday even-
ing last, however, a mishap occurred, near Potsdam, to
the mail train from Cologee, due in. Berlin at about ten
a.m. Four passenger carriages got off the rails, and two
of them upset, one of them getting broken completely in
two. Fortunately and strangely considering the
nature of the accident—no one was killed, and the in-
juries suffered were generally slight, except in two or
three eases, one of these being that of an unlucky
bridegroom, who had lust started on his -wedding trip,
and whose leg was broken. The telegraph was set to
work, the passengers got into Berlin an hour after mid-
night, and by great exertion the line was. cleared and
open. again on the following day. On the previous night
a singular accident happened on the same line, near the
Bielefeld station. As the mail teein to Cologne was
passing along, a one-horse vehicle dashed down a steep'
side read which leads across the railway, broke through
the gate, which was badly secured, became entangled
with the train, and was dragged along with it for some
distance. Two women who were in the cart or gig,
'broke their necks; the driver had several ribs frac—
tured; and the:horse and cart were, so the accounts say,
literally knocked to pieces.—.Letter from Berlin.
THE FEDERAL ARMY.—When Colonel McMurdo told
his volunteers the other night that there was neither
drill nor discipline in that mass of stupidity and inhu-
manity, the American army, as he is reported to have
done, he committed an error as well as an injustice,, and
it is rarely he does- either. As a mass the American
volunteer army is- the very reverse of stupid, and the
men are not inhuman any more than we are, though
the United States' service is as disgraced by such
wretches as 11PNeil as their government is tainted, with
infamy by retaining them in its employment. As to
drill, there is only too much of it. 'Let Colonel
111`Murdo ask the English officers who have visited Ame-
rican camps what their opinion is on that point, and he
will be astonished to hear such acccunts of brigade and
division field-days as they will give, when he reflects
that the mass of these men are volunteers. With
respect to real discipline there is indeed little enough,
though there is a delusive outward show of it. In cen-
suring the want of principle displayed in the American
battles, Gol. lll'Murdo would do well to remember that
we have only received accounts of them from very igno-
rant men, with the exception, perhaps, of M`Dowell's
report of Bull Run, which is admitted by military critics
to have been well conceived and carried out up to the
point when the fresh troops under Johnston threw them-
selves on the Federal right and rear, and doubled it up.
Colonel M‘Murdo has praised the movements of Stone-
wall Jackson and Stuart, so that we must refer his
remarks to the Federal leaders only; and, in our
opinion, 11I‘Clellan's fault was looking too much to
strategy and too little to action.—Armg and Navy
Gazette.

THE MURDER OF A POLICEMAN IN STIFFOLK.—On
Saturday the body of the policeman Tye, who was so
brutally murdered in the course of last week at Hales-
worth, Suffolk, was interred in the• cemetery. On
Friday the prisoner John Ducker, who, as stated in the
Times of Saturday, has been committed for trial on the
charge of wilfully murdering the deceased, was brought
up for examination before the local magistrates. The
evidence • adduced was substantially the same as that
given before the coroner, and at the close Captain
Hatton, chief constable, asked for a remand. A man
named Stephen Warne and his wife were then brought
up. The man is a chirainey-sweep, and a shirt belong-
ing to the prisoner, which had been recently washed,
was found in his house on Tuesday morning. The
couple had been in custody since Wednesday. No
witnesses were called, but Captain Hatton stated that
he had evidence to bring forward which would show
them to hare been accessories after the fact in the
murder, and he wished, therefore, to have them re-
manded, The Bench assented to the application. On
Thursday evening the prisoner Ducker sent for Mr.
Reward, the surgeon who had been called in, and made
a statement to him as follows I, John Ducker, say
it was old Ben Warne. He asked me 'Had I seen the
policeman?' and he said.' I'll be - if I haven't done
for him." The authorities do not consider this state-
ment worthy of much attention, as there appears to be
no evidence to corroborate it.

THE ROMAN CATHOLICS OF LONDON.-A pastoral
letter, from the pen of Cardinal Wiseman, was read on
the 30th ult. in the
.various places of Roman catholic
worship in the metropolis. Ris eminence entered fully
into the origin and causes of the present distress in the
cotton manufactory districts, dwelt with much feeling
upon its extent, and after speaking in highly compli-
mentary terms of the class who are now so deeply
suffering, he urged his flock to contribue generously to
the fund now being raised l on their behalf, Liberal
collections were made at the conclusion of the services.

articles.title: I MB. DU CITAITIU AM) THE I GORILLA.
articles.text:
I MB. DU CITAITIU AM) THE
I GORILLA.

The following letter appeared in the Times
Snt,—l had hoped that I should never have to
trouble you again in my personal vindication, but my
enemies in this country have not ceased to assail me,
and now a letter has been published from a Mr. 'Win-
wood Reade, s‘ho claims to have spent five months in
the gorilla, and to be in a position to deny my state-
ments. As Mr. Reade concludes by candidly admitting
in my behalf that many of the. calumnies previously
heaped upon me are false, and as he claims to be a
competent witness on the subject of my success in hunt-
ing, &c., I offer a reply to him which I have not
condescended to others.

Mr. Rea e says he spent five months in the gorilla
1 country. What are five months to traverse and explore
' the immense tracts of country I visited, to ascend
rivers, scale mountains, become intimate with numerous
tribes, learn to understand their various dialsth,
occupy many days in palaver with each in succession,
make the stay with each which is necessary to acquire
their confidence, and pass on to others; and how can
any one with such a limited experience only venture to
contradict such experiences as mine?
Moreover, we are not told that Mr. Reacle had ever
been in a tropical climate previously, still less in that
of West Africa; whether or not any of his time was
, consumed by fever' or, if not, by what miracle he es-
caped it; and we have not a single proof that he had
any of the qualifications as a hunter to pass judgment
upon other hunters, still less to warrant him in denying
what I say I actually heard, did, and witnessed.
He does, indeed, say that he hunted the gorilla him-
self, but always unsuccessfully,' and I will tell him
how I can account for his failure. The old African
hunters will not take you to the gorilla's haunts unless
they have confidence in your nerve and skill, and Mr.
Reade did not allow them sufficient time to acquire this
confidence, if his nerve and skill fully entitled him to it.
Ile admits that he heard (from them, I presume) that I
was a good marksman' (which some of my English
assailants would deny), that I was possessed of no
common courage and endurance,' that I had won the
affection of the natives,' &c.; and perhaps such antece-
dents will explain my own success, while Mr. Reade
crawled for hours' after the gorillas in vain.
Mr. Reade does not pretend that he ever saw a gorilla,
yet he disputes my description of the animal and its
habits. On these points I simply compare my oppor-
tunities with his, being willing to wait for the con-
firmation of my representations hereafter. He does
seem to contradict me as regards 111 ongilomba, who he
says is not a native hunter at all,' but, as he is never
described by me as such, and is only mentioned twice in
my book (pages 242 and 307), there is no difference of
statement whatever between us in this respect.
Mongilomba was a boy of about 14 year of age, who
accompanied me only in one portion of one expedition,
and who was instructed by me and employed solely in
the same capacity of steward and natural history
assistant' in which he served Mr. Reade, without,
however, having any gorilla skins intrusted to his
custody by that gentleman. Had he betn present when
I actually shot gorillas, I should not be surprised if he
or any other African in his place fitted his statements to
the fancy of his interlocutor, especially if he never
expected to see me again, and had an ind,finite hope of
rum or tobacco. Mongilomba, however, never accom-
panied me in hunting; when he was in my service he
remained solely in charge of my depot, from which I
was sometimes distant as much as 100 miles, and his
statements, one way or the other, are not of the slightest
consequence.

As to Mr. Iteade's statement that I was at Gaboon
-while I affected to be at Camma, this is the old rtharge,
founded on a hasty passage in my first edition, in which
I was not sufficiently explicit, but which is now cor-
rected.

I have nothing mere to say to Mr. Reade separately,
but, in common with all the assailants of my veracity, I
invite him to consider this. I brought home twenty-
one skeletons and skins of the gorilla, among other
novelties, when there had been no perfect skin of the
beast seen in Europe before. It was suggested that
bought them of the natives, whence more would be
forthcoming; and yet,. with every museum and show-
man ready to purchase, not one gorilla or gorilla skin
fit for • stuffing has reached Europe in the eighteen
months since this controversy arose. How comes it
that I alone obtained perfect specimens, and such a
number of thcra' and that no one has bought, shot, or
seen 3 gorilla in the meantime—not even Mr. Reade or
the famous Indian hunter, his companion, after five
active months in the gorilla country F'
I will prove how I got my specimens, by the simple
expedient of hunting and shooting others as I hunted
and shot these, under certain conditions, which involve
a fair offer. If Dr. Gray and his friends will raise
among them and deposit in a bank £2,000, I will
deposit £l,OOO on my side. I will start fom the gorilla
country, and if I do not kill five or six gorillas in the
course of two years (I allow so long for fevers and
other contingencies), and bring their skins and skeletons
home preserved with a preparation which these gentle.
men shall give me (provided it is ascertained to be
suitable for the purpose), I will forfeit to them my
£l,OOO. On the other hand I shall claim their £2,000
to repay my expenses if I succeed, and I shall be happy
of the company of the bravest of them in making the
venture.

This is all the answer I shall make for the future to
any of my assailants, and I trust that all England will
deem it sufficient.

I have the honour to be, your obedient servant,
Nov. 28. P. B. CIIAILLU.

The Neva was covered with a thin coating of ice on
the sth, and in consequence the bridges of boats were
removed. A steamer which had left for Cronstadt in
the morning was stopped at five miles from the capital
by blocks of ice.
TnE FRENCH GAME LAWS. Th 3 Prefect of the
Aisne has consulted a committee of sportsmen upon
the question whether, in consequence of the scarcity of
game in the department, it would not be desirable to
close the shooting season on New Year's Day. The com-
mittee has reported that such a measure is greatly to
be deprecated, as it would surely lead to the destruc-
tion of what little game is left. They represent that
the poacher's bag is at all times better filled than the
sportsman's, and that at the latter end of the season
when birds get wild nothing conduces so much to their
preservation:as being well shot at. The gun brings down
a very few, but the disturbance of the game in their
haunts thwarts the manceuvres of the poacher, who
does not know where to lay his snares. They also
urge that it is undesirable to check a source of public
alimentation. But here they refute their former argu-
ment by proving too much. The poacher, as they have
already shown, would provide the public with more
game than they could do if their sporting did not spoil
his sport.
LOST IN A. SNOW-STOR3I.—The Aigle, of Toulouse,
states that a shepherd, who was keeping his flock in
the mountains near Martre (Haute Garonne), last week
perceived two horses in harness lying dead under the
snow at the foot of a precipice. He at once informed
the mayor of what he had seen, and that functionary,
accompanied by several gendarmes, lost no time in
proceeding to the spot to search for the owner of the
horses, who was also supposed to have perished. At a
distance of about 300 paces they, found a man and
woman in the snow, quite dead, closely locked tin each
other's arms, and near them was a cart containing a
wool-combing machine and other articles. On the
cart was the name 'Joseph ißouquier, proprietor, at
Miraval-Cabardes.' It appears that the unfortunate
couple, Rouquier and his wife, on returning home from
a fair at Mamezet, had been overtaken by a snow-
storm, and finding it impossible to proceed with their
cart, had detached the horses in the hope of reaching
the next village, but were unable to find their way, and
all perished together.
RUMOURED RETIREMENT OF SIR HUGH ROSE. —lt
is strongly rumoured at the clubs that Sir Hugh Rose
is about to resign his appointment as Commander-m-
Chief of her Majesty's Forces in Bengal, and that Sir
Hope Grant will be his successor.-- Unite I Service
Gazette.

Major-General Lord G. Paget, 0.13., having pro-
ceeded on leave of absence, the command of the cavalry
brigade at Aldershot has devolved upon Major-General
Brook Taylor..

We learn from a paper in Thomas Hoofs 'Saturday
Night' that Mr. Torn Taylor's play of Our American
Cousin' was originally written for Mr. Webster, and
was by him transferred to the late Mr. Josh. Silsbee,
who will be remembered as a second-rate Yankee
comedian, playing for a short time, some years ago, at
the old Adelphi theatre, and afterwards at the Mary-
lebone. The piece was to have been produced at the
latter house; and it is mentioned as a fact that Mr.
Belford, now the Strand mimic of Mr. Sothern, was
then proposed as the original representative of Lord
Dundreary. The play, however, was not brought out
in England, but was carried to New York, where it
first appeared at Laura Neene's Theatre. There,
Sothern, then a mere walking gentleman,' was cast
for this insignificant part, but his genius soon raised
it to that wondrous ideal which has filled the Hay-
market for a year, and added a new word to the Eng-
lish language.
A crock, containing from 1,200 to 1,500 ancient coins,
was discovered last week by two Belgians while work-
ing in the wood of Collinances, near Thury-en-Valois
(Oise.) They consist principally of coins of the eleventh
and twelfth centuries, and include, among others, some
bearing the effigies of Gauthier 1., Bishop of Meaux,
1045-1082; Thibaut 1., struck at Troyes, 1048 • Thibaut
I. or 11., struck at Proving; Burcard, Bishop Of Meaux,
1120-1175; Henry I. or 11., struck at Proving and at,
Troyes; Louis VI. or VII., struck at Sens. The whole '
cre generally in a bad state of preservation.

small, but of foreign large. To.day's market was very

METROPOLITAN CATTLE MARKET.

DECEMBER I .—The total imports of foreign stock into
London last week amounted to 12,453 head. In the-cor-
responding week in 1861 we received 8128; in 1860,
6,661; in 1859. 5,387; in 1858, 5,387; in 1857, 1,721;
and in 1856, 3,518 head.

There was only a moderate supply of foreign stock on
offer in to-day's market, and its general quality was but
middling. The demand ruled very inactive, at about
previous quotations. From our own grazing districts the
receipts of beasts fresh up were rather limited for the time
of year; bat the weight and condition of most breeds
was tolerably good. There was a fair average number
of beasts in the market, both from Ireland and S3otland.
The attendance of buyers was far from numerous, and
the beef trade ruled inactive. However, compared
with Monday last, no quotable change took place in.
prices. The beat Scots and Crosses sold at ss. per albs.
Owing to the falling off in the arrivals from abroad, the
show of sheep was rather limited. The Downs and half-
breeds appeared in good saleable condition; but most other
breeds exhibited a want of quality. Newgate and Leaden-
hall MarKets beinc, heavily supplied, the mutton trade
was by no inn= brisk; nevertheless, a fair clearance was
effected, at previous rates. Thotop figure for mutton was
ss. Bd. per 81bs. Calves were in moderate supply and
slow request, on former terms. The highest quotation
was 4s. 6d. per Sibs. Prime small pigs were firm in price;
but large hco.s were very dull, at late rates. From Lin-

ceived 2,590 Shorthorns, &c.; from other parts of
England, 800 various breeds; from Scotland, 110 Scotts

THE PRINCE AND PRINCESS OF iiESSE.—The follow-
ing communication has been received by Lieutenant-
Colonel Gladdish, commandant of the is t Kent (Graves-
end) Volunteer Artillery :---` Sir,—l have received the
commands of her Royal Highness the Princess Louis of
Hesse to thank the Kent Volunteer Artillery, which
under your command turned out on the 14th ult, to do
honour to her Royal Highness and Prince Louis,on
their highnesses' first visit to Gravesend since their
marriage. Will you be good enough to communicate
the above to the Officers, non commissioned officers, and
privates of the brigade. The duty appeared to me to be
most efficiently performed.-4 have the honour to remain,
your obedient servant, ,
—SYDNEy.
SHIPMENT OF
GUNPOWDERi FOR THE CONFEDERATE
GOVERNMENT.—There s no doubt that a ship left Cardiff
last week having on board a considerable quantity of
gunpowder intended for the Confederate government.
The ship in question was partly loaded with coal, and
received, one day last week, a consignment of 220 to
of gunpowder, which was shipped from alongside. The
Bute Dock authorities, knowing the danger of such a
large quantity of combustible matter being near the
shipping, urged the immediate departure of the vessel.
Application was made to the Customs fir a clearance to
Nassau, but on the contents of the cargo being known it
was refused. In the meantime the ship bad obtained
the dock clearance, and had put out of Penarth Roads.
The ship soon afterwards sailed, and nothing more has
been beard of her, although she was minus the usual
Custom-house papers. The person who was in comman. d
of the vessel was an unqualified captain.— Westeen Datly
Tress.
ROBBERY OF THE MAID IN SWITZERLAND.—BERNE,
Nov. 25.—1 n the night of Sunday and Monday last the
Federal mail carriage which runs between Lugano and
Como was attacked by fifteen brigand.s from Lombardy,
who afterwards returned (at least so it is supposed) to
their own country. The outrage occurred on Swiss
territory, at a spot near Chiana, on the Ticino frontier.
Highway robberies are so rare in Switzerland, that the
mail guards never think of carrying guns. It is at
least 200 years since a mail was robbed in Sivitzerlatd.,
On this occasion the guard made a stout resistance with
his fists, but he was overpowered by numbers and sadly
ill-used. A lady (a countess) who was travelling in
the coupe were robbed of 4,0001. The other travellers,
four or five in number, lost what valuables they had
about them. It is rumoured that the authors of this
crime belong to a new band of brigands let loose upon
Northern Italy by the Bourbons of Rome, who work
under the protection of Napoleon 111.

articles.title: LATER F.ROII AMERICA.
articles.text:
LATER F.ROII AMERICA.

NEW YOEX, Nov. 22.—The Army of the Potomac has
danced to Falmouth, the suburb of Fredericksburg.
Fredericksburg has been summoned to surrender, and
sixteen hours have been allowed for the departure of the
women, children, and other non-combatants. The civic
authorities have applied for an extension of time. Gen.
Lee is in the vicinity at the head of a large Confederate
force. The Federals have made no attempt to cross the
Rappahannock. The Monitor has left the Potomac, it
is supposed for the James River, to co-operate with the
land forces against Richmond. There have been heavy
rains during the whole week. The storm has extended
over the whole North, and as far south as Virginia.
The Potomac is no longer fordable at any place above
Harper's Ferry. There is no truth in the report that
General Sigel had been attacked and defeated by'Stone-
wall Jackson. It is stated in the Republican journals
that the President, in his forthcoming Message to Con-
greS; will reiterate and re-argue his Emancipation
policy, both as reourds slavery in the Border States and
the liberation of °the slaves in all States that may be in
rebellion on the Ist of January.
NEW YORX, Nov. 21, Evening.—The Federals have
occupied the north side of the Rappahannock. The Con-
federates occupy the south side, and are occupying the
positions lately evacuated by the Federals. The Con-
federates are also making movements in the neighbour-
hood of Harper's Ferr7. The New York Herald expresses
•• doubts of success resulting from the change of the base
of operations' and thinks that in efforts to capture Rich-
mond care should be taken to prevent Washington falling
into the hands of the Confederates. The roads in
'Virginia are in bad condition. The Federal fleet lately
in the Gulf of Mexico has returned to the Mississippi.
It is rumoured in New Orleans that a military expedition
will shortly leave that city. A brisk engagement has
• occurred above Brashear City, up the river Teche, iii
Louisiana, between Federal gunboats and Confederate
gunboats, assisted by batteries on shore. Both com-
batants received considerable damage. A Federal land
expedition will proceed to Brashear City from Thibodeaux.
General Butler has visited the British steamer Rinaldo
at New Orleans. The Southein journals state that the
Federals attacked St. Marys, Georgia' but were repulsed.
The Federals, being unable to land, destroyed the town
by gunboats. General M'Clellan's staff officers have
been released from arrest.
The New York Toms says The time will come
when America will enforce reparation from. England for
the Alabama's depredations. The most effective cure
for sectional heartburnings will be a foreign war for a
year or two. England has done all she can to break
down America in her day of agony, and America will
hate England for it till the last American now living
goes to his grave.' General M'Clellan has arrived at
New York.' He was serenaded at the Fifth Avenue
Hotel, and made an unimportant speech to a large con-
.bourse of people, amid much enthusiasm. The steamer
'California, with a cargo•of cotton from Mobile, has been
captured by Federal cruisers. The steamer Kate has
•arrived at Nasstau with a cargo of cotton. The Persia
.and the Teuttmia have arrived out.
NOVEMBER. 22. The Confederates still occupy
Fredericksburg. General Sumner has demanded from
the Mayor of Fredericksburg the surrender of the city,
and insisted that the inhabitants should cease aiding the
Confederates. He declared that if the city was not
surrendered in 'l6 ,hours he would shell it. The
Municipality replied that the inhabitants would cease
assisting the Confederates, but would not surrender the
city. They also complained of the .short time allowed
for the removal of women and children. General Long-
street is encamped outside Fredericksburg, and
a battle is' expected• for possession of the city.
The Confederates are planting batteries.alang the south
side of the Rappahannock to prevent the Federals from
crossing. The Federals are at Falmouth. General
'Stonewall' Jackson's movements are still mysterious.,
An engagement is sexpected near Holly Springs, Mis-
sissippi. Upwards of 100,000 Federal soldiers are on
the sick list. The Southern journals estimate the Con-
federate loss by disease and battles within the last 10
months at 75,000. The trial of Police-Superintendent
Kennedy for the illegal imprisonment of Mrs. Brine-
made is progressing dn. New York.

IRON RA/MAT 'CARRIAGES. The Pennsylvania
Railroad Company are havingriron cars constructed for
We on their road. It is supposed that they will be much
lighter and stronger than wooden cars, last much longer,
and be much more secure from accident.
A great feat in telegraphing was performed on the
13th ult., when a message was sent direct from New
York to San Francisco, a distance of 3,500 miles, at half-
past 4 in the afternoon, andan.answer.was received by
half-past 6 the same evening. It is believed that a
message from San Francisco could be sent direct to Cape
Race, a distance of 5,000 miles, and that Europe could
hear from California in five or six days.
THE RIBCELESTER MuRDER.,--During Monday, after
the five prisoners in custody on the charge of murdering
Ann \Value, of Ribchester, near Blackburn, had been
remanded for examination till this morning (Wednes-
day), one of them, Benjamin Hartley,,desired to see
Mr. Higgs, the superintendent of the county police for
the district, and when waited upon by Mr. Higgs
expressed a wish to confess the full particulars of the
murder' on condition that he be admitted approver,
stating that he had not,intlicted the fatal injuries upon
the deceased. Having received an affirmative answer,
he proceeded to give a very minute statement of the facts
of the murder, showing that they had entered the house
with a view to rob her of her money only, but as she
persistently declined to tell them where it was
secreted, two of them commenced to abuse her,
threatening also to kill her if she did not at once
reveal the Aecret. They told. her they knew she had
a quantity of money in the house, and that they were
determined to have it. Still refusing to inform them,
they carried out their threat, and murdered herby blows
and suffocation. We understand that Hartley described
who committed this outrage but we could not elicit the
information further than that two of the party (M`Phail
and another) had suggested and carried it out. Hartley
also described the search for money and the amount
which they obtained and other minor details, in several
of which he will be corroborated by two or throe wit-
nesses. M`Phail and Carr are returned convicts, and
George Woods and Hartley are said to be poachers.
William Woods, and not Hartley, as reported, is the man
to be indicted for being an _accessory after the facts,
joining the rest in drinking the money away.
THE CREAP COUNTRY.—Complaints are raised in

every part of the Federal. States d the increased cost of
making newspapers,' as they-phrase it. The war has
- caused a great increase in the expenditure upon come-
6Pondence and telegraphic communications, and now
Paper has risen 50 per cent., and continues to rise,
owiLc to the tax upon it and upon all the chemicals used
in its taanufacture, and, it is said, to the Government
contractors using rags for the manufacture of blankets
and cloth for the army. The Baltimore American says
the probability is that the white sheet it uses will soon
cost more than the purchaser pays for the printed news-
paper- Some papers have raised their price, but some
of the New York dailies propose to try an increase in
the charge for advertisements.
CULTIVATION or COTTON Dr NEW SOUTH WALES.—
A company has been established in New South Wales
for the cultivation of cotton in-that colony. The corn-
has solicited from the Local Government the con-
cession of 5,000 acres of waste land for the purposes of
cultivation of the plant. The company asked to have
the possession of the laud en certain conditions which
were clearly and definitely stated. In case, at the ex-
piration of the five years the design should not succeed,
the losses sustained were proposed to be covered by the
sale of the whole or part of the land that had been oe-cu-
pied. If, on the contrary, the scheme succeeded, the
lands, as cultivated, were to return to the State. A bill,
presented to the Legislature on this subject, has been
greatly opposed, but has at length passed, and the com-
pany is about to commence its labours with the hope of
immediate return of profit.—Soeial Science Review.
A SALT WELL—According to American accounts, a
novel salt mine has been discovered at Wellsville, in the
county of Columbiana, Ohio. A-well was being sunk,
on the artesian principle, for extracting rock oil, when,
at a depth of 488 feet, a column of gas made its escape
'with such violence that the boring rods and some 200

months, when it occurred to the proprietors to utilise
the waters for the manufacture of salt. The gas itself
being conducted into a furnace by pipes is lighted, and

and furnishes one barrel of salt per hour. The gas is
