articles.title: BEitiEDY.
articles.text:
BEitiEDY.

SHORT, SHARP, AND IHMEDIATB

1E: a correspondent of the Times, urges one Pro-
posed remedy for garotting:-IThe remedy is obvious.
Furnish for violence an additional penalty that shall be
short, sharp, and above all, immediate. It has not
escaped, nor is it condemned by so experienced an
inquirer as Mr. Adderley, but it has been regarded for
some time in England with so much superstitious a
dislike that I will not name it at once. I will only say
that it is a punishment well-known and well tried, the
very instrument by which it is inflicted subject to strict
regulation; that it is proved by an immense experience
to be productive of no lasting injury, and that it sup-
pressed the very kind of motive most likely to be effec-
tive in the kind of villains who can maltreat their
fellow-creatures for the sake of a few shillings. In our
own times the threat of it arrested at once a particular
sort of crime which every loyal subject viewed with
hatred. Every man of experience must have known mu-
tineers put oown by its agency. Most educated, pro-
bably all Well-educated men, have been liable in wrath
to its infliction; and in grave cases it is applied to our
soldiers and sailors. But what was good enough in
their early days for the most eminent among us, and is
good enough, in case of need, tor our gallant defenders,
is too bad, it seems, for our criminals. A fellow stretches
an unoffending pa,isenger half dead on the pavement,
and must not be flogged for fear it should brutalise him.
Butitis because he is a brute all eady that he didit. How-
ever I shall say no more. All my friends assure me that it
is in vain, for the public mind is not prepared
for corporal punishment. I would merely hope each
successive outrage will be considered part of the
preparation. Our criminals will not be backward to in-
struct us in our weak placeg. In the meantime let us
continue to be garotted and knuckle-dusted; let us see
our friends maimed, and even old and humble women
flung headlong on the road for the sake of the-few pence
that may be in their pockets; and let us console ourselves
with the recollection that at all events we do nothing to
lower the self-esteem of those who perpetrate these
deeds. We only inform them meekly that many years
hence, instead of being then at liberty, they will have
to remain for a while longer in the exercise of a trade
which we shall have taught them, well housed, well fed,
nursed in sickness, enjoying plenty of fresh air, and paid"
for their trouble, for the convicts receive a sort of wages
for their labour. This course may .show a kind of bene-
vOleiace, but certainly not 'humanity in its proper mean-.
ing ; for that word denotes a concern' for the whole of
our race, a sympathy for the innocent as well as for the
wicked, and no disposition .to stifle in our breasts, for
the sake of wrong-doers, our sense of the eternal princi-
ples o.f justice, both human and 'divine.'

TEE PRESENT STATE OF GREECE.

A •correspondent• of the Nord, writing from A'aiens,
gives the following description of the present state of
Greece:—

Already a month has elapsed since the ex-Ring Otho
qaiitted the country, and during that time the Greeks,
, who were suspected by everybody of revolutionary and
anarchical sentiments, have done everything to contra-
dict the opinions entertained of them and to prove that,
.although they have' expelled their King, it was simply
because his reign was 'incompatible with the happi-
ness of the country. The October revolution' accom-
plished without bloodshed, without robbery, and
.
without property being either injured or Threatened,
.shows at once the intelligence of the Greek people,
and their readiness in becoming calm, and in sub-
mitting to the laws. For who can dtny that in
that moment of confusion, when no authority ex-
isted, when everything appeared to be ,demolished,
and the army was 'without officers to 'direct it—
who can deny that the people and soldiers displayed
under such circumstances a full and complete abnegation,
and a respect for law-and the public tranquillity beyond
all praise? And it has not been here only that this has
occurred. t have jest made a tour in the environs of
Athens, and I was struck in every village, with the same
spirit of order. At ,Cephissia the people 'organised a
civic guard of themselves and among themselves. They
formed nine companies of fifteen men each, which mount
guard by turns evelynight. On all sides I hear that
not even the most trifling robbery has been committed
this month, and that .every one sleeps in more security,
than before the revolution.

A friend of mine recently visited the plain of Argos,
Mycena, and Nauplia; he then went to Tripolitza, and
thence to Sparta, returning by Gythion. Several per-
sons had tried to dissaude him from such ,a journey in
so critical a time. , ,Despite of their advice he went,
and he has come back not only safe and sound, but de-
lighted with the welcome he everywhere received, and
with the order and security he met on his way. In all the
• towns, he tells me, a civic guard is established; not the
least disorder is anywhere seen; not the slightest evi-
-dence that a revolution has just occurred. Everybody
:attends to his business in the usual way, anl the change
would be-nowhere apparent but for some few enthusi-
asts desirous of office or of seat in the National As-
sembly. Everywhere, he says, the speedy arrival of a
Xing is desired, a King such as is demanded by the
national wants. Not .a voice is raised in favour of a
republic, or of any other 'regime than a liberal and con-
stitutional monarchy. There can be no doubt the people
were justified in complaining of the incapacity of the
Government that has been overthrown, he says, for in
all his journey he found but one road really worthy
of .the name—that from Nauplia to Tripolitza. Else-
where he saw nothing but mere beaten tracks, adapted
only for mules. How could the country people prosper
without any other outlet for their produce than the
wretched villages to which that produce belonged?
The correspondent of the Nord does not say a word
about the enthusiasm in ,favour of Prince Alfred, but
mentions that the public are much interested in the forth-
coming elections, and that the Government will in .no
way influence the popular will.

articles.title: NEW ROPE FO.ll LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
NEW ROPE FO.ll LANCASHIRE.

There are well-constituted and responsible authorities
for receiving and transmitting moneys to Lancashire,
and the benevolent need not be at any loss as to how to
proceed. For those who have nobly exerted themselves
to collect subscriptions, and enforce the claims of Lanca-
shire upon the people, the principal duty now is to see
that every avenue has been explored, and that none are
passed by in the general appeal. At nearly all the places
of worship in the City there have been collections, and if
the distress continues long there must be collections again.
In like manner, Lancashire must have mention in all
clubs, societies, at everyplace of meeting, whether secular
or religious, so that every class is reached at last, and
none left with the excuse, that not having been asked is
the reason they have not given. If it could be demon-
strated beyond all cavil that the wealth of Lancabire
has been fairly taxed for this cause, the charity of the
.country at large would flow Ns ith more spontaneity.
But while this point remains unsettled the gaunt fea-
tures of famine are seen in all the cotton towns, and we
had better give more than our share than leave one of
these helpless ones to perish. But the whole case is
brightening; the stook of cotton is now augmented to a
respectable amount, and there are heavy cargoes on the
'seas on their way to Liverpool. This should be an ad-
ditional inducement to renewed energy and cheerful
sacrifice, for the point of extreme danger is probably
passed, and a little more help may bring the sufferers
through their trial.—City Press.

THE PRINCE OF WALES IN BERLIN.—In the lonigs-
burger Zeitung, a gentleman who had been staying at
Berlin during the sojourn of Prince of Wales in 1859,
relates the following little anecdote illustrative of the
good sense and liberal opinions of the future King of
England. The Prince happened to call at a bookseller's
shop in Tinter der Linden, where he looked over the
latest publications of German literature, and evinced the
highest satisfico.tion at the many vainable and precious
'works of art with which the premises were adorned.
Then suddenly noticing the narrator of the anecdote,
who chanced to be present, the Prince took off his hat,
and, addressing his companions in English, begged them
to follow his example, as the German gentleman might
be offended by their infringing on the customs of the
country. The Prince subsequently asked for a copy of
Schiller's 'William Tell,' and on its being handed to
him by the assistant, requested his companions to read
the play, saying that it was 'a capital drama, full of
liberal tendencies and manly and ennobling thoughts.'
Here ends the story, the German reader being invited by
the obliging chronicler to compare the good nature and
amiable frankness of the Prince with the very different
qualities but too frequently prominent in the heirs-
apparent to a tenth-rate Crown.

articles.title: MAZZINLIN M_ANIFESTO.
articles.text:
A MAZZINLIN M_ANIFESTO.

The Cittadino d' Asti publishes a long letter addressed
by Mazzini to some of his intimate friends
He declares that the work of organisation is urgent,
and that the means of action must be changed. Aspro-
monte has closed a period—viz., that of legal action,
and has inaugurated the period of extra 'legal action.
The Emancipation Society has abdicated, aid there-
fore better elements must be sought for, and espe-
cially among the boldest Garibaldians. The essential
point is to act in concert with him (Mazzini) who will
organise the second degree' of the Republican associa-
tions. The first degree' is to be constituted by an asso-
tion to be called the Sacred Legion,' and already
commenced at Lugano. Hence one of his adherents,
whom he designates by L—, together with D.--,
' N—, and M should proceed to Naples to orga-
nise the Legion. After the reconvocation of the
Chamber, the Mazzinian deputies should commence a
violent debate on the past, and call for a vote of censure
on Ministers, and then collectively resign their seats.
Their position,' he adds,' is false. One cannot preach
action to the people against the will of the Govern-
ment while crying, "The Constitution and the King!"
Garibaldi has proved that but too unfortunately.' He
then recommends the emission of notes of 5f., 10f., 20f.,
Of., 100 f., 500 f., and 1,000 f., to be signed, if possible,
by Garibaldi; but, at all events, money must be col-
lected. Let shells be manufactured of zinc and gun-
powder, which will not cost more than 2f., each at
most. There must be,' he observes, in conclusion,
union, discipline, and absolute unanimity.'

articles.title: BRUTAL 21URDE1? AT FALMOUTH.
articles.text:
BRUTAL 21URDE1? AT FALMOUTH.

On Monday William Beggerman, a Russian Finn, was
charged before the magistrates at Falmouth with the
wilful murder of William Henry Jones, mate of the
American ship Emma Jane, lying
.in Falmouth docks.
The evidence was voluminous ; the following is an
outline of the facts :—On Wednesday evening last the
deceased was reading in his cabin, the "ship then being
moved close to the dock wharf. He heard a noise at his
back, and turning round saw the prisoner, who was the
ship's carpenter, near the stove. Deceased asked him
what he was doing there, and he replied Putting on
some fire.' The mate told him there was no need to do
that; and prisoner went towards the do,r. In a minute
after the deceased received a, tremendous blow on the
back of his head with a maul,' a massive pointed
iron hammer, which penetrated the skull, inflicting
a Tearful wound, from the effects of which. the poor
fellow, after lingering in a ,comatose state; expired on
Sunday afternoon, his deposition to the foregoing facts
being previously taken during a lucid interval. The
prisoner appears then to have left.the Emma Jane, gone
on board the Russian bark Kurland, and induced two of
the seamen to take him out to an English brig then
lying in the roads, and just about to sail. To these
two men he ,confessed he had 'struck' the mate. 'The
police having learned the occurrence, visited the last--
mentioned vessel the some night, and after a two hour.-3'
search found the prisoner in the coal-bunker, covered
with some ;boards, and with two feet of coal on the top
of him.

The ,prisoner, in his defence, steed that he was
sitting on his, chest cutting some tobacco, when he saw
a man4n the shape of the second mate' go into the
cabin where deceased was, and the first thing he 'heard
was, '4iYou die, you-die!' The mat, then sung out
or his pistol, when the man ran off over the ship's
side, followed by two other men dressed in blue.
Prisoner then dropped his pipe, ran along the pier, and
went on board the Russian barque.
The prisoner was fully •committed to take .I.is trial
for wilful murder.

BIGAMY, DfVORCE, AND 311,..DR1A.GE.--It will be re-
membered that some eighteen months or so ago a young
man of respectable family, and supposed to be a
bachelor, came as curate to aerector in the upper part of
this diocese. After a while ie became engaged,te a
young lady, a sister of a clergyman in the neighbourhood
of Bristol, and whom he met at Brighton. The wedding
day was fixed, and a large party invited ,to the break-
fast, but the ceremony did not take place, owing to the
non-appearance of the bridegroom, who ,wrote to say
that he was detained by his father's illness.; another day
for the ceremony was named, but once more he was not
forthcoming, upon a somewhat similar excuse. Having
been strongly remonstrated with, he appeared upon a
third and last day named and was married. However,
about two months afterwards it was discovered that he
had another wife living, and upon this discovery the de-
faulter fled. The friends of the lady with whom he had
committed bigamy, however, did not proceed against
him, but his first wife commenced a suit of divorce on
the ground of adultery, &c., and obtained it a few
months ago, upon which he renewedhis addresses to the
lady whom he married in the second instance, who of
course could not be considered as a wife, and she
accepting his second offer, they were again this week
united in wedlock, we trust to remain longer together,
and with no such untoward interruption as after their
first (but on the bridegroom's part) fictitious wedding.—
Bristol Times.

A letter from Athens, after describing the enthusiasm
for Prince Alfred, says :—‘ In this state of things it is
desirable that the British Government should come to a,
determination on the subject, and express their deter-
mination in clear language. Any other course would
maintain expectations which, if deceived at the last
moment, might lead to lamentable confusion. As it is,
the sire for an English prince has taken such pro-
portions that it will be difficult to lead it into another
regular channeL While there is hope of an English
prince no faction is possible; take away that possibility,
and behind is Chaos. If illusions cherished 60 ardently
and unanimously are to be dispelled, let it be done soon
that time ma q be given to shape the chaos.'
THE BREADALBANE STICCESSION.—The Dundee Adver-
tiser says :—` A rumour has obtained circulation with
regard to a new claimant to the title and entailed estates
of the late Marquis of Breadalbane which seems
almost too romantic to be true. It is asserted—on what
authority we are not aware— the Marquis, a few hours
before his death, married a woman with whom, before
his engagement and marriage to the late Marchioness '
he had had an affectionate intimacy, and who at that
time had presented him with an illegitimate son. By
his lawful marriage with the pious and amiable Eliza
Baillie, of the Jarviswoode family, he had no children,
and it is generally understood that he regarded with
considerable aversion the succession of Glenfalloch as
heir entail, which seems to be attested by the fact of the
Duke of Buckingham succeeding to the large unentailed
property and appearing at the Marquis's funeral as chief
mourner, Campbell of Glenfalloch not even being pre-
sent. The existence, of such a feeling between the
Marquis and his recognised successor gives in the mean-
time an air of probability any rumour indicating a
desire to change the descent of the Breadalbane property
and lawyers are already discussing what would be the
effect of such a irarriage as is alleged to have occurred
in Switzerland between the Marquis and his supposed
first love.'

THE POLIC.E AND THE GAROTTERS.

We must be careful not to throw too heavy a burden
of responsibility upon the police, in reference to this
matter. The police are not responsible for the mistaken
leniency of prison disciplinarians, who have let loose
upqi. the streets abandoned characters who have yet,
acc3iding to the sentence of the law, some years of
imprisonment to endure. Nor is it possible for the
police to engage suddenly in the capture of men pre-
pared for murder, unless they are assisted by the public
in the performance of their desperate duties. What is
one policeman against a gang of three experienced
ruffians? He is but a splinter in their hands, to be dis-
abled at a blow, and he has but the strength of a man,
though the bystanders too often expect him to perform
the deeds of a giant. In that awful encounter of Mr.
Burt, how many strong men must he have passed, while
striking at the man Leet, from Crutched-friars to St.
Mary-axe at the hour of half-past sev, n in the even-
ing? There must have been abundant means of hclp
on every hand, but the feariof a blow had prevented its
exercise. It is certainly no small matter to be called
suddenly to cope with highway robbers, who have
everything to gain and nothing to lose by a murderous
outrage for robbery in the first instance, and escape
in the second. But it has now come to a sheer
question of self-defence, and there is a moral
obligation upon us all to a mutual share of dangers,
until this new fashion of garotting is completely
crushed, and the streets made once more as safe as
they used to be. In several cases of the capture
of highway ruffians, the police have been left to struggle
single-handed, when the moral countenance of the by-
standers would almost have sufficed to bring the strife to
an end without harm to the preservers of the peace, and
with the capture of the offenders; but if moral support
does not suffice, we are not greatly in doubt as to the.
duty of every citizen to use his strength, and risk some-
what, when he suddenly becomes a spectator of one of
these outrages. The conviction that if help is needed
it will be given, will give the police new courage, and
these candidates for the hulks and the gallows will be
struck with awe, and turn to other and less violent
methods of plunder in the pursuit of their professional
avocations.—aty .Press.

articles.title: 21-ORIfaLVS.
articles.text:
THE 21-ORIfaLVS.

The Mormons have been holding their annual fair
seed conference at Salt Lake city, and the attendance is
said to have been the largest even seen since their first
earganisation. Visitors from the East who happened to
be present declare that the exhibition of agricultural
and mechanical products would hare been creditable to
any of the old States of America. • It is a mistake to
suppose Utah to be a desert it may be true of the small
portion which is of volcanic origin, bordering upon the
great Salt Lake, but the slopes of the extensive valley
beyond are capable of produciug in abundance all the
great staples of that latitude. The collection of fruits
and vegetables at the fair consisted of the finest varieties,
and indicated a most luxurant growth—with the excep-
tion of grapes alone, fully equal to those of California,
which is admitted to be the best fruit-growing region
in the world. Tee cereal specimens were also of
superior quality. The product of wheat and ether
grain in .the present season in Utah has been enormous,
enough to supply the people with breadstuffs for
two years to tome, besides making a liberal allowance
-for immigration. Fine samples of tobacco, flax, and
cotton were also on exhibition, as well as domestic
manufactures of the latter, such as .cloths and counter-
panes, equal to the finest fabrics of the eastern States.
The mechanical arts are the forte of the Mormons, and
-coming, as many of them do, from the great manufac-
turing districts of Europe, they are probably the most
skilful artificers in America. Cotton of excellent fibre
is of easy growth in the valley, a large surplus of
which for export, has been raised in the present year; and,
as theprice of factory cloth is now 60c. per yard in that
remote region, the Saints are about to engage largely in
the cotton manufacturing enterprise on their own ac-
count. To that end they are preparing and setting up ex-
tensive machinery, .and expect by the time the Pacific Rail-
road is built not only to supply with their fabrics all
the new settlements east of the Rocky Mouirtains
but to compete in. the California and Pregon markets.
The fair lasted ten days. Before the adjournment of
conference the ieeople voted that Brigham Young should
have the entire direction of their labour throughout
the territory, for the better development of the re-
sources of the country and a better equalisation of
la 'ar. Up to the present time the great majerity of
th ii inigrantsehave gone into wheat raising and term-
ini, m a general way, and the consequence was a super-
abundance of certain cereals and a ,great absence of
others. In ~,fature Brigham is to say, where
they shall go and raise cotton, where flax, and
where every other thing. In illustration of the
manner in which the community is suppl;ed with
proselytes' the Boston Commercial Bulletin vouches for
the truth of the followeng statement com-
pany of immigrants lately passed through Boston,
on their way to Utah. Among them was noticed
a young man, • more distinguished in his appear-
ance than the remainder of the company, and two
young women, deeply veiled, whose delicate grace
and ieserve indicated them as belonging to a superior
social position. The young man is the son of a rich
landowner in Norway, and the two young ladies
orphans, who were brought up with.thim in his father's
family, until he left for •college, .at Drontheina, where
he remained some years, and, afterwards travelling over
the greater part of Europe, his former playmates were
forgotten. lteturnbag at last to :his home, he was
astonished to find two beautiful women. He was
struck to the heart as svith an arerow. He was in
but with which one. Both were spiendidl§
beautiful. He was enamoured of both. He was in a.
whirlpool of doubt, indecision, and perplexity. In an
.exoess of desperate frankness he related to the two young
girls the state of his feelings. They laughed at him at
first; then they reflected ;and the result of their reflec-
tion was that they both loved Ludwig, and were as
• embarrassed as he. The sequel is soon told. A Mormon
apostle preached.to willing .ears, and the trio departed
for Utah.'

OLUARING OUT THU EXHIBITION.—The work of clear-
ing.out the interior has made very rapid progress during
the last few days. ,On the English half of the building,
both from floor and galleries, nearly everything has
been removed, except, of course, such massive objects
as the ;Skidmore roodscreen or the granite obelisks,
which still keep their places in the nave and tran-
septs. Minton's fountain also remains intact, but,
waterless and silent now, is quite in keeping with the
cold, inanimate aspect of the ..v.hole interior. Most
of the trophy cases are in process of removal, very
many have gone; even the timekeeper of the building
and general rendezvous for meetings and appointments
—Benson's great clock—has at last ceased to strike,
and gone the way of all the other clocks. With the
general removal, however, the fine proportions of the
building, thus seen comparatively clear for the first
time, become more striking every day. On the foreign
side, Portugal, Switzerland, Hamburg, Mecklenburg,
and Bavaria have diatirely departed, and Austria's
splendid show is only represented by a few costly
articles, which have been bought in this country, but
not yet delivered. Her very small stock of unsold goods
was removed from the building a few days after the
closing. France is likely to be the last to leave the
field; she has sent off more than 2,000 packages during the
last fortnight—a very great amount of goods to get away
in such a time —an amount too, which shows her ill
success in this market..

THE UNDERGROUND LINE.—The Washington corres-
pondence of a New York paper states that in the last ten
days of October not leas than ten persons were known to
have arrived in Washington from Richmond, engaged in
smuggling goods into the Southern States. 'The facility
and extent of this contraband trade,' says the cones-
pondent, is really surprising. Those who profess to
know estimate that not less than 500,000 dols. worth of
goods have been smuggled across the Lower Potomac
since the Ist of September, and it is known the business
is still carlied on on a largtr scale than ever. These
adventurous parties gather up all the Federal currency
around Richmond at a slight premium, and with it pur-
chase their goods on this side the lines; in some instances
they buy with Confederate notes both here and in Balti-
more. Thera are now several hundred persons engaged
in running the blockade in this quarter, and, though some
are almost daily caught, many succeed in carrying im-
mense stocks of goods to Richmond. How they manage
it is a secret, but it is well known that the underground
route is somewhere on'the Lower Potomac. The articles
now most needed in Dixie, and commanding the best
prices, are boots, shoes, clothing, tea, coffee, sugar, salt,
and medicines, and every contraband cargo consists of
these exclusively. The trade in medicines has been more
extensive than any, owing to the facility of transporting
them in small bulk. Large quantities of quinine have
lately found a market in Richmond, transported thither
in small quantities on the persons of those passing the
line, every traveller carrying more or less. The article
was once worth its weight in gold, but owing to the
quantity lately smuggled through it has fallen to six
dollars an ounce.'

DEATH OFMR. SIIERIDANKROWL_ES.

James Sheridan Knowles died at Torquay on the Ist
of December. Mr. Knowles was born in Cork in the
year 1784, being the eldest son of Mr. James Knowles,
the author of a Dictionary of the English Language,'
and a man of eminence both for talent and learning.
He received the name of Sheridan in consequence of his
connection. with the family which has been renderel
illustrious by the high and varied talents both ef its
male and female branches. When only twelve years
old his mind began to display its inherent in-
clination for that sort of literature in which he after-
wards became so distinguished, having composed a
play for a company of juvenile performers, of whom
he was the leader. Soon afterwards he compos4
the libretto of an opera founded on the history or
the Chevalier de Grillon. At fourteen he wrote the
ballad of the 'Welsh Harper.' It was about this time that
he became acquainted with William Hazlitt, by whose
advice and free but friendly criticisms he was aided, in
many of his earlier productions. By Hazlitt he was
introduced to Charles Lamb; And his qualities both of
head and heart, were warmly appreciated. Mr. qualities,
made his first appearance as an actor on the boards of
Crow-street Theatre, Dublin, and he afterwards per-
formed in Waterford, Swansea and various other places.
As an actor he never achieved much eminence. He
subsequently assisted his father at the Belfast Academi-
cal Institution. While in that city his first dramatic
efforts were submitted to the ordeal of public favour.
The first of these pieces was Brian Boroihme, rather a
rifacciamento of a piece by another author than an
original play. The next was Cains Gracchus,' first
performed in Belfast on the 13th of February, 1815, and
acted about eight years afterwards in London with great
success. The third of Mr. Knowles's plays was Vir-
ginius. In several of these plays Mr. Knowles himself
appeared; in some of them he sustained the leading cha-
racters. Under the Ministry of the late Sir Robert Peel a
literary pension of £2OO per annum was bestowed upon
him as an acknowledgment by the Crown of his labours
in the cause of literature and virtue. Mr. Know lea has
also written some novels and tales and two works on
subjects of polemical theology, The Rock of Rume' and
The Idol Demolished by its own Priests,' both written
in opposition to the tenets of the Church of Rome. The
.Northern Whig of Belfast says For many years Mr.
Knowles was a martyr to rheumatism, which almost
entirely robbed him of the use of his limbs. His suf-
ferings were severe, but were borne with exemplary
patience; and his last moments, we are happy to learn,
were tranquil and resigned, supporthd by the hopes
which he had often laboured to impart to other minds.
Those who differ most widely from his religious views
will rejoice that they brought him peace and comfort;
and every one who knew him will acknowledge that a
soul more genial or a heart more warm never resided in
an earthly tenement than that which beat in the bosom
of James Sheridan Knowles.'

Do TREES ETEEt. DIE A NATURAL DEATH ?—M. de
Candolle maintained that trees were not individual
plants, but bodies corporate, and, as such, may live for
ever.; and that -each bud on a tree represents, and
in its season ,produces, an individual tree plant, which,
fully equipped with all the appurtenances of a perfect
plant—with stem, roots, leaves, and flowers, and bear-
ing wood for forming buds, or both, lives but a season—
shooting up in spring, and dying in autumn; and that
thus dying, rootand branch, its constituent parts wither
and are cast off, save only the roots and the buds which
remain attached to the parent stock—the roots per-
manently, to add to the store of timber already amassed,
and which is nothing else than a mass of roots; the
buds temporarily, for the evolution of the plants on tee
same stock the following season; and further, that this
formation of buds and evolution of plants going succes-
sively year by year, in endless perpetuity, there
is no natural limit either to the size which any
tree may attain, or to the number of years it may live.
How HE ESCAPED THE DRAUGHT.—The .Reading
(Pennsylvania) Times says.: —lt is well known that
Commissioner Knapp .was very precise and exact in his
proceedings, always keeping an eye to the interest of
the country, while dealing honourably with all. Now,
it happened that among the able-bodied men draughted
from one of the Heidelbergs there was an obese speci-
men of humanity, but whom the chances hit as one of
the elect. When he received his ticket for draught'
he hastened to .13,eading, and, knowing where lived the
, cutest specimen of a lawyer, he went straight to his
office. Said he, I'm draughted.' 'The deuce you
are; it must have been a strong man that draughted
you ! " Well, I'm draughted, and I want to get out.
Can't march. I'll pay well.' 'Very well.' Tne twain
proceeded to the .office of the Commissioner. Here,'
said the lawyer, 4 Commissioner, I have a substitute.'
Commissioner looked at the wheezy specimen for some
time. He won't do; ean't march.' 'But he must
do,' blundered out the lawyer; and you know he will.'
He .can't march—he won't do—and I can't take him.'
This is what our smart friend wanted. He won't do,
eh ? " No, he won't.' 'Well, then, scratch his name
off the list—he is draughted, and wants to be exempted.'
The -Commissioner looked at the lawyer for about a
minute; then regarded the fat draught, and, without
speaking a word, scratched off his name!
THE MURDER OF MR. BULLION.—A letter received
from the British Consulate at Marseilles, dated the 27th
of November, confirms the reported death by violence at
that place, on the 18th of November, of Mr. Allan Bul-
lion, assistant-engineer of Her Majesty's ship Pysche.
Mr. Bullion had been on shore with Mr. Gray, another
engineer from the same vessel. They were returning on
board at about ten o'clock at night, when they were set
upon by a gang of men, and left for dead on the quay.
Mr. Gray was discovered about midnight on the quay by
the police, dangerously wounded in the lower pal t of the
body with a knife. He was conveyed to the hospital,
and is recovering. Mr. Bullion was found about one
a.m., in a state of insensibility, and was conveyed by
thepolice to the Town-hall, and afterwards to the hospital,
where he expired the same evening without having re-
covered consciousness. A post-mortem examination was
held on the body by a French medical man and the surgeon
of the Pysebe, when it was found that death had been
caused by the fracture of the back part of the skull, which
was completely battered in. The unfortunate deceased
was buried on the following evening by the resident
chaplain, the Rev. Mr. Mayers, many of the officers and
men of the Pysche attending the ceremony. The autho-
rities have arrested three men, upon whom the strongest
suspicions rest of being the perpetrators. Mr. Bullion
was Much respected in his profession. He was of in-
offensive manners, and abstemious in his habits.

trains. It appsars that three trains are due at this

luggage from Bridlington, and a luggage train from
Scarborough. On Saturday evening the Bridlington
luggago train was the first to arrive at the station,

turned completely over and remained wheels up wards.
rile traffic on the line was completely stop ed. The

leave their train and enter the one which wouid other-
wise have come to Hull. A number of men were at

strewed on the line that it was not until np q•ly noon on

PARIS Permanent "Traversal Fain-
TO BE OPENED IN 1863.
For many years National Exhibitions have beeen held
in various cities, with universal success iu stimulating
industry' and developing trade between the countries
represented by the Exhibitions.
The central position of Paris, and the vast number of
visitors passing through the city every year, have sug-
gested there the establiihment there of a Permanent
Exhibition: where specimens of the manufactures and
products of every country will be collected together in
one spacious building, in order that dealers and con-
sumers from all parts of the world may see them, and
base their orders upon the quality and cost of the arti-
cles exhiAted.
The project has met with the entire approval of the
Emperor Napoleon 111. and a special license has been
granted by the Ministers of Finance and Commerce for
admission to the Permanent Universal Exhibition,
during the entire period that it is opel, of all Foreign
Products, Free of Duty, ,sith liberty to re-export them
without payment of duties, or to sell them on the spot,
on paying the duties imposed by the new International
Tariff.
The whole of the capital, amounting to £600,000, has
been subscribed in France, and the Palace (now in
course of construction) will be opened early in the sum-
mer of 1863.
The amount of space allotted to France and several
Other continental countries has al:eady been taken up.
Admission will be gratuitous on at least five days of
the week.
The British Exhibitors will be reyresented by a Com-
mittee of twenty members, who, with those appointed by
other countries will form a Gener..l Committee, to
organise the distribution of space, and frame a code of
rules for general observance; and agencies will be esta-
blished in Paris to receive orders.
All products and manufactures will be classified, so
that those of the same nature from different countries,
being placed in jolts-position, may be easily compared.
Two rates of rental (payable annually In advance)
will be charged, the space being taken for six years.
The first rate (.C2 per square metre per annum) will
apply to all products and manufactures,
TIIC second rate (£1 per square metre per annum)
will apply to wall surface for advertisements.
N.B.—Five square metres are equal to six square
yards.
Drawings of the Building can be seen at the principal
Railway Stations and Exchanges in London and the
Country; in the Refreshment-rooms of the present
London Exhibition; and at the Offices of Messrs. J.
STUDDY LEIGH & CG., 27. Leadenhall-street, London.
Agents for Great Britain, lreland, and the Colonies, from
whom forms of agreement and full information may be
obtained.

THE LONDON OPERATIVE
ROPEMAKERS' Appeal to the Metropolitan
Trades, and Trades of the United Kingdom.
BROTHER WORKING MEN: It is with a feeling of
reluctance that we, the London Operative Ropemakers,
venture to draw your attention to our present position,
knowing as we do the great depression of trade in
almost every degartment of manufacture, and yet we
feel encouraged to lay our cases before you. soliciting
your sympathy and aid, by the conviction that we are
well known by the London trades, and to many trades
in the country, for our willingness to assist others in
times of difficulty. We will therefore simply state our
case to you, hoping that you will deem it worthy of
your kind consideration
On the 11th of June last one of our employers offered
a reduction of sevenpence per day, or three and six-
pence per week, from our wages, and we, having a
well organised trade society, could not submit to any
reduction of wages, recognising, as fair workmen should
do that a fair day's work is entitled to a fair day's pay,
and having enjoyed the present rate of wages for the
last seven years, and there being no reasonable plea
given why such reduction should take place.
Haying sent deputations to the employers to reason.
the matter with them and used every effort to pre-
vent a strike, but finding that the employers were
determined if possible to effect a general reduction of
wages throughout the trade, there was no other course
left us but to withdraw the whole of the journeymen
from the firm, viz.—Messrs. J. H. Baker, Bermon.l-
- This is the eighth week of the strike, and our
men are firm and in good spirits, being convinced of the
justness of their claims and ultimate success, for al-
though the firm has resorted to all kinds of misrepre-
sentation to obtain men their shop is stiil empty, for
as fast as the men come up from the country through
their agents and advertisements in the country local
papers, they '(the men) after having the question of
dispute explained to them, leave their work, and by
our assistance leave London again, which creates a
large expense over the actual cost of keeping our own
members on strike. We have expended over £l5O, a
large sum for only ono firm, but then we are fighting
for the whole trade, for. some of the other employers
have already given notice to their men, that as soon
as Messrs. Baker and Brothers get supplied with men
at the reduction that they will give no more for their
work than the Messrs. Baker's, and if we are com-
pelled to submit to this reduction we shall lose
£1,500 per year irr wages (then leaving a large surplus
of men out of work), a sum you will admit worth
sttuggling for.
Having thus briefly stated our rpresent position we
earnestly appeal to the sympathy of our fellow workmen
another trades. soliciting their assistance to enable us to
defend successfully our right of wages and trade against
these grasping employers. In appealing to our fellow
working men, we may say that we have had always a
Willing heart and ready hand to assist other trades
placed in similar eircnmstances ; indeed, since 1853 there
has not been a question affecting the interest of the
working classes, or a dispute in any other trade, but
Whet we have supported and sustained to our utmost
ability. We therefore make this appeal. with some
sregree of confldene, that you will readily respond to us
in our present difficulties, and show to the employing
classes that there is a spirit of union aud brotherhood
amongst the working men of England, that will enable
them to rally round their fellow but oppressed brother
workmen.
We beg to remain yours very respectfully, on behalf of
the trade. Thomas Hay, Charles Howe, William Matthews,
Charles Terdre, Robert Still, committee; Richard Bur
ridge, treasurerr Daniel Smith, secretary.
P. S.—We shall be most happy to send a deputation
to any society to give the information that may be re-

dispute, by applying to
